16153.q: What was the main aim of the German Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain in 1940?
a: To win control of the air for a planned invasion
To sink the British fleet in the Pacific
16153.e: Control of the air over the English Channel and southern England was a precondition for a German landing. The Royal Air Force prevented this.
16153.m: Without control of the air, a German landing in England was not possible.

16154.q: What was the German plan for an invasion of Great Britain called?
16154.e: Hitler ordered preparations on 16 July 1940. In September 1940 the operation was postponed indefinitely.
16154.m: Operation Sea Lion was never carried out.

16155.q: What was the German Luftwaffe's major offensive from “Eagle Day” in August 1940 meant to achieve?
a: To decisively weaken the Royal Air Force
To sink the US fleet in the Atlantic
16155.e: Eagle Day on 13 August 1940 was meant to decisively weaken the Royal Air Force. This did not succeed.
16155.m: Eagle Day in August 1940 opened the major German offensive.

16156.q: Which technology helped the Royal Air Force spot approaching German formations early?
a: The Chain Home radar network on the coast
16156.e: The Chain Home radar stations reported attacks early. This allowed the British fighters to be used where they were needed.
16156.m: Radar gave the Royal Air Force an important advantage.

16157.q: To whom was Churchill referring with the sentence “Never was so much owed by so many to so few”?
a: The pilots of the Royal Air Force
The sailors of the merchant navy
The ministers of his war cabinet
16157.e: In August 1940 Churchill paid tribute to the few fighter pilots who were defending the country. The sentence became one of the best-known quotations of the war.
16157.m: With this sentence, Churchill honoured the pilots of the Royal Air Force.

16158.q: Which day is commemorated in Great Britain as “Battle of Britain Day”?
16158.e: On 15 September 1940 the Royal Air Force fought off large German attacks on London. Shortly afterwards the planned landing in England was postponed.
16158.m: 15 September is seen as the turning point of the Battle of Britain.

16159.q: Which English city was badly destroyed by a German air raid on 14 November 1940?
16159.e: The raid on Coventry destroyed large parts of the city centre and the cathedral. The ruins of the cathedral are today a place of reconciliation.
16159.m: In 1940 Coventry became a symbol of destruction by air raids.

16160.q: Which change of strategy by the Luftwaffe from September 1940 took pressure off the British airfields?
a: The switch to attacks on London and other cities
The withdrawal of all aircraft to Africa
Concentrating on attacks on ships in the Atlantic
16160.e: At the start of September 1940, Hitler ordered attacks on London. This gave the Royal Air Force time to rebuild its bases and fighters.
16160.m: The switch to attacks on cities took pressure off the Royal Air Force.

16161.q: On which date did the German attack on the Soviet Union begin?
16161.e: With Operation Barbarossa, Germany broke the Hitler-Stalin Pact. About three million German soldiers crossed the border.
16161.m: On 22 June 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union.

16162.q: Into how many army groups was the German attack on the Soviet Union in 1941 divided?
a: Three army groups, North, Centre and South
Two army groups, East and West
16162.e: Army Group North aimed at Leningrad, Army Group Centre at Moscow and Army Group South at Ukraine.
16162.m: Three army groups attacked the Soviet Union in 1941.

16163.q: Why do historians call the war against the Soviet Union a “war of annihilation”?
a: Because from the start it was designed for murder, starvation and expulsion of the population
Because only weapons were to be destroyed
Because both sides took no prisoners
Because it lasted only a few days
16163.e: The Nazi leadership planned racially motivated mass murder and the starvation of millions of people. Rules of international law were deliberately ignored.
16163.m: The war against the Soviet Union was planned as a racist war of annihilation.

16164.q: What did the “Commissar Order” of 6 June 1941 command?
a: To murder captured political commissars of the Red Army immediately
To treat Soviet commissars as allies
To give German officers political training
To treat prisoners of war according to the Geneva Convention
16164.e: The order deliberately broke the laws of war. It shows that the Wehrmacht leadership took part in criminal orders.
16164.m: The Commissar Order was an order to murder that broke international law.

16165.q: Roughly how many Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity?
16165.e: Of almost six million Soviet prisoners of war, about three million died, mainly from hunger, cold and disease. Their deaths were deliberately accepted.
16165.m: About half of the Soviet prisoners of war did not survive German captivity.

16166.q: How long did the siege of Leningrad by German troops last?
16166.e: The siege lasted from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944. According to most estimates, about 1.1 million civilians died, most of them of hunger.
16166.m: The siege of Leningrad cost about a million civilians their lives.

16167.q: What was the “Road of Life” during the siege of Leningrad?
a: A supply route across the frozen Lake Ladoga
A secret tunnel under the Neva
16167.e: In winter, an ice road ran across Lake Ladoga into the city. Food came in along it, and civilians were evacuated.
16167.m: The Road of Life across Lake Ladoga supplied the besieged city of Leningrad.

16168.q: Which Soviet operation encircled the 6th Army at Stalingrad in November 1942?
16168.e: Operation Uranus began on 19 November 1942. Within a few days the 6th Army under Friedrich Paulus was surrounded.
16168.m: With Operation Uranus, the Red Army encircled the 6th Army at Stalingrad.

16169.q: Of the roughly 90,000 to 110,000 German prisoners from Stalingrad, about how many returned home after the war?
16169.e: The last parts of the 6th Army surrendered on 2 February 1943. Most of the prisoners died of exhaustion, hunger and disease in captivity.
16169.m: Only a small number of the prisoners from Stalingrad came back.

16170.q: On which date did Japan attack the US base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii?
16170.e: On the morning of 7 December 1941, Japanese carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet. After that, the USA entered the war.
16170.m: The attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the USA into the war.

16171.q: Which Japanese admiral is seen as the author of the plan to attack Pearl Harbor?
16171.e: Yamamoto was commander-in-chief of the Combined Fleet and developed the idea. Vice Admiral Nagumo led the attack force.
16171.m: Admiral Yamamoto planned the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16172.q: Which US measure in summer 1941 greatly sharpened the conflict with Japan?
a: A complete oil embargo against Japan
The declaration of war on Germany
16172.e: Japan depended heavily on imported oil. The embargo threatened its warfare in China and Southeast Asia and contributed to the decision to attack.
16172.m: The American oil embargo of 1941 sharpened the conflict with Japan.

16173.q: Roughly how many Americans died in the attack on Pearl Harbor?
16173.e: In total, 2,403 military personnel and civilians died. Almost half of them died on the battleship USS Arizona.
16173.m: About 2,400 Americans died in the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16174.q: Why was the attack on Pearl Harbor not a complete military success for Japan?
a: The US aircraft carriers were not in the harbour
All the Japanese aircraft were shot down
The battleships had been moved away beforehand
The attack took place at night and missed all its targets
16174.e: The carriers Enterprise and Lexington were at sea, and the Saratoga was on the US west coast. In the Pacific War, aircraft carriers became more important than battleships.
16174.m: The American aircraft carriers escaped the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16175.q: Which battleship, now a memorial, was destroyed at Pearl Harbor by an explosion in its ammunition magazines?
16175.e: A bomb set off the Arizona's ammunition, and more than 1,100 sailors died. The wreck still lies in the harbour today and is a memorial.
16175.m: The USS Arizona is today a memorial to the victims of Pearl Harbor.

a: Germany and Italy declared war on the USA
The USA declared war on the Soviet Union
16176.e: Four days after Pearl Harbor, Germany and Italy declared war on the USA. This finally turned the war into a world war.
16176.m: With Germany's declaration of war on the USA, the war became global.

16177.q: How did President Roosevelt describe 7 December 1941 in his speech to Congress?
a: As “a date which will live in infamy”
16177.e: In his speech on 8 December 1941, Roosevelt called the day a date which will live in infamy. Congress then declared war on Japan.
16177.m: Roosevelt called the day of Pearl Harbor a date which will live in infamy.

16178.q: How many European Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
16178.e: Researchers give figures of 5.6 to 6.3 million murdered Jews. That was about two thirds of the Jews living in Europe at the time.
16178.m: About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.

16179.q: What does the Hebrew word “Shoah”, often used for the Holocaust, mean?
16179.e: In Hebrew, Shoah means the catastrophe or the great disaster. Many prefer this term because “Holocaust” originally referred to a religious burnt offering.
16179.m: Shoah is the Hebrew word for the catastrophe.

16180.q: What was discussed at the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942?
a: The organisation and coordination of the murder of the European Jews
16180.e: Under the leadership of Reinhard Heydrich, senior officials coordinated the carrying out of the so-called “Final Solution of the Jewish Question”. Adolf Eichmann took the minutes.
16180.m: At the Wannsee Conference, the genocide of the Jews was coordinated organisationally.

16181.q: What was the task of the Einsatzgruppen of the Security Police and the SD in the Soviet Union from 1941?
a: They carried out mass shootings, above all of Jews
They built roads for the Wehrmacht
They supplied the civilian population with food
They only guarded prisoners of war
16181.e: Einsatzgruppen A to D followed behind the front and murdered hundreds of thousands of people. They were supported by the Wehrmacht, police and local helpers.
16181.m: The Einsatzgruppen committed mass murder behind the Eastern Front.

16182.q: When did the November pogroms take place, in which synagogues were destroyed and Jews persecuted in Germany?
16182.e: In the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, synagogues were set on fire and Jewish shops destroyed. Hundreds of people were murdered or died as a result.
16182.m: The November pogroms of 1938 were a step towards open violence against Jews.

16183.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 lay down?
a: They took away Jews' civic rights and banned marriages with non-Jews
They set out the punishment of war criminals
16183.e: The Nuremberg Laws made Jews second-class citizens in law. They were the basis for further exclusion and persecution.
16183.m: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 turned discrimination against Jews into law.

16184.q: When did the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising begin?
16184.e: Jewish fighters under Mordechai Anielewicz put up armed resistance against the deportations. The SS crushed the uprising by mid-May 1943.
16184.m: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 was an act of Jewish resistance.

16185.q: Which Swiss diplomat in Budapest saved tens of thousands of Jews from deportation with protective letters?
16185.e: Carl Lutz was vice-consul in Budapest and saved more than 60,000 people with protective letters and safe houses. Yad Vashem honoured him as Righteous Among the Nations.
16185.m: The Swiss Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest.

16186.q: Which measure did Switzerland agree with Germany in autumn 1938?
a: Marking the passports of German Jews with a “J”
Opening the borders to all refugees
16186.e: Switzerland wanted to recognise Jewish refugees at the border and threatened to require visas for all Germans. Both countries then agreed on the J stamp, which made it easier for Swiss officials to turn Jewish refugees away.
16186.m: The J stamp made it easier for Switzerland to turn Jewish refugees away.

16187.q: What do many Roma call the genocide of the Sinti and Roma in the Nazi era?
16187.e: In Romani, Porajmos means roughly “the devouring”. Several hundred thousand Sinti and Roma were murdered.
16187.m: Sinti and Roma were also victims of a Nazi genocide.

16188.q: Which St Gallen police commander let Jewish refugees into Switzerland in 1938 and 1939 against instructions?
16188.e: Paul Grüninger backdated the entry of many refugees to before the border closure and so saved several hundred people. He was dismissed, convicted in 1940 and only cleared by a court in 1995; Yad Vashem honoured him in 1971 as Righteous Among the Nations.
16188.m: Paul Grüninger defied the rules to save Jewish refugees.

16189.q: Which camp was set up in March 1933 as one of the first permanent concentration camps and later served as a model?
16189.e: Dachau concentration camp opened on 22 March 1933. Its organisation served as a model for other camps in the Reich.
16189.m: Dachau concentration camp was a model for the whole camp system.

16190.q: Who was mainly imprisoned in the first concentration camps in 1933?
a: Political opponents such as communists and social democrats
16190.e: The first camps served to eliminate and intimidate political opponents. Later Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals and many other groups were added.
16190.m: The first concentration camps were directed mainly against political opponents.

16191.q: What does the term “extermination through labour” mean in the concentration camp system?
a: The deliberate death of prisoners through forced labour, hunger and disease
16191.e: In concentration camps, many prisoners died of exhaustion, malnutrition and disease. Their deaths during forced labour were deliberately accepted.
16191.m: In the concentration camps, forced labour was used deliberately as a means of extermination.

16192.q: When was Dachau concentration camp liberated by US troops?
16192.e: Soldiers of the US 7th Army liberated Dachau on 29 April 1945. In total more than 200,000 people were imprisoned in the camp, and about 41,500 died.
16192.m: Dachau concentration camp was liberated at the end of April 1945.

16193.q: How did extermination camps such as Treblinka differ from most concentration camps?
a: They served mainly to murder the deported people immediately
Only prisoners of war were held there
They were all in Western Europe
16193.e: In extermination camps, most people were murdered straight after they arrived. Only a few had to work to keep the camp running.
16193.m: Extermination camps were places of immediate mass murder.

16194.q: Which three extermination camps belonged to “Operation Reinhard”?
16194.e: Operation Reinhard began in March 1942 and aimed to murder the Jews in the General Government. Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka were built for this purpose.
16194.m: Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka were the camps of Operation Reinhard.

16195.q: Roughly how many people were murdered in the Auschwitz camp complex?
16195.e: About 1.1 million people were murdered in the Auschwitz camp complex, the great majority of them Jews. Auschwitz became the symbol of the Holocaust.
16195.m: Auschwitz was the largest site of murder in the Holocaust.

16196.q: Which army liberated the Auschwitz camp on 27 January 1945?
16196.e: Soviet troops reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. This day is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
16196.m: 27 January commemorates the liberation of Auschwitz.

16197.q: What happened from December 1941 in the Kulmhof (Chelmno) camp in occupied Poland?
a: The systematic mass murder of Jews with gas vans began there
Only prisoners of war were made to work there
Jews were gathered there to leave for Switzerland
Arms were made there for the Wehrmacht
16197.e: In Kulmhof in the annexed Wartheland, systematic murder with gas vans began in December 1941. It is regarded as the first extermination camp; others followed later.
16197.m: Kulmhof was the first extermination camp.

16198.q: Which lone assassin carried out a bomb attack on Hitler in the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich on 8 November 1939?
16198.e: The carpenter Georg Elser built a time bomb into a pillar on his own. Hitler left the hall about 13 minutes before the explosion and survived.
16198.m: Georg Elser acted alone in 1939 and only narrowly missed Hitler.

16199.q: Where was Georg Elser arrested on the evening of his assassination attempt?
a: In Konstanz, just before the Swiss border
On the French border near Strasbourg
16199.e: Elser wanted to flee to Switzerland and was stopped by customs in Konstanz. He was murdered in Dachau concentration camp in April 1945.
16199.m: Georg Elser was arrested at the border with Switzerland.

16200.q: How did the resistance group “White Rose” in Munich mainly act?
a: It distributed leaflets against the Nazi regime
It carried out bomb attacks on barracks
It spied for the Soviet Union
16200.e: The group around Hans and Sophie Scholl wrote and spread six leaflets. They called for resistance against Hitler and the war.
16200.m: The White Rose resisted with leaflets.

16201.q: When were Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst executed?
16201.e: After the Scholls were arrested on 18 February 1943, the three were sentenced to death by the People's Court. The sentence was carried out on the same day, 22 February 1943.
16201.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in February 1943.

16202.q: Where did Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg set off his bomb on 20 July 1944?
a: At the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia
16202.e: Stauffenberg put the briefcase with explosives down in a briefing hut. The case was moved, and the heavy map table shielded Hitler.
16202.m: The assassination attempt of 20 July 1944 took place at the Wolf's Lair.

16203.q: What was “Operation Valkyrie” in connection with 20 July 1944?
a: A plan for internal unrest that the conspirators wanted to use for a coup
The German plan to attack England
A plan to free prisoners of war
16203.e: Valkyrie was an official plan of the Replacement Army in case of internal unrest. The conspirators adapted it to take power after Hitler's death.
16203.m: The conspirators of 20 July wanted to use Operation Valkyrie for the coup.

16204.q: Which Catholic bishop publicly denounced the murders of sick and disabled people in 1941?
16204.e: The Bishop of Münster made the so-called euthanasia public in his sermons. The centrally organised Aktion T4 was then officially stopped, but the murders continued in other ways.
16204.m: Bishop von Galen made the murders of patients publicly known.

16205.q: How did the protest by non-Jewish wives in Berlin's Rosenstrasse in 1943 end?
a: Their arrested Jewish husbands were released
The women were allowed to leave for Switzerland
16205.e: For days the women gathered in front of the building where their Jewish husbands were being held. The men were released; how far this was due to the protest is disputed among historians.
16205.m: The Rosenstrasse protest is a rare example of public protest in the Nazi state.

16206.q: On which date did the Allies land in Normandy?
16206.e: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, the largest amphibious landing in history began. On the first day, about 170,000 soldiers went ashore.
16206.m: The Normandy landings began on 6 June 1944.

16207.q: Who was commander-in-chief of the Allied forces in Operation Overlord?
16207.e: As Supreme Allied Commander, General Eisenhower led the invasion. Montgomery commanded the land forces in the first phase.
16207.m: Eisenhower was commander-in-chief of the invasion of Normandy.

16208.q: On which landing beaches did the American troops go ashore on D-Day?
16208.e: The Americans landed at Utah and Omaha. The British landed at Gold and Sword, and the Canadians at Juno.
16208.m: The Americans landed on the Utah and Omaha beaches.

16209.q: Because of the deception operation “Fortitude”, where did the German leadership expect the main Allied landing?
16209.e: With an invented army group under Patton, the Allies faked a landing in the Pas-de-Calais. German reserves were kept back there.
16209.m: The Fortitude deception drew the Germans' attention to the Pas-de-Calais.

16210.q: What were the “Mulberry harbours” in the invasion of Normandy?
a: Artificial harbours built off the coast for supplies
16210.e: Because no large port had been captured, the Allies built two artificial harbours. Troops and materiel were landed through them.
16210.m: Artificial Mulberry harbours secured supplies after the landing.

16211.q: Which German field marshal was responsible for strengthening the coastal defences in northern France in 1944?
16211.e: Rommel took over Army Group B at the start of 1944. He had the Atlantic Wall strengthened with obstacles and mines.
16211.m: Erwin Rommel strengthened the Atlantic Wall in 1944.

16212.q: When was Paris liberated after the Normandy landings?
16212.e: After the breakout from Normandy, Allied and French troops reached Paris. The city was liberated on 25 August 1944.

16213.q: What was the second Allied landing in France, on the Mediterranean coast on 15 August 1944, called?
16213.e: In Operation Dragoon, Allied troops landed between Toulon and Cannes. They then pushed quickly north through the Rhône valley.
16213.m: With Operation Dragoon, the Allies also landed in southern France.

16214.q: When did the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht come into force?
16214.e: The surrender was signed in Reims and Berlin-Karlshorst. It came into force on all fronts on 8 May 1945 at 23:01 Central European Time.
16214.m: The war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945.

16215.q: Why is victory celebrated in Russia on 9 May rather than 8 May?
a: Because of the time difference, it came into force on 9 May in Moscow
Because the Soviet Union only surrendered a month later
Because Stalin saw 8 May as an unlucky day
Because the surrender was only signed in Moscow
16215.e: At 23:01 Central European Time it was already after midnight in Moscow. In addition, the surrender was only announced there after the signing in Karlshorst.
16215.m: Because of the time difference, 9 May is Victory Day in Russia.

16216.q: Who signed the first instrument of surrender for the Wehrmacht in Reims in the night before 7 May 1945?
16216.e: Jodl had been authorised by Grand Admiral Dönitz. In Berlin-Karlshorst the surrender was signed again by Wilhelm Keitel and other representatives.
16216.m: Alfred Jodl signed the surrender in Reims.

16217.q: Whom did Hitler name in his political testament as his successor at the head of the state?
16217.e: After Hitler's suicide on 30 April 1945, Grand Admiral Dönitz led a caretaker government based in Flensburg. It was removed in May 1945.
16217.m: After Hitler's death, Karl Dönitz briefly became head of state.

16218.q: Where did American and Soviet troops meet on 25 April 1945, an event known as “Elbe Day”?
16218.e: The first contacts were at Strehla and Torgau. The meeting on the Elbe cut the German Reich in two. It became a symbol of Allied victory.
16218.m: Americans and Soviets met at Torgau on the Elbe.

16219.q: What did the Berlin Declaration of 5 June 1945 lay down?
a: The four victorious powers took over supreme authority in Germany
Germany became a sovereign state again
Berlin became the capital of the UN
16219.e: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France took over governmental authority. Germany was divided into occupation zones.
16219.m: After the war, the four victorious powers took power in Germany.

16220.q: According to estimates, how many people died in total in the Second World War?
16220.e: Estimates give more than 65 million dead, and up to 80 million if all the effects of the war are included. Most of the victims were civilians.
16220.m: The Second World War was the deadliest war in history.

16221.q: What happened in Switzerland on 1 April 1944?
a: American bombers bombed Schaffhausen by mistake
16221.e: US bombers mistook Schaffhausen for a German target. 40 people died in the attack.
16221.m: Even neutral Switzerland was hit by a mistaken bombing raid in 1944.

16222.q: On which date was the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima?
16222.e: On the morning of 6 August 1945 at 8.15 local time, a US bomber dropped the bomb. Nagasaki followed three days later.
16222.m: Hiroshima was destroyed by an atomic bomb on 6 August 1945.

16223.q: What were the atomic bombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki called, and which fissile material did they use?
a: Little Boy with uranium and Fat Man with plutonium
Fat Man with uranium and Little Boy with plutonium
Trinity with hydrogen and Gadget with uranium
Little Boy and Fat Man, both with hydrogen
16223.e: Little Boy was a uranium bomb and fell on Hiroshima. Fat Man was a plutonium bomb and fell on Nagasaki.
16223.m: Little Boy contained uranium, Fat Man contained plutonium.

16224.q: What was the name of the bomber that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima?
16224.e: The B-29 “Enola Gay” was flown by Paul Tibbets. The bomb on Nagasaki was dropped by “Bockscar”.
16224.m: The Enola Gay dropped the bomb on Hiroshima.

16225.q: Why did the second atomic bomb fall on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945?
a: Clouds and smoke blocked the view over the actual main target
Nagasaki was the capital of Japan
The emperor's headquarters were in Nagasaki
The bomb was accidentally released too early
16225.e: The main target was the city of Kokura. Because clouds and smoke prevented an aimed drop, the crew flew to the alternative target, Nagasaki.
16225.m: On 9 August 1945, Nagasaki was only the alternative target.

16226.q: What was the American research programme in which the first atomic bombs were developed called?
16226.e: From 1942, researchers worked on the Manhattan Project under the scientific leadership of Robert Oppenheimer. The first test, Trinity, took place on 16 July 1945.
16226.m: The atomic bomb was developed in the Manhattan Project.

16227.q: According to estimates, how many people had died as a result of both atomic bombings by the end of 1945?
16227.e: About 100,000 people died immediately, and more than 100,000 more by the end of 1945 from injuries and the effects of radiation. Most of the victims were civilians.
16227.m: By the end of 1945, the atomic bombs had killed more than 200,000 people.

16228.q: What are the survivors of the atomic bombings called in Japan?
16228.e: Hibakusha means roughly “explosion-affected people”. Many suffered all their lives from radiation damage and social exclusion.
16228.m: The survivors of the atomic bombs are called hibakusha.

16229.q: When did Japan sign the surrender that ended the Second World War?
a: On 2 September 1945 aboard the USS Missouri
16229.e: Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender on the radio on 15 August 1945. The document was signed in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945.
16229.m: The Second World War ended with Japan's surrender on 2 September 1945.

16230.q: In which treaty did the European powers recognise Switzerland’s permanent neutrality on 20 November 1815?
a: In the Second Peace of Paris
16230.e: On 20 November 1815 in Paris, the signatory powers recognised and guaranteed the permanent neutrality and the inviolability of Swiss territory. The groundwork had been laid at the Congress of Vienna.
16230.m: Switzerland’s permanent neutrality was recognised internationally in 1815.

16231.q: In which set of treaties were the rights and duties of neutral states in war laid down in 1907?
a: In the Charter of the United Nations
16231.e: The law of neutrality was codified in the Hague Conventions in 1907. It also applied to Switzerland in the Second World War.
16231.m: The law of neutrality comes from the Hague Conventions of 1907.

16232.q: What duty does a neutral state have under the law of neutrality?
a: It may provide neither troops nor its territory to parties at war
It must stop all trade with parties at war
It may not keep an army of its own
It must supply all parties at war with the same number of weapons
16232.e: A neutral state may not take part militarily in a war, provide troops or open its territory to parties at war. Private trade, however, remained allowed in principle, which raised tricky questions during the war.
16232.m: A neutral state does not take part militarily in any war.

16233.q: What did Switzerland’s return to “integral neutrality” in 1938 mean?
a: It no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions
It made an alliance with France
16233.e: Since joining the League of Nations in 1920, Switzerland had followed a “differential” neutrality that included taking part in economic sanctions. In 1938 it returned to full, integral neutrality and no longer joined in sanctions.
16233.m: From 1938 Switzerland no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions.

16234.q: What does the term “armed neutrality” mean?
a: Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own army
Switzerland supplies weapons only to neutral states
Switzerland lets foreign armies into the country for protection
Switzerland does without any arms industry
16234.e: Swiss neutrality is self-chosen, permanent and armed. The state intends to defend its independence with its own army if necessary.
16234.m: Switzerland protects its neutrality with its own army.

16235.q: What was Switzerland’s geographical situation from the summer of 1940?
a: It was surrounded by the Axis powers and territories they controlled
It bordered an unoccupied, Allied France
It had free access to the Mediterranean
It was completely surrounded by Allied states
16235.e: After France’s defeat in 1940, Switzerland was enclosed by Germany, Italy and territories they controlled. From the end of 1942 it was completely surrounded.
16235.m: From 1940 Switzerland was surrounded by the Axis powers.

16236.q: Which President of the Confederation gave a radio speech on 25 June 1940 that many saw as adapting to a Nazi-ruled Europe?
16236.e: Shortly after France surrendered, Pilet-Golaz spoke of an “inner rebirth”. Terms such as armed neutrality and independence were missing, which many interpreted as adapting to the new situation.
16236.m: Pilet-Golaz’s speech in June 1940 was criticised as adapting to Nazi Germany.

16237.q: Which meeting held by Federal Councillor Pilet-Golaz in September 1940 caused fierce criticism?
a: Receiving leaders of the Frontist National Movement of Switzerland
16237.e: Pilet-Golaz received representatives of the pro-Nazi National Movement of Switzerland. The movement was banned in November 1940.
16237.m: Pilet-Golaz receiving Frontists in 1940 caused outrage.

16238.q: Which diplomatic task did Switzerland take on for many states in the Second World War?
a: As a protecting power, it represented the interests of states at war with each other
It led the negotiations on Germany’s surrender
It provided peacekeeping troops for the Allies
It chaired the League of Nations Council in Geneva
16238.e: Especially after the USA entered the war, Switzerland took on many protecting power mandates. It represented the interests of states that no longer had direct relations with each other.
16238.m: As a protecting power, Switzerland represented the interests of many states in the war.

16239.q: Which political and cultural movement from the 1930s was meant to strengthen Swiss values against totalitarian ideologies?
16239.e: Spiritual National Defence stressed multilingualism, democracy and freedom as a defence against Nazism and fascism. It shaped culture and politics into the 1960s.
16239.m: Spiritual National Defence strengthened Swiss identity against dictatorships.

16240.q: Which event is considered the most powerful expression of Spiritual National Defence?
a: The National Exhibition of 1939 in Zurich
The World Exhibition of 1937 in Paris
The 1928 Olympic Games in St Moritz
16240.e: The “Landi” of 1939 in Zurich gave a strong sense of national independence shortly before the war began. People therefore speak of the “Landi spirit”.
16240.m: The Landi of 1939 became a symbol of Switzerland’s will to stand firm.

16241.q: What is the name of the form of government in which the Federal Council governed largely without parliament during the war, using extraordinary powers?
16241.e: The Federal Assembly gave the Federal Council extraordinary full powers on 30 August 1939. After the popular initiative “Return to direct democracy” was accepted in 1949, the regime of full powers was completely lifted by the end of 1952.
16241.m: During the war the Federal Council governed with extraordinary full powers.

16242.q: What did General Guisan do on the Rütli on 25 July 1940?
a: He called on the officers to resist and presented the Réduit
He signed a treaty with Germany
He announced his resignation as general
He announced the end of active service
16242.e: At the Rütli Report, Guisan gathered the senior officers at the symbolic place. He made it clear that Switzerland would defend itself, if necessary from the Alpine Réduit.
16242.m: With the Rütli Report in 1940, Guisan strengthened the will to resist.

16243.q: Shortly before which event was Henri Guisan elected general in 1939?
a: Before the German attack on Poland
Before the attack on Pearl Harbor
16243.e: The United Federal Assembly elected Guisan on 30 August 1939, two days before the German attack on Poland.
16243.m: Guisan became general shortly before the war began in 1939.

16244.q: Which body elects the general in Switzerland?
16244.e: The general is elected jointly by the National Council and the Council of States, that is, by the United Federal Assembly. This is also what happened with Henri Guisan in 1939.
16244.m: The general is elected by the United Federal Assembly.

16245.q: What was the result of Henri Guisan’s election as general in 1939?
a: A clear majority of the Federal Assembly
A narrow lead of one vote
Drawing lots because of a tie
No election, appointment by the Federal Council
16245.e: Guisan received 204 of 229 valid votes. The clear result showed broad support in parliament.
16245.m: Guisan was elected general with a clear majority.

16246.q: What is special about the rank of “general” in the Swiss Army?
a: A general is only elected in times of serious threat or war
The general is elected directly by the people
The general is also President of the Confederation
16246.e: In peacetime the Swiss Army has no general. Only when a large number of troops are called up to protect the country does the Federal Assembly elect a commander-in-chief.
16246.m: Switzerland only has a general in times of serious threat.

16247.q: Which canton did Henri Guisan come from?
16247.e: Guisan was born in Mézières in the canton of Vaud in 1874. He later lived on the Verte Rive estate in Pully.

16248.q: What job did Guisan do before his military career?
16248.e: Guisan worked as a farmer, among other places in Chesalles-sur-Oron, and took over an estate in Pully in 1902. As was usual in the militia army, he pursued a military career alongside.
16248.m: Guisan was a farmer and a militia officer.

16249.q: After which event did Guisan hold the Rütli Report in July 1940?
a: After the end of the war
After the Allied landings in Normandy
After the German attack on the Soviet Union
16249.e: After the fall of France, Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. On 25 July 1940 Guisan wanted to strengthen the army’s will to resist.
16249.m: The Rütli Report followed the fall of France in 1940.

16250.q: What did Guisan announce at the Rütli Report?
a: The will to resist and the new Réduit strategy
16250.e: Guisan called for resistance and announced defence in the Alpine region, the Réduit. The report was seen as a counterpart to Pilet-Golaz’s speech, which was felt to be timid.
16250.m: On the Rütli in 1940, Guisan called for resistance.

16251.q: Why did Guisan choose the Rütli meadow for his report in 1940?
a: It is the symbolic place of the founding tradition of the Confederation
It was at the centre of the Gotthard fortress
He had started his military service there himself
16251.e: According to tradition, which is partly legend, the first Confederates swore their alliance on the Rütli. The place was meant to express unity and the will to be free.
16251.m: Guisan used the Rütli as a symbol of freedom and unity.

16252.q: When did Henri Guisan’s time as general end?
a: After the end of the war in summer 1945
In 1943 after the landings in Italy
16252.e: Active service ended on 20 August 1945. With that, Guisan stepped down as general.
16252.m: Guisan’s time as general ended in August 1945.

16253.q: How does Switzerland still remember General Henri Guisan today?
a: With monuments and streets and squares named after him
With a national holiday of its own
With his picture on all coins
With a permanent seat for his family on the Federal Council
16253.e: Guisan died in 1960, and his funeral was a great national event. Many places have an Avenue Général-Guisan or a General-Guisan-Quai.
16253.m: Many streets and monuments recall General Guisan.

16254.q: How does more recent historical research judge Guisan’s role?
a: It questions the myth that he alone saved Switzerland from occupation
It considers him a supporter of Nazism
It denies that he was ever general
It sees him as the founder of neutrality
16254.e: People who lived through the time often saw Guisan as the saviour of the country. More recent historians also stress other factors such as economic relations and put the myth around him into perspective.
16254.m: Research today sees Guisan’s role in a more nuanced way than before.

16255.q: Which troops did the Federal Council call up at the end of August 1939, even before general mobilisation?
16255.e: On 28 August 1939 the Federal Council ordered the mobilisation of the border guard with about 80,000 men; the border troops reported on 29 August. General mobilisation only followed after the German attack on Poland.
16255.m: The border troops were the first to be called up at the end of August 1939.

16256.q: When did the general war mobilisation of the Swiss Army begin?
16256.e: After the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939, the whole army was called up. The first day of mobilisation was 2 September 1939, and a second general mobilisation followed on 10 May 1940.

16257.q: Roughly how many soldiers were called up in the general mobilisation of 1939?
16257.e: In the general mobilisation about 430,000 combat troops reported for duty. Over the whole war, about 450,000 soldiers were called up.
16257.m: About 430,000 soldiers reported for duty in the general mobilisation of 1939.

16258.q: Which group also supported the regular troops in large numbers in 1939?
a: about 200,000 men in the auxiliary service
16258.e: In the general mobilisation, about 200,000 men liable for auxiliary service reported alongside the combat troops; over the whole war about 250,000 were called up. They took on guard, transport and medical duties, for example.
16258.m: Men in the auxiliary service supported the army during active service.

16259.q: What was the organisation founded in 1939 in which at times over 20,000 women served the army voluntarily?
16259.e: In the Women’s Auxiliary Service, women worked in administration, communications, transport, kitchens or aircraft spotting, for example. At the end of 1941 about 23,000 women were serving, which freed men for duty with the troops.
16259.m: In the Women’s Auxiliary Service, women served the army voluntarily.

16260.q: On average, how many days of active service did Swiss soldiers do in the Second World War?
16260.e: On average the soldiers did about 800 days of service. This is why people speak of the “active service generation”.
16260.m: The active service generation did about 800 days of service on average.

16261.q: Which social scheme replaced soldiers’ lost wages from 1940 and is seen as paving the way for the AHV?
a: The Wage and Earnings Compensation Scheme
16261.e: Unlike in the First World War, soldiers received compensation financed by wage contributions from employers and employees as well as public money. This model influenced the financing of the AHV in 1948.
16261.m: The wage compensation scheme supported soldiers’ families and was a model for the AHV.

16262.q: How were troop numbers mostly organised from autumn 1940?
a: Through about 80 partial mobilisations with troops taking turns
Through permanent full mobilisation of all troops
Through a professional army of 20,000 men
16262.e: After the move into the Réduit, the number of troops called up fell sharply. Throughout active service there were about 80 partial mobilisations, so that industry and agriculture kept enough workers.
16262.m: From 1940 troops took turns in partial mobilisations.

16263.q: How did the air battles between the Swiss Air Force and the German Luftwaffe go in May and June 1940?
a: 11 German aircraft were shot down, 3 Swiss were lost
Switzerland lost all its fighter aircraft
16263.e: During violations of Swiss airspace, the Air Force shot down 11 German aircraft and lost 3 of its own. Germany responded with a sharp protest.
16263.m: The air battles of 1940 led to a crisis with Germany.

16264.q: What did General Guisan order the Air Force to do on 20 June 1940 under German pressure?
a: He banned it from air combat over Switzerland
He ordered attacks on German airfields
He placed it under the French army
16264.e: After sharp German protests about the air battles, Guisan banned the Air Force from air combat over Switzerland. After that, mainly the anti-aircraft defence protected the airspace; the ban lasted until the end of 1943.
16264.m: From June 1940, under German pressure, the Air Force was no longer allowed to fight in the air.

16265.q: How many Swiss soldiers died during active service from 1939 to 1945?
16265.e: About 4,050 soldiers died during active service, mainly through accidents and illness. Switzerland was not drawn into fighting on the ground.
16265.m: Even without war in the country, about 4,000 soldiers died during active service.

16266.q: How many Swiss sentenced to death for treason were executed in the Second World War?
16266.e: In 1940 the death penalty in military criminal law was extended to espionage and treason. Of 33 death sentences, 17 were carried out.
16266.m: In the Second World War, 17 traitors were executed in Switzerland.

16267.q: Which three fortress areas formed the cornerstones of the Réduit?
16267.e: Sargans in the east, St-Maurice in the west and the Gotthard in the centre were the most important fortresses. The Gotthard was considered the heart.
16267.m: Sargans, St-Maurice and Gotthard were the cornerstones of the Réduit.

16268.q: Where did General Guisan explain the Réduit strategy to senior officers on 25 July 1940?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
16268.e: At the Rütli Report, Guisan gathered the commanders at the symbolic place of the Confederation. He called for resistance and explained the withdrawal into the Réduit.
16268.m: At the Rütli Report in 1940, Guisan explained the Réduit strategy.

16269.q: Which general led the Swiss Army when it moved into the Réduit in 1940?
16269.e: Henri Guisan was general of the Swiss Army from 1939 to 1945. In 1940 he pushed through the Réduit strategy.
16269.m: General Henri Guisan led the army into the Réduit.

16270.q: Roughly what part of Swiss territory lay within the Réduit?
16270.e: The Réduit covered about a quarter of the country, mainly mountain areas. The densely populated regions lay outside it.
16270.m: The Réduit covered about a quarter of Switzerland.

16271.q: Which criticism of the Réduit is made most often?
a: The Central Plateau, with most of the population, would largely have been given up
It was too close to the German border
It was far too small for the army
It was never manned with troops
16271.e: In an attack, the army would hardly have defended the cities and economic centres of the Central Plateau. The civilian population would largely have been left unprotected.
16271.m: Under the Réduit plan, the Central Plateau would hardly have been defended.

16272.q: What idea was the effect of the Réduit mainly based on?
a: Deterrence through a long and costly mountain war
The superiority of the Swiss Air Force
16272.e: The Réduit was meant to make an attack so costly that it would not be worth it. Such a strategy is called dissuasion.
16272.m: The Réduit was meant to deter an attacker.

16273.q: Which means of pressure on the Axis powers was linked to the Réduit?
a: The prepared destruction of the Alpine crossings such as Gotthard and Simplon
The threat of an alliance with the Soviet Union
16273.e: In case of an attack, tunnels, bridges and railway lines were to be blown up. Germany and Italy would then have lost the important north-south link through the Alps.
16273.m: The Alpine transit routes were an important means of pressure for Switzerland.

16274.q: What was the name of the German plan for an attack on Switzerland from summer 1940?
16274.e: After the victory over France, the German general staff drew up attack plans, called “Tannenbaum” (fir tree) from September 1940. Italian troops were to attack from the south.
16274.m: With Operation Tannenbaum, Germany planned an attack on Switzerland in 1940.

16275.q: Which reasons helped ensure that Operation Tannenbaum was not carried out?
a: Other war aims and German interest in Swiss industry and Alpine transit
A peace treaty between Germany and Switzerland
16275.e: The Wehrmacht concentrated on other aims such as the planned invasion of Great Britain. In addition, Swiss deliveries and the Gotthard transit were useful to Germany.
16275.m: Economic interests helped ensure that Switzerland was not attacked.

16276.q: Which British military commander called the Réduit impractical nonsense?
16276.e: Montgomery thought the strategy made no military sense, because it gave up the Central Plateau. Opinions on the Réduit are still divided today.

16277.q: Until when were the course and boundaries of the Réduit kept secret?
a: Until the end of the war in 1945
16277.e: The installations remained important during the Cold War and were kept secret. Especially since the army reform of 1995 many have been dismantled, and some are museums today.
16277.m: The Réduit remained secret into the 1990s.

16278.q: What did the federal government want to prevent with a purchase ban on sugar, fats and grain shortly before the war began in 1939?
16278.e: With the purchase ban of 29 August 1939, important foods could temporarily no longer be sold. This was meant to prevent panic buying, and regular rationing followed shortly afterwards.
16278.m: A purchase ban prevented panic buying in 1939.

16279.q: From when were basic foods such as sugar, pulses and fats officially rationed?
16279.e: Rationing with ration cards began at the end of October 1939. Without ration coupons you could no longer buy these goods.

16280.q: Why was Switzerland better prepared for supplies in the Second World War than in the First?
a: The war economy system was ready to operate as early as 1938
It had enough oil wells of its own
It got all its food free from the USA
16280.e: In the First World War rationing only began hesitantly in 1917, and in 1918 there was hardship. Learning from this, the federal government prepared the war economy early.
16280.m: Learning from the mistakes of the First World War, Switzerland prepared early.

16281.q: How many meat-free days per week applied from May 1941?
16281.e: From May 1941 there were two meat-free days per week. From March 1942 meat was also rationed.
16281.m: From 1941 there were two meat-free days per week.

16282.q: From when was bread rationed in Switzerland?
16282.e: From July 1940 bread could no longer be sold fresh, so that people would eat less. From October 1942 it was rationed.
16282.m: Bread was rationed in Switzerland from 1942.

16283.q: What did you need in Switzerland in the Second World War, as well as money, to buy sugar or fat?
a: A voucher from the municipality for every purchase
16283.e: Every person received monthly ration cards with coupons. Without the right coupons you could not buy rationed goods, even if you had enough money.
16283.m: Rationed goods were only available for coupons and money.

16284.q: What daily calorie requirement for an adult did wartime nutrition plans assume?
16284.e: The planners assumed 2,160 calories per day. From 1943 this figure was reached only in a few months; things were tightest in the post-war period.
16284.m: Rationing assumed about 2,160 calories per day.

16285.q: When were the last foods released from rationing?
16285.e: Rationing was gradually lifted from spring 1945. The last foods only became freely available again in July 1948.

16286.q: By which name is the wartime programme to expand arable farming known?
16286.e: The agronomist Friedrich Traugott Wahlen drew up the plan to increase self-sufficiency. He later became a Federal Councillor.
16286.m: With the Wahlen Plan, Switzerland grew more of its own food during the war.

16287.q: Where in Zurich were potatoes planted in the middle of the city during the Cultivation Battle?
a: In the courtyard of the National Museum
16287.e: For the Wahlen Plan, parks, sports grounds and squares in the cities were also planted. The picture of potatoes on the Sechseläutenplatz became a symbol of the Cultivation Battle.
16287.m: During the Cultivation Battle, potatoes even grew on the Sechseläutenplatz.

16288.q: How did Switzerland’s open arable land change from 1940 to 1945?
16288.e: The arable land almost doubled. Parks and sports grounds were also planted, but the planned target of 500,000 hectares was not reached.
16288.m: The Cultivation Battle almost doubled the arable land.

16289.q: Roughly how did the degree of self-sufficiency in food change because of the Cultivation Battle?
a: From about 52 to about 70 per cent
From about 10 to about 100 per cent
From about 90 to about 50 per cent
From about 30 to about 40 per cent
16289.e: Self-sufficiency rose from about 52 per cent in 1939/1940 to about 70 per cent in 1945. Figures vary depending on the estimate, but Switzerland remained dependent on imports.
16289.m: The Cultivation Battle clearly increased self-sufficiency, but not completely.

16290.q: What was the so-called J stamp?
a: A mark in the passports of German Jews that made them identifiable at the border
A stamp on Swiss ration cards
A visa for Jewish refugees to the USA
16290.e: From October 1938 the passports of German Jews were marked with a “J”. This was based on an agreement between Germany and Switzerland.
16290.m: The J stamp made Jewish travellers immediately identifiable at the border.

16291.q: Which independent commission of experts examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War in the 1990s?
16291.e: The Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland Second World War, led by the historian Jean-François Bergier, examined refugee policy among other things from 1996. Its final report appeared in 2002.
16291.m: The Bergier Commission examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War.

16292.q: According to more recent research, why did the German authorities propose the J stamp in 1938?
a: To avoid a general visa requirement for Germans in Switzerland
To make it easier for Jews to emigrate
16292.e: Switzerland threatened a visa requirement for all Germans. Germany wanted to avoid this and offered to mark Jewish passports, which the Federal Council approved on 4 October 1938.
16292.m: Switzerland agreed to the J stamp so as not to have to introduce a general visa requirement.

16293.q: What position did Heinrich Rothmund hold during the Second World War?
a: Head of the Police Division in the Department of Justice and Police
Chief of the General Staff of the army
16293.e: Rothmund led the Police Division, including the aliens police, and shaped the restrictive refugee policy. Historians criticise his attitude as antisemitic.
16293.m: As head of police, Heinrich Rothmund shaped refugee policy.

16294.q: What did the directive of 13 August 1942 order?
a: Closing the border to refugees who fled only “for reasons of race”
Opening the border to children from France
16294.e: Refugees “only for reasons of race”, meaning mainly Jews, were not considered political refugees and were to be turned away. This happened when deportations to the extermination camps were already under way.
16294.m: With the border closure of 1942, Jewish refugees were turned away.

16295.q: How did the Federal Council react shortly after the border closure of August 1942?
a: After public protests it temporarily eased the turning back of refugees
It closed the border to diplomats too
16295.e: The directive caused fierce protests among the population, churches and press. On 23 August 1942 the turning back of refugees was temporarily eased.
16295.m: Public protests led to an easing of the border closure in 1942.

16296.q: Which slogan is often used to sum up Switzerland’s harsh refugee policy in the Second World War?
16296.e: In 1942 Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a small lifeboat that could not take everyone. This became the well-known slogan “The boat is full”.
16296.m: “The boat is full” stands for the refugee policy of turning people away during the war.

16297.q: Roughly how many people did Switzerland host in total during the war, including military internees?
16297.e: They included over 100,000 interned soldiers, refugees at the border, children on recovery stays and civilian refugees. Their stay was often limited in time.
16297.m: During the war Switzerland at times hosted about 300,000 people seeking protection.

16298.q: Roughly how many civilian refugees did Switzerland take in during the Second World War?
16298.e: About 51,000 civilian refugees were taken in, about 21,000 of them Jews. At the same time, many were turned away at the border.
16298.m: About 51,000 civilian refugees found refuge in Switzerland.

16299.q: Why do the estimates of the number of refugees turned away vary so widely?
a: Because of incomplete records and different ways of counting
Because Switzerland had no border controls
Because all records are published and clear
Because only refugees from Italy were counted
16299.e: Depending on the study, the estimates differ many times over. Repeated attempts by the same person, destroyed records and different definitions make an exact number difficult.
16299.m: With refugee numbers, you must check sources and ways of counting critically.

16300.q: How did the St Gallen police captain Paul Grüninger help refugees in 1938 and 1939?
a: He backdated entries so that refugees could stay legally
He hid refugees in the Réduit
He issued letters of protection in Budapest
16300.e: Grüninger enabled several hundred refugees to enter by backdating entry dates or falsifying documents. He was dismissed in 1939 and fined in 1940.
16300.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees by getting round the rules.

16301.q: When was Paul Grüninger acquitted by a court?
a: In 1945, shortly after the end of the war
In 1971, while he was still alive
16301.e: The St Gallen district court overturned the verdict in 1995. Yad Vashem had already honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations” in 1971.
16301.m: Paul Grüninger was only fully rehabilitated in 1995.

16302.q: Roughly how many Hungarian Jews did the Swiss vice-consul Carl Lutz save in Budapest in 1944?
16302.e: Lutz issued letters of protection that saved people from deportation. In 1964 Yad Vashem honoured him as “Righteous Among the Nations”.
16302.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest with letters of protection.

16303.q: Which agreement did Switzerland conclude with Germany on 9 August 1940?
16303.e: The economic agreement secured supplies of coal and raw materials. In return Switzerland supplied industrial goods, including armaments, to the Axis powers.
16303.m: From 1940 an economic agreement tied Switzerland closely to Germany.

16304.q: What is meant by clearing in trade between Switzerland and Germany?
a: Settling payments through state offices without direct payment in foreign currency
16304.e: In clearing, exports and imports were offset against each other through state accounts. Swiss clearing credits allowed Germany to obtain goods before it paid.
16304.m: In clearing, payments between states were offset against each other.

16305.q: What did Switzerland get in return for the clearing credit to Germany of February 1941?
16305.e: Switzerland granted a credit of 165 million francs. In return it was promised 150,000 tonnes of coal per month.
16305.m: Coal from Germany was vital for the Swiss economy.

16306.q: According to the Bergier Commission, how much gold did the Swiss National Bank buy from the Reichsbank between 1940 and 1945?
16306.e: The National Bank bought gold worth about 1.23 billion francs, and commercial banks about 100 million. Part of it was looted gold.
16306.m: During the war the National Bank bought over a billion francs’ worth of gold from the Reichsbank.

16307.q: Why was the Swiss franc important to Germany during the war?
a: It was freely convertible and was used to buy raw materials such as tungsten and oil
It was the official currency throughout Europe
It was tied to the Reichsmark
16307.e: With francs, Germany could buy raw materials in neutral countries such as Portugal or Spain. Gold was therefore exchanged for francs in Switzerland.
16307.m: Germany needed freely convertible francs to buy raw materials.

16308.q: Which goods were among the most important Swiss exports in the Second World War?
a: Machine tools, watches and precision parts
16308.e: Precision goods such as machine tools, watches and jewel bearings were in demand, also for fuses and aiming devices. Electricity and dairy products were added to this.
16308.m: Swiss precision goods were in great demand during the war.

16309.q: When did Switzerland stop exporting war material?
16309.e: Under Allied pressure, the Federal Council banned the export of war material in autumn 1944. Before that, Switzerland had supplied mainly the Axis powers.
16309.m: Switzerland only stopped exporting war material in 1944.

16310.q: What was the largest share of German armaments production that Swiss arms deliveries ever reached?
16310.e: The deliveries never reached more than about one per cent of German production. For some individual goods, however, they could still be significant.
16310.m: Compared with German production, Swiss arms deliveries were small.

16311.q: Which transport link through Switzerland was particularly important for Germany and Italy?
a: The Gotthard Railway as a north-south transit route
16311.e: Goods traffic between the Axis partners ran over the Alpine railways, especially coal to Italy. War material and troops could not be transported for reasons of neutrality.
16311.m: The Gotthard transit was of great importance to the Axis powers.

16312.q: How did the Allies punish Swiss companies that traded with Germany?
a: By excluding them from the ICRC
By having the Federal Council seize them
16312.e: Companies on blacklists were boycotted by the Allies. The lists were only lifted with the Washington Agreement of 1946.
16312.m: The Allies boycotted companies by putting them on blacklists.

16313.q: What measure did the USA take against Swiss assets in 1941?
a: It froze Swiss assets, including a large part of the gold reserves
It introduced the franc as a second currency
16313.e: About three quarters of the Swiss gold reserves were held in the USA and were frozen. Only the Washington Agreement released them.
16313.m: During the war the USA froze Swiss assets.

16314.q: What sum did Switzerland pay the Allies under the Washington Agreement of 25 May 1946?
16314.e: The payment was made as compensation for the gold purchases, but expressly without accepting any legal obligation. In return, Swiss assets were released.
16314.m: Under the Washington Agreement, Switzerland paid 250 million francs in 1946.

16315.q: What did the Washington Agreement of 1946 decide about German assets in Switzerland?
a: They were to be sold off and the proceeds shared between the Allies and Switzerland
They were to be returned to Germany
They went entirely to the Soviet Union
16315.e: One half was to go to the Allies for rebuilding Europe, the other to Switzerland for its claims against Germany.
16315.m: After 1946, German assets in Switzerland were to be shared.

16316.q: What is the official name of the Bergier Commission?
a: Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland Second World War
16316.e: The commission is named after its president Bergier; officially it is called the Independent Commission of Experts (ICE). It examined Switzerland’s role in the Second World War.
16316.m: The Bergier Commission’s official name is the Independent Commission of Experts.

16317.q: When did the Federal Council set up the Bergier Commission?
16317.e: It was based on a federal decree passed by parliament in December 1996. The Federal Council set up the commission on 19 December 1996.
16317.m: The Bergier Commission was created at the end of 1996.

16318.q: What was the profession of Jean-François Bergier, the president of the Independent Commission of Experts?
16318.e: Bergier taught economic history at ETH Zurich. The commission is named after him.
16318.m: Jean-François Bergier was an economic historian at ETH Zurich.

16319.q: Why did the Bergier Commission also include historians from abroad?
a: To strengthen its independence and credibility
Because there were too few historians in Switzerland
Because the records were only available in English
16319.e: The commission had an international membership, including Saul Friedländer and Harold James. That way, nobody could accuse it of going easy on Switzerland.
16319.m: The Bergier Commission had international members so that it would be credible.

16320.q: Which debate in the 1990s was the main trigger for setting up the Bergier Commission?
a: The debate about dormant assets of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks
The dispute about joining the EEA
The debate about joining the UN
A dispute about abolishing the army
16320.e: The World Jewish Congress and lawsuits in the USA accused Swiss banks of holding back assets belonging to Holocaust victims. The international pressure led to a reappraisal of the past.
16320.m: The dormant assets triggered the reappraisal of the past in the 1990s.

16321.q: Which special right did the Bergier Commission get for its research?
a: Access to the archives of private companies such as banks and insurers
The right to overturn court verdicts
16321.e: The companies had to open their archives and were not allowed to destroy records from the period. This was unusual for historical research in Switzerland.
16321.m: The commission was also allowed to study the archives of private companies.

16322.q: Apart from looted gold and banking business, what else did the Bergier Commission examine?
a: Neutrality in the First World War
The founding of the federal state in 1848
16322.e: Its mandate was extended, and the budget rose from 5 to 22 million francs. The commission also examined how Switzerland dealt with refugees.
16322.m: The Bergier Commission also examined refugee policy.

16323.q: When did the Bergier Commission present its final report?
16323.e: The final report is called “Switzerland, National Socialism and the Second World War”. Many individual studies had appeared before it.
16323.m: The Bergier final report appeared in 2002.

16324.q: According to the Bergier Commission, where did part of the looted gold that reached Switzerland come from?
a: From the central banks of occupied countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, and from persecuted people
16324.e: The Reichsbank had stolen gold from the central banks of occupied states and from private individuals. Gold from victims of the extermination policy also ended up in its stocks.
16324.m: Part of the gold sold to Switzerland was looted gold.

16325.q: According to the Bergier Commission’s final report, how many refugees did Switzerland turn away or deport during the war?
16325.e: The commission gave a figure of over 20,000 refusals. Other studies arrive at lower or higher numbers, which shows how difficult the sources are.
16325.m: According to the Bergier Commission, Switzerland turned away over 20,000 refugees.

16326.q: What did the security guard Christoph Meili do at the Union Bank of Switzerland in January 1997?
a: He saved bank records from being destroyed
He published account data on the internet
He set up a foundation for refugees
16326.e: Meili took away records that were to be shredded, even though destroying them had been banned since December 1996. The case increased international pressure on the banks.
16326.m: In 1997 Christoph Meili saved records from the shredder.

16327.q: Which sum did the major Swiss banks agree to in the global settlement of 13 August 1998?
16327.e: The settlement ended class actions in the USA. The money was intended for Holocaust survivors and their descendants.
16327.m: In the 1998 global settlement the banks paid 1.25 billion dollars.

16328.q: Which picture of Switzerland in the Second World War did the Bergier Commission call into question?
a: That Switzerland was spared only thanks to its army and neutrality
That Switzerland took an active part in the war
That Switzerland was occupied by Germany
That Switzerland took in no refugees
16328.e: The commission showed that economic relations, gold deals and a harsh refugee policy also played a role. The Bonjour Report from 1965 onwards had already partly corrected this picture.
16328.m: The Bergier Commission showed that Switzerland was not spared thanks to the army alone.

16329.q: On which day did the Charter of the United Nations come into force?
16329.e: After ratification by the required states, the UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945. Since then this day has been marked as United Nations Day.
16329.m: 24 October is seen as the birthday of the UN.

16330.q: In which city was the Charter of the United Nations signed on 26 June 1945?
16330.e: At the San Francisco Conference, which began on 25 April 1945, the Charter was drawn up and signed on 26 June 1945.
16330.m: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in 1945.

16331.q: How many founding members did the United Nations have?
16331.e: 50 states were represented in San Francisco, and Poland signed shortly afterwards. That makes 51 founding members.
16331.m: The UN started in 1945 with 51 member states.

16332.q: Which international organisation was the UN meant to replace because it had not prevented the Second World War?
16332.e: The League of Nations had been founded after the First World War and failed to prevent war. It was formally dissolved in April 1946 and handed its tasks over to the UN.
16332.m: The UN is the successor to the failed League of Nations.

16333.q: Which two politicians announced the Atlantic Charter in August 1941, an important forerunner of the UN?
a: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill
Harry S. Truman and Clement Attlee
Franklin D. Roosevelt and Charles de Gaulle
16333.e: In 1941 Roosevelt and Churchill set out common principles for a post-war order. These ideas later went into the UN Charter.
16333.m: The Atlantic Charter of 1941 prepared the way for founding the UN.

16334.q: Who first suggested the name “United Nations”?
16334.e: US President Roosevelt suggested the name to Churchill in December 1941. It was first used officially in the Declaration by United Nations of 1 January 1942.
16334.m: The name “United Nations” comes from Franklin D. Roosevelt.

16335.q: What did the term “United Nations” originally stand for from 1942?
a: The wartime alliance against the Axis powers
The members of the League of Nations
16335.e: On 1 January 1942, 26 governments committed themselves to fighting together against Germany, Italy and Japan. Only in 1945 did this become the peace organisation UN.
16335.m: Originally the United Nations were an alliance against the Axis powers.

16336.q: Which four powers jointly drew up the basic structure of the UN in 1944?
a: USA, Great Britain, Soviet Union and China
USA, Great Britain, France and Canada
USA, Soviet Union, France and India
Great Britain, France, China and Brazil
16336.e: The four big Allies met in Washington in 1944 to discuss the new organisation. France later joined as the fifth veto power.
16336.m: The four big Allies planned the UN in 1944.

16337.q: At which conference in February 1945 did Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agree on the veto in the Security Council?
16337.e: Stalin insisted on a veto for the great powers, and Roosevelt agreed at Yalta. Without this compromise, the Soviet Union would probably not have joined.
16337.m: The veto in the Security Council goes back to the Yalta Conference.

16338.q: Which five states are permanent members of the UN Security Council?
a: USA, Russia, China, France, United Kingdom
USA, Russia, India, France, United Kingdom
USA, Canada, China, France, United Kingdom
16338.e: The victorious powers of the Second World War received permanent seats with a veto. Russia took over the Soviet Union's seat in 1991.
16338.m: The five veto powers are the victorious powers of 1945.

16339.q: Who was the first Secretary-General of the United Nations?
16339.e: The Norwegian Trygve Lie took office in February 1946 and resigned in 1952. His successor was the Swede Dag Hammarskjöld.
16339.m: The first UN Secretary-General was the Norwegian Trygve Lie.

16340.q: In which city did the UN General Assembly meet for the first time on 10 January 1946?
16340.e: The first session took place in Methodist Central Hall in London. The headquarters in New York was only occupied in the early 1950s.
16340.m: The first UN General Assembly met in London in 1946.

16341.q: How many members has the UN Security Council had since it was enlarged in 1965?
16341.e: In 1965 the number of non-permanent members rose from 6 to 10. Together with the 5 permanent members, that has made 15 ever since.
16341.m: The Security Council has 5 permanent and 10 non-permanent members.

16342.q: For how long are the non-permanent members of the Security Council elected?
16342.e: Each year the General Assembly elects about half of the non-permanent members. Immediate re-election is not allowed.
16342.m: Non-permanent members sit on the Security Council for two years.

16343.q: Which UN body is the only one that can decide on binding enforcement measures under Chapter VII of the Charter?
16343.e: Only the Security Council may order binding measures such as sanctions or military action when peace is threatened. Resolutions of the General Assembly, by contrast, are recommendations.
16343.m: Only the Security Council decides on binding enforcement measures.

16344.q: Which main body of the UN stopped its work in 1994 because its task was done?
16344.e: The Trusteeship Council looked after territories on their way to independence. When Palau, the last trust territory, became independent in 1994, it stopped its work.
16344.m: The Trusteeship Council has been inactive since there have been no more trust territories.

16345.q: How did the UN get the land for its headquarters in New York?
a: John D. Rockefeller Jr. paid for the purchase
The US government seized a harbour
The City of New York auctioned it
Great Britain gave it as a gift
16345.e: With his father's money, Nelson Rockefeller bought a site on the East River and gave it to the UN. That is why it chose New York instead of Philadelphia.
16345.m: The UN headquarters stands on land given by the Rockefellers.

16346.q: Why was the Soviet Union absent from the Security Council vote on the Korean War in 1950?
a: It was boycotting the Council over the China question
It was not yet a member
16346.e: The Soviet Union stayed away from the Council because China's seat was held by the Republic of China in Taiwan. So the Council could decide on action in Korea without its veto.
16346.m: Because of the Soviet boycott, the Security Council was able to act in Korea in 1950.

16347.q: In which year did China's UN seat pass from the Republic of China to the People's Republic of China?
16347.e: Until 1971 the government in Taiwan represented China in the UN. After that the People's Republic of China took over the seat, including the permanent seat on the Security Council.
16347.m: Since 1971 the People's Republic of China has represented its country in the UN.

16348.q: When did Switzerland join the United Nations as a full member?
16348.e: After the popular vote of 3 March 2002, Switzerland became a member in September 2002. Before that it had long only had observer status.
16348.m: Switzerland has only been a full member of the UN since 2002.

16349.q: By what result did Swiss voters accept joining the UN on 3 March 2002?
16349.e: 54.6 percent voted yes. The majority of the cantons was also only narrowly reached, which shows many people's doubts because of neutrality.
16349.m: Switzerland's decision to join the UN in 2002 was a close one.

16350.q: In which Geneva building, once the seat of the League of Nations, is the United Nations Office located today?
16350.e: The Palais des Nations was built in the 1930s for the League of Nations. The UN has used it since 1946, and Geneva is one of its most important locations.
16350.m: The Palais des Nations in Geneva first housed the League of Nations and today the UN.

16351.q: For which years was Switzerland a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the first time?
16351.e: The General Assembly elected Switzerland to the Security Council in 2022. It was its first term on this body.
16351.m: Switzerland sat on the Security Council for the first time in 2023 and 2024.

16352.q: How many member states does the United Nations have today?
16352.e: Since South Sudan was admitted in 2011, the UN has had 193 member states. Almost every sovereign state in the world is a member.

16353.q: In which year did the Federal Republic of Germany and the GDR both become members of the UN at the same time?
16353.e: Both German states were admitted on 18 September 1973. This was a sign of the policy of détente between East and West.
16353.m: Both German states joined the UN in 1973.

16354.q: On which day did the UN General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
16354.e: The Declaration was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948. Since then this day has been International Human Rights Day.

16355.q: In which city did the UN General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948?
16355.e: In 1948 the General Assembly met in the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. The headquarters in New York was not yet finished.
16355.m: The Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in Paris in 1948.

16356.q: How many articles does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights have?
16356.e: The Declaration consists of a preamble and 30 articles. It covers civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.
16356.m: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has 30 articles.

16357.q: How did the vote on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights turn out in 1948?
a: With no votes against, but with some abstentions
Narrowly, with a majority of just one vote
It was rejected and only adopted in 1950
16357.e: 48 states voted in favour, none against, and eight abstained. They included South Africa, Saudi Arabia and several Eastern Bloc states.
16357.m: The Declaration of Human Rights was adopted with no votes against.

16358.q: Which state abstained in the 1948 vote on the Declaration of Human Rights, partly because of its policy of racial segregation?
16358.e: South Africa was just introducing apartheid and rejected equal rights for all. It was one of the eight states that abstained.
16358.m: South Africa abstained in 1948 because of its apartheid policy.

16359.q: Who chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights, which drew up the Universal Declaration?
16359.e: The former US First Lady, Eleanor Roosevelt, chaired the commission. She skilfully mediated between the different world views.
16359.m: Eleanor Roosevelt shaped the making of the Declaration of Human Rights.

16360.q: Why is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights not seen as a purely American work?
a: Authors from many countries and cultures took part
It was written only by Europeans
The USA voted against the Declaration
It was translated from an old Chinese constitution
16360.e: Besides Eleanor Roosevelt, contributors included the Frenchman René Cassin, the Canadian John Peters Humphrey, the Chinese Peng Chun Chang and the Lebanese Charles Malik. Cassin received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1968.
16360.m: People from many cultures helped write the Declaration of Human Rights.

16361.q: Which body drew up the text of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: A commission of the United Nations
The League of Nations in Geneva
The Council of Europe in Strasbourg
The International Committee of the Red Cross
16361.e: The UN Commission on Human Rights under Eleanor Roosevelt drew up the text. The first draft was written by the Canadian lawyer John Peters Humphrey.
16361.m: The Declaration of Human Rights was created in a UN commission.

16362.q: Which tradition of thought did the Chinese diplomat Peng Chun Chang bring into the Declaration of Human Rights?
16362.e: P. C. Chang was vice-chairman of the commission. Using ideas from Confucianism, he worked to make sure the Declaration did not only reflect Western traditions of thought.
16362.m: Peng Chun Chang made the Declaration of Human Rights more open to the world.

16363.q: What legal effect does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights have?
a: It is a resolution with no direct legal force
It is a treaty ratified by all states
It is part of the UN Charter
It is enforced by the Security Council
16363.e: Resolutions of the General Assembly are not binding. But the Declaration acts as a moral standard and as the basis for later binding treaties.
16363.m: The Declaration of Human Rights is an ideal and not a binding treaty.

16364.q: With which idea does Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights begin?
a: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights
Everyone has the right to work
No one may be arbitrarily arrested
Everyone has the right to education
16364.e: Article 1 states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
16364.m: The Declaration begins with the equal dignity of all people.

16365.q: Which basic rights does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights put first at the very start of its list of rights?
a: Life, liberty and security of person
Property, trade and free choice of job
Right to vote, asylum and nationality
16365.e: Article 3 protects life, liberty and security of person. Many other rights build on these basic goods.
16365.m: Life, liberty and security are the basis of all human rights.

16366.q: What does Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights prohibit?
a: Torture and cruel or degrading treatment
The death penalty in any form
16366.e: No one may be tortured or treated inhumanely. The ban on torture is today seen as a peremptory rule of international law.
16366.m: The ban on torture is at the core of human rights.

16367.q: According to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, what is explicitly part of freedom of religion?
a: The right to change one's religion
