The right to places of worship paid for by the state
The right to one's own religious school
Only the freedom to practise one's faith in private
16367.e: Article 18 guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion. It explicitly includes the right to change one's religion, which led Saudi Arabia to abstain.
16367.m: Freedom of religion also includes the right to change one's faith.

16368.q: Which freedom, according to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, explicitly applies across national borders too?
a: To seek and spread information and opinions
To work in any country without a permit
16368.e: Article 19 guarantees freedom of opinion and information. This includes seeking and spreading information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.
16368.m: Article 19 protects free opinion and free access to information.

16369.q: Which two binding UN covenants turned the rights of the Universal Declaration into international law in 1966?
a: Convention on the Rights of the Child and Convention on Women's Rights
16369.e: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights were adopted in 1966. Together with the Declaration they form the so-called International Bill of Human Rights.
16369.m: The Civil and Social Covenants made human rights binding.

16370.q: Why did the UN human rights covenants of 1966 only come into force ten years later?
a: Enough states first had to ratify them
The Security Council used its veto
The text first had to be translated into every language
The UN waited for the end of the Vietnam War
16370.e: The covenants were adopted in 1966. Only by 1976 had 35 states ratified them, so that they could come into force.
16370.m: It took ten years from adoption until the UN covenants came into force.

16371.q: When and where was the European Convention on Human Rights signed?
16371.e: The ECHR was signed in Rome within the framework of the Council of Europe on 4 November 1950 and came into force in 1953.
16371.m: The European Convention on Human Rights dates from 1950.

16372.q: What distinguishes the European Convention on Human Rights from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: It is binding and has its own court
It applies worldwide to all UN states
It was adopted by the UN
16372.e: The ECHR is a treaty that binds its member states. Individuals can bring cases before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
16372.m: The ECHR makes human rights in Europe enforceable in court.

16373.q: What, among other things, delayed Switzerland's accession to the European Convention on Human Rights until 1974?
a: The lack of women's right to vote
Rejection by the Council of Europe
Not being a member of the UN
16373.e: Switzerland joined the Council of Europe in 1963 but only ratified the ECHR in 1974. One obstacle was the lack of women's right to vote, which was only introduced in 1971.
16373.m: The ECHR has applied in Switzerland since 1974.

16374.q: Which UN body based in Geneva replaced the Commission on Human Rights in 2006?
a: International Committee of the Red Cross
16374.e: The Human Rights Council has 47 members and regularly reviews all states. It meets in Geneva.
16374.m: The UN Human Rights Council has met in Geneva since 2006.

16375.q: Which states does the UN Human Rights Council review in its regular review procedure?
a: Every member state of the UN
Only the members of the Security Council
16375.e: In the Universal Periodic Review, every state takes its turn about every four and a half years. All states are treated equally.
16375.m: In the Universal Periodic Review, every state has to give an account of itself.

16376.q: Which historical experience was a main reason for drawing up the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: The crimes of National Socialism and the Holocaust
16376.e: The preamble speaks of barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind. This refers above all to the crimes of the Second World War and the Holocaust.
16376.m: The Declaration of Human Rights is a response to the crimes of the Second World War.

16377.q: Into how many languages has the Universal Declaration of Human Rights been translated so far?
16377.e: According to the United Nations, there are now well over 500 language versions. This makes it one of the most translated texts in the world.
16377.m: Hardly any text has been translated as often as the Declaration of Human Rights.

16378.q: Which group of states mostly abstained in 1948 because it rejected the emphasis on civil liberties?
a: The Soviet Union and several Eastern Bloc states
16378.e: The Soviet Union, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia abstained. They gave more weight to social rights and state sovereignty.
16378.m: The Eastern Bloc abstained on the Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

16379.q: What was the official name of the Marshall Plan?
16379.e: The aid programme was officially called the European Recovery Program, ERP for short. The name Marshall Plan comes from US Secretary of State George C. Marshall.
16379.m: The Marshall Plan was officially called the European Recovery Program.

16380.q: Where did George C. Marshall present his plan for rebuilding Europe on 5 June 1947?
16380.e: Marshall gave a speech of only about ten minutes at Harvard University. In it he offered Europe extensive help if the states worked together.
16380.m: The idea of the Marshall Plan was announced at Harvard in 1947.

16381.q: Which office did George C. Marshall hold when he proposed the Marshall Plan?
16381.e: Marshall was US Secretary of State from 1947 to 1949. Before that, during the Second World War, he had been Chief of Staff of the US Army.
16381.m: George C. Marshall was US Secretary of State when he presented the plan.

16382.q: Which award did George C. Marshall receive in 1953?
16382.e: Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953, above all for his contribution to rebuilding Europe.
16382.m: Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize for the Marshall Plan.

16383.q: Over which period did the Marshall Plan run?
16383.e: Congress approved the programme in April 1948. The aid flowed to Europe until 1952.
16383.m: Marshall Plan aid flowed from 1948 to 1952.

16384.q: Roughly how much was the Marshall Plan aid in total?
16384.e: A sum of about 13.1 billion dollars is usually given. Depending on how it is counted, figures vary between about 10 and 14 billion.
16384.m: The Marshall Plan amounted to about 13 billion dollars.

16385.q: Which US President put the Marshall Plan into force in April 1948?
16385.e: Congress passed the law on 3 April 1948, and President Truman signed it into force on the same day.
16385.m: President Truman put the Marshall Plan into force in 1948.

16386.q: Which basic US foreign policy statement of 12 March 1947 came before the Marshall Plan?
16386.e: Truman promised support to countries resisting communist pressure. The Marshall Plan put this policy into practice economically.
16386.m: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 came before the Marshall Plan.

16387.q: What is the US policy of stopping the spread of Soviet influence called, which the Marshall Plan was also part of?
16387.e: Containment means holding something back. Economically stable democracies were expected to be less open to communism.
16387.m: The Marshall Plan was also a tool of the policy of containment.

16388.q: According to Marshall's Harvard speech, what was American policy explicitly directed against?
a: Against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos
Against the Soviet Union and communism
16388.e: Marshall said the policy was directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. That the plan was nevertheless also meant to contain communism shows how important it is to look critically at such sources.
16388.m: Officially, the Marshall Plan was directed against hardship and chaos in Europe.

16389.q: Which organisation did the receiving states found in Paris on 16 April 1948 to share out the aid?
16389.e: The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation coordinated the aid among the European states. It required the countries to plan together.
16389.m: The OEEC shared out the Marshall Plan aid among the receiving states.

16390.q: Which present-day organisation grew out of the OEEC?
16390.e: In 1961 the OEEC was turned into the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which also includes the USA and Canada.
16390.m: The OECD is the successor to the OEEC.

16391.q: What was the task of the US agency Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) from 1948?
a: It organised the Marshall Plan aid deliveries
It ran the intelligence service in Europe
It administered the occupation zones in Japan
16391.e: The Economic Cooperation Administration, ECA for short, organised the aid deliveries. Paul G. Hoffman headed it until 1950.
16391.m: The ECA carried out the Marshall Plan on the American side.

16392.q: How did the Soviet Union react to the offer of the Marshall Plan?
a: It refused and banned the Eastern Bloc states from taking part
It took part and received aid
16392.e: Foreign Minister Molotov walked out of the Paris negotiations in 1947. The Soviet Union saw the plan as an attempt to weaken its influence in Eastern Europe.
16392.m: The Marshall Plan deepened the division of Europe into East and West.

16393.q: Which economic organisation did the Soviet Union found in January 1949 in response to the Marshall Plan?
16393.e: The CMEA, often called Comecon in the West, linked the economies of the Eastern Bloc states with the Soviet Union.
16393.m: Comecon was the Eastern counterpart to the Marshall Plan.

16394.q: Why did Spain receive no Marshall Plan aid?
a: Because of the dictatorship of Francisco Franco
Because it belonged to the Eastern Bloc
Because it had not been damaged in the war
Because it wanted to stay neutral
16394.e: Spain was excluded because of the Franco regime. Only at the end of the 1950s did it receive help from a special OEEC fund.
16394.m: The Franco regime shut Spain out of the Marshall Plan.

16395.q: Why did Finland not take part in the Marshall Plan?
a: Out of consideration for the Soviet Union and its neutrality
Because it had no war damage
Because it was ruled by Franco
Because it already belonged to NATO
16395.e: Finland bordered the Soviet Union and had to take its powerful neighbour into account. It followed a cautious policy of neutrality.
16395.m: Finland stayed out of the Marshall Plan out of consideration for Moscow.

16396.q: How did Switzerland take part in the Marshall Plan?
a: It refused to take part at all
16396.e: Switzerland took part in the Paris talks in 1947 and became a member of the OEEC in 1948. As a country hardly damaged by the war, it initially received no aid.
16396.m: Neutral Switzerland was a founding member of the OEEC.

16397.q: Which basic principle shaped the Marshall Plan?
a: A planned economy on the Soviet model
16397.e: The recipients were to rebuild their economies themselves. To do so they had to free up trade and stabilise their currencies.
16397.m: The Marshall Plan relied on help for self-help.

16398.q: What did the receiving states pay into so-called counterpart funds for the goods delivered?
a: The equivalent value in their own currency
16398.e: The governments paid the value of the deliveries in their own currency. This money was used to finance investment in the country.
16398.m: The counterpart funds made the aid doubly useful in the receiving country.

16399.q: Which German development bank still manages the ERP Special Fund, which comes from the Marshall Plan, on behalf of the federal government?
16399.e: The KfW began its work in Frankfurt am Main on 16 December 1948. The ERP Special Fund still mainly supports small and medium-sized businesses today.
16399.m: Through the KfW, the Marshall Plan's money still has an effect in Germany today.

16400.q: Which reservation do researchers have about the idea that the Marshall Plan alone triggered the “economic miracle”?
a: Other factors such as currency reform and workers were just as important
The aid consisted only of weapons
16400.e: Historians stress that the sums were limited compared with economic output. Also important were the currency reform, well-trained workers and the effect on confidence.
16400.m: The Marshall Plan was an important but not the only reason for the boom.

16401.q: In what form did the recipients receive most of the Marshall Plan aid?
a: As grants for imports from the USA
16401.e: Most of the funds were used as grants for imports of raw materials, food and industrial goods from the USA. The US economy also benefited from this.
16401.m: Marshall Plan aid came to Europe mainly as deliveries of goods.

16402.q: What benefit did the USA itself get from the Marshall Plan?
a: Stable markets in Europe for its exports
It got seats in European parliaments
16402.e: An economically strong Europe bought American goods and was politically stable. In this way the plan also served the interests of the USA.
16402.m: The Marshall Plan strengthened Europe and at the same time the US economy.

16403.q: Which three heads of government were negotiating at the end of the Potsdam Conference in summer 1945?
16403.e: The conference met from 17 July to 2 August 1945. Churchill lost the British election during the conference, so from the end of July Clement Attlee represented Great Britain.
16403.m: At Potsdam, Truman, Stalin and Attlee decided on Germany's future.

16404.q: Which victorious power was not involved in the Potsdam Conference but received an occupation zone?
16404.e: France was not invited. Its zone was formed from parts of the American and British zones.
16404.m: France got an occupation zone but did not sit at the table in Potsdam.

16405.q: Which goals for Germany are known as the “four Ds” of the Potsdam Conference?
16405.e: Germany was to be disarmed, freed from National Socialism, and built up democratically and decentrally. Sometimes dismantling is mentioned as well.
16405.m: The four Ds of Potsdam describe the Allies' goals for Germany.

16406.q: Which line was to mark the boundary of the territories under Polish administration according to the Potsdam Agreement?
16406.e: The territories east of the Oder and the Lusatian Neisse came under Polish administration. A peace treaty was to bring the final settlement.
16406.m: The Oder-Neisse line became Poland's western border.

16407.q: Which occupation zones were merged economically into the Bizone in 1947?
16407.e: From 1 January 1947 the American and British zones formed the Bizone. Later the French zone joined, and it became the Trizone.
16407.m: With the Bizone, the merger of the western zones began in 1947.

16408.q: When was the Deutsche Mark introduced in the western zones?
16408.e: The currency reform replaced the Reichsmark with the Deutsche Mark. Berlin was excluded at first, and the Soviet Union responded with the blockade.
16408.m: The currency reform of 1948 was a step towards the division of Germany.

16409.q: How long did the Berlin Blockade last?
16409.e: The Soviet Union blocked all land and water routes to West Berlin. After almost eleven months, it lifted the blockade.
16409.m: The Berlin Blockade lasted almost a year.

16410.q: Which US military governor ordered the Berlin Airlift in June 1948?
16410.e: General Lucius D. Clay gave the order on 25 June 1948. The Western powers then supplied West Berlin from the air.
16410.m: Lucius D. Clay is regarded as the father of the airlift.

16411.q: Which goods made up almost two thirds of the Berlin Airlift's cargo?
16411.e: Coal was needed for electricity, heating and industry. That is why it was the planes' most important load.
16411.m: The airlift flew mainly coal into Berlin.

16412.q: Why did Berlin children call the airlift planes “raisin bombers”?
a: Because pilots dropped sweets on little parachutes
Because they only carried dried fruit
Because they came from raisin factories
16412.e: The US pilot Gail Halvorsen dropped chocolate on handkerchief parachutes for children. This grew into the “Little Vittles” operation.
16412.m: The raisin bombers became a symbol of friendship between Berlin and the West.

16413.q: Who was president of the Parliamentary Council, which drew up the Basic Law?
16413.e: The Parliamentary Council met in Bonn on 1 September 1948 and elected Konrad Adenauer as its president. In 1949 Adenauer became the first Federal Chancellor.
16413.m: Adenauer led the Parliamentary Council and then became Federal Chancellor.

16414.q: Which lawyer got the sentence “Men and women shall have equal rights” into the Basic Law in the Parliamentary Council?
16414.e: Elisabeth Selbert was one of the four “mothers of the Basic Law”. With public pressure she got the equal rights article included.
16414.m: Elisabeth Selbert fought for equal rights in the Basic Law.

16415.q: On which day was the Basic Law proclaimed, founding the Federal Republic of Germany?
16415.e: The Parliamentary Council adopted the Basic Law on 8 May 1949. It was proclaimed on 23 May 1949, which is seen as the founding day of the Federal Republic.
16415.m: The Federal Republic was founded on 23 May 1949.

16416.q: On which day was the German Democratic Republic founded?
16416.e: The GDR was created on 7 October 1949 out of the Soviet occupation zone. This completed the division of Germany into two states.
16416.m: Two German states were created in 1949.

16417.q: What triggered the uprising of 17 June 1953 in the GDR?
a: A 10 percent increase in work quotas
The building of the Berlin Wall
The introduction of the Deutsche Mark
16417.e: The higher quotas effectively meant a pay cut. Building workers on Stalinallee in East Berlin stopped work on 16 June, and on 17 June the protest spread across the whole GDR.
16417.m: The uprising of 17 June 1953 began as a protest against higher work quotas.

16418.q: How was the uprising of 17 June 1953 ended?
a: By a compromise with the government
16418.e: Soviet troops and the Barracked People's Police crushed the uprising, and a state of emergency was declared. At least about 55 deaths are documented.
16418.m: Soviet tanks crushed the uprising of 17 June.

16419.q: What did 17 June become in the Federal Republic from 1954 to 1990?
a: The Day of German Unity, a public holiday
A day to remember the airlift
16419.e: In memory of the uprising, 17 June was a public holiday in West Germany. Since 1990 it has been 3 October.
16419.m: Until 1990 the Federal Republic celebrated the Day of German Unity on 17 June.

16420.q: What did Stalin offer the Western powers in the Stalin Note of 10 March 1952?
a: Withdrawal from the whole of Eastern Europe
The return of the eastern territories
16420.e: Stalin proposed negotiations on a reunited but neutral Germany. The West and Adenauer refused; whether the offer was meant seriously is still disputed today.
16420.m: Historians still disagree about how serious the Stalin Note was.

16421.q: With which principle did the Federal Republic threaten from 1955 to break off relations with states that recognised the GDR?
16421.e: The Federal Republic claimed to be the only one to speak for Germany. The Hallstein Doctrine was meant to isolate the GDR internationally.
16421.m: With the Hallstein Doctrine, Bonn wanted to isolate the GDR.

16422.q: Which alliances did the two German states join in 1955?
a: The Federal Republic joined NATO and the GDR the Warsaw Pact
The Federal Republic joined EFTA and the GDR Comecon
16422.e: The Federal Republic became a member of NATO in May 1955. A few days later the Eastern Bloc founded the Warsaw Pact with the GDR.
16422.m: In 1955 the two German states were tied into opposing military alliances.

16423.q: Roughly how many people fled from the GDR to the West between 1949 and the building of the Wall in 1961?
16423.e: The mass flight, above all of young, well-trained people, greatly weakened the GDR. This was a main reason for building the Wall.
16423.m: The flight of people from the GDR led to the building of the Wall.

16424.q: Which GDR politician said on 15 June 1961 “No one has the intention of building a wall”?
16424.e: Walter Ulbricht said this at a press conference. Two months later, on 13 August 1961, building of the Wall began.
16424.m: Ulbricht's famous sentence was proved wrong two months later.

16425.q: What did the GDR leadership officially call the Berlin Wall?
16425.e: The SED presented the Wall as protection against the West. In reality it was meant above all to stop its own citizens from fleeing.
16425.m: The GDR used the glossing-over name “Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart” for the Wall.

16426.q: Which treaty regulated relations between the Federal Republic and the GDR in 1972?
16426.e: In the Basic Treaty both states effectively recognised each other, without the Federal Republic regarding the GDR as a foreign country. It was part of Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik.
16426.m: The Basic Treaty of 1972 eased tensions between the German states.

16427.q: Which treaty of 12 September 1990 made German reunification possible in terms of foreign policy?
16427.e: In it, the two German states and the four victorious powers settled the external aspects of unity. Germany gained full sovereignty and confirmed the Oder-Neisse border.
16427.m: The Two Plus Four Treaty ended the post-war era in Germany.

16428.q: On which day did the division of Germany end with reunification?
16428.e: On 3 October 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic. Since then this day has been the Day of German Unity.
16428.m: Germany has been united again since 3 October 1990.

16429.q: Which author wrote the novel “Nineteen Eighty-Four” about a totalitarian surveillance state?
16429.e: George Orwell published “Nineteen Eighty-Four” in 1949. In 1945 he was also one of the first to use the term “cold war”.
16429.m: In “Nineteen Eighty-Four”, Orwell warned against the totalitarian state.

16430.q: Why is the conflict between the USA and the Soviet Union called a “cold” war?
a: Because the two superpowers never fought each other directly
Because it was fought without a declaration of war but with open battles in Europe
Because both sides only imposed economic sanctions and disarmed
Because the two states officially remained allies until 1991
16430.e: The USA and the Soviet Union were hostile to each other, built up their arms and supported proxies, but did not wage a direct war against each other. The fear of nuclear war acted as a deterrent.
16430.m: In the Cold War, the superpowers threatened each other without firing directly at each other.

16431.q: In which place did Winston Churchill give his famous “Iron Curtain” speech on 5 March 1946?
16431.e: At Westminster College in Fulton, Churchill said that an iron curtain had descended across Europe from Stettin to Trieste. In Zurich he gave a speech on the unity of Europe in September 1946.
16431.m: Churchill's Fulton speech made the Iron Curtain the symbol of Europe's division.

16432.q: Which aim did US President Truman announce with the Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947?
a: Containing communism by supporting threatened states
The complete withdrawal of US troops from Europe
A joint world government with the Soviet Union
16432.e: Truman promised free peoples help against communist pressure, at first Greece and Turkey. This gave rise to the policy of “containment”.
16432.m: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 founded the American policy of containment.

16433.q: What is meant by a proxy war in the Cold War?
a: A war in which the superpowers support allied parties instead of fighting each other directly
A war that the UN fights instead of a member state
A war in which mercenaries of a neutral power strengthen both sides
A war fought only with propaganda and without weapons
16433.e: In conflicts such as Korea, Vietnam or Afghanistan, allies or troops of one superpower faced forces supported by the other side. In this way the USA and the Soviet Union avoided a direct clash.
16433.m: In proxy wars, others did the fighting while the superpowers supplied and steered from the background.

16434.q: Which Soviet party leader began far-reaching reforms with glasnost and perestroika from 1985?
16434.e: Gorbachev became General Secretary of the CPSU in 1985. His reforms and the easing of tensions with the West played a major part in ending the Cold War.
16434.m: Gorbachev's reforms opened the way to the end of the Cold War.

16435.q: With which event is the Cold War usually said to have ended?
a: With the break-up of the Soviet Union at the end of 1991
With the end of the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962
With the US withdrawal from Vietnam in 1973
16435.e: After the fall of the Wall in 1989 and the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact, the Soviet Union also fell apart in December 1991. This ended the two-sided rivalry of the superpowers.
16435.m: With the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Cold War came to an end.

16436.q: Which economic system shaped the Soviet Union?
16436.e: In the Soviet Union, the state decided in five-year plans what was produced and at what prices. Factories and land largely belonged to the state.
16436.m: The Soviet Union ran its economy with state plans.

16437.q: Which two thinkers published “The Communist Manifesto” in 1848?
16437.e: In it, Marx and Engels described history as a history of class struggles and called for the abolition of private ownership of the means of production. Their work became the basis of communist movements.
16437.m: The Communist Manifesto by Marx and Engels appeared in 1848.

16438.q: Which feature marks a capitalist economic system?
a: Private ownership of the means of production and competition in markets
State ownership of all factories and land
Binding five-year plans for all businesses
Fixed standard prices set by a party
16438.e: In capitalism, businesses belong to private owners, and prices are formed by supply and demand. In the Cold War the West combined this with democracy and a multi-party system.
16438.m: In capitalism, private people own businesses and the market decides prices.

16439.q: What was the aim of the Marshall Plan, which US Secretary of State George C. Marshall announced on 5 June 1947?
a: The economic rebuilding of Europe, partly to weaken communism
The dismantling of all German industrial plants
Building a joint army with the Soviet Union
Europe repaying its war debts to the USA
16439.e: The USA offered Europe extensive reconstruction aid. Prosperity was meant to weaken communist movements; the Soviet Union rejected the aid for its sphere of power.
16439.m: The Marshall Plan helped Western Europe rebuild and tied it to the USA.

16440.q: Which organisation did the Soviet Union and its allies found in 1949 as an economic response to the Marshall Plan?
a: The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA)
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC)
16440.e: The CMEA, often called “Comecon” in the West, was meant to coordinate the planned economies of the Eastern Bloc. The OEEC, by contrast, was the Western organisation for distributing Marshall Plan aid.
16440.m: Comecon was the economic alliance of the Eastern Bloc.

16441.q: What were the Eastern European states that were under Soviet control after 1945 called?
16441.e: States such as Poland, Hungary or Czechoslovakia were formally sovereign, but their politics were largely decided by Moscow. They circled the Soviet Union like satellites, so to speak.
16441.m: The satellite states of Eastern Europe largely followed orders from Moscow.

16442.q: Which party held the monopoly on political power in the Soviet Union?
a: The Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU)
The Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED)
The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party
16442.e: The CPSU was the only permitted party and controlled the state, the economy and the media. The SED played a similar role in the GDR.
16442.m: In the Soviet Union, the CPSU ruled as the only party.

16443.q: What does the Russian word “glasnost”, one of Gorbachev's slogans, mean?
16443.e: Glasnost stood for more freedom of speech and more open information about problems. Perestroika, by contrast, meant “restructuring” and referred to reforms of the economy and the state.
16443.m: Glasnost means openness, perestroika means restructuring.

16444.q: When was the North Atlantic Treaty signed, which created NATO?
16444.e: The treaty was concluded in Washington on 4 April 1949. It was a response to the growing tension with the Soviet Union, for example during the Berlin Blockade.

16445.q: How many states signed the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949 as founding members?
16445.e: The founding members were Belgium, Denmark, France, Great Britain, Iceland, Italy, Canada, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and the USA.
16445.m: NATO began with twelve founding states.

16446.q: What does Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty lay down?
a: An attack on one member counts as an attack on all, who give assistance
Every member must have its own nuclear weapons
Members may not trade with the Eastern Bloc
The Secretary General is appointed by the US President
16446.e: Article 5 is the alliance's mutual defence clause. It formed the core of mutual deterrence in the Cold War.
16446.m: Under Article 5, all NATO states come to the aid of a member that is attacked.

16447.q: In which year did the Federal Republic of Germany join NATO?
16447.e: Membership was formally completed in Paris on 9 May 1955, made possible by the Paris Agreements. This firmly tied West Germany into the Western alliance.
16447.m: West Germany became a member of NATO in 1955.

16448.q: Which country withdrew from NATO's military integration in 1966 and only fully returned in 2009?
16448.e: Under President de Gaulle, France left the integrated command structure on 1 July 1966, but remained a member of the alliance. It returned in 2009.
16448.m: In 1966 France went its own way militarily but still stayed in NATO.

16449.q: Where has NATO's headquarters been since 1967?
16449.e: NATO was first based in London, and from 1952 in Paris. After France withdrew from military integration, it moved to Brussels in 1967.
16449.m: NATO has had its headquarters in Brussels since 1967.

16450.q: When was the Article 5 collective defence clause invoked for the first time?
a: After the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001
During the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962
After the building of the Wall in 1961
16450.e: During the whole Cold War, the collective defence clause was never triggered. This happened for the first time after the attacks in the USA in 2001.
16450.m: NATO only invoked Article 5 in 2001, not during the Cold War.

16451.q: Why is Switzerland not a member of NATO?
a: Because joining a military alliance is incompatible with its neutrality
Because NATO only admits states with a coastline
Because Switzerland belonged to the Warsaw Pact
16451.e: Armed neutrality forbids Switzerland from joining an alliance with a duty of mutual defence. But since the 1990s it has worked with NATO in the Partnership for Peace.
16451.m: Neutral Switzerland stays outside military alliances such as NATO.

16452.q: When was the Warsaw Pact founded?
16452.e: The treaty was signed in Warsaw and came into force on 4 June 1955. It was the military counterpart to NATO.
16452.m: The Warsaw Pact was created in May 1955 as a counter-alliance to NATO.

16453.q: Which development was a direct reason for founding the Warsaw Pact?
a: The Federal Republic of Germany being admitted to NATO
The building of the Berlin Wall
The start of the Vietnam War
16453.e: The Paris Agreements of 1954 made West Germany's rearmament and its entry into NATO in 1955 possible. The Soviet Union responded with an alliance of its own.
16453.m: West Germany joining NATO led to the founding of the Warsaw Pact.

16454.q: Which Hungarian prime minister declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact on 1 November 1956?
16454.e: During the popular uprising, Nagy declared Hungary neutral. A few days later Soviet troops crushed the uprising; Nagy was executed in 1958.
16454.m: The Hungarian uprising of 1956 was crushed by Soviet troops.

16455.q: Which reform movement did Warsaw Pact troops end with an invasion in August 1968?
a: The workers' uprising in the GDR
16455.e: In Czechoslovakia, the leadership around Alexander Dubček wanted “socialism with a human face”. Troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria marched in.
16455.m: The Prague Spring was ended by Warsaw Pact troops in 1968.

16456.q: What did the Brezhnev Doctrine, formulated after 1968, state?
a: The sovereignty of socialist states is limited, and intervention to protect socialism is allowed
Every Eastern Bloc state may decide freely to leave the pact
The Soviet Union gives up the use of nuclear weapons
The Eastern Bloc aims for a common currency with the West
16456.e: With the doctrine, the Soviet Union justified military intervention if an allied state threatened to leave the socialist path. Gorbachev gave up this policy at the end of the 1980s.
16456.m: The Brezhnev Doctrine allowed Moscow to intervene militarily in fellow socialist states.

16457.q: Which country formally left the Warsaw Pact in 1968?
16457.e: Albania had fallen out with the Soviet Union, and its membership had been suspended since 1962. After the invasion of Czechoslovakia, it left in September 1968.
16457.m: Albania left the Warsaw Pact in 1968.

16458.q: Which socialist state in Europe never belonged to the Warsaw Pact?
16458.e: Yugoslavia under Tito had fallen out with Stalin in 1948 and went its own way. It later became a leading country of the Non-Aligned Movement.
16458.m: Tito's Yugoslavia stayed outside the Warsaw Pact.

16459.q: When was the Warsaw Pact formally dissolved?
16459.e: The military structures were dissolved on 31 March 1991, and the alliance itself on 1 July 1991. The GDR had already left with reunification in 1990.

16460.q: How long did the Soviet blockade of the western sectors of Berlin last?
16460.e: The Soviet Union blocked all land and water routes to West Berlin. After almost eleven months it lifted the blockade.
16460.m: The Berlin Blockade lasted from June 1948 to May 1949.

16461.q: Which measure by the Western powers did the Soviet Union use in 1948 as a reason for the blockade?
a: The currency reform introducing the Deutsche Mark in the western zones
Stationing American nuclear weapons in Berlin
16461.e: On 20 June 1948 the Deutsche Mark replaced the Reichsmark in the western zones. The Soviet Union reacted a few days later with the blockade.
16461.m: The introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the West triggered the Berlin Blockade.

16462.q: How did the Western powers supply West Berlin during the blockade?
a: Through an airlift with transport planes
Through a tunnel under the sector border
By ships on the Elbe into the city centre
By lorry convoys protected by tanks
16462.e: For almost a year, American and British planes brought food, coal and goods into the city. Berliners called the planes “raisin bombers”.
16462.m: The airlift saved West Berlin during the blockade.

16463.q: Which American military governor ordered the airlift in June 1948?
16463.e: General Clay ordered the setting up of the air supply on 25 June 1948. In Berlin he is regarded as one of the fathers of the airlift.
16463.m: General Lucius D. Clay got the Berlin Airlift going.

16464.q: Why did US pilot Gail Halvorsen's sweets operation during the airlift become a symbol?
a: It showed how former enemies in war became partners
It broke the blockade by land
It showed the strength of the Soviet air force
16464.e: Halvorsen dropped sweets on little parachutes for Berlin children. The “Little Vittles” operation showed how enemies from the World War became partners.
16464.m: Gail Halvorsen became famous as the “Candy Bomber” of the airlift.

16465.q: At which Berlin airport did the airlift planes mainly land?
16465.e: Tempelhof was in the American sector and was the centre of the airlift. Schönefeld, by contrast, was in the Soviet-controlled area.
16465.m: Tempelhof airport is closely linked with the airlift.

16466.q: Which longer-term consequence did the Berlin Blockade have for Germany?
a: It sped up the founding of two German states in 1949
It led to the immediate reunification of Germany
It ended the Allied occupation of Berlin
It caused the Soviet Union to leave the UN
16466.e: The Federal Republic of Germany was founded in May 1949, and the GDR in October 1949. The blockade had deepened the division and brought the West closer together.
16466.m: After the blockade, the Federal Republic and the GDR were created in 1949.

16467.q: When did the Korean War begin with North Korea's attack on South Korea?
16467.e: North Korean troops crossed the border to the south. The war became the first major hot conflict of the Cold War.
16467.m: The Korean War began in June 1950.

16468.q: Which line divided the Soviet and American occupation zones in Korea after the Second World War?
16468.e: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. Today's ceasefire line also runs close to it.
16468.m: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel.

16469.q: Why was the UN Security Council able to decide on military intervention in Korea in 1950?
a: Because the Soviet Union was boycotting the meetings and did not use its veto
Because the Soviet Union explicitly agreed to the mission
Because North Korea was a UN member and asked for help itself
Because the UN General Assembly outvoted the Security Council
16469.e: The Soviet Union stayed away from the Security Council in protest because China's seat was held by the government in Taiwan. So the resolutions were passed without a Soviet veto.
16469.m: The Soviet boycott made the UN mission in Korea possible in 1950.

16470.q: Which US general turned the course of the war with the landing at Inchon in September 1950?
16470.e: The landing behind the North Korean troops made the advance north possible. MacArthur commanded the UN troops.
16470.m: With the landing at Inchon in 1950, MacArthur turned the tide.

16471.q: Which state entered the war on the North Korean side at the end of October 1950 with so-called “volunteer units”?
a: The Soviet Union with regular ground troops
16471.e: When the UN troops approached the Chinese border, China sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers. As a result the war became a long war of position.
16471.m: China's entry into the war in 1950 prevented a victory for the UN troops.

16472.q: Why did US President Truman dismiss General MacArthur in April 1951?
a: Because MacArthur demanded extending the war to China and defied the government
Because MacArthur had refused the landing at Inchon
Because MacArthur had made a separate peace with North Korea
Because MacArthur ran for president against Truman
16472.e: MacArthur wanted to extend the war to China and also considered nuclear weapons. Truman removed him on 11 April 1951, confirming the priority of civilian leadership.
16472.m: Truman dismissed MacArthur to prevent a bigger war.

16473.q: When and where was the armistice in the Korean War signed?
16473.e: The armistice ended the fighting, but a peace treaty was never signed. Korea is still divided today.
16473.m: Since the armistice of 1953, Korea has been divided, but without a peace treaty.

16474.q: Which task has Switzerland carried out in Korea since 1953?
a: It is a member of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC) at Panmunjom
It provides the UN troops on the border with North Korea
It runs the demilitarised zone on its own
It represents North Korea at the UN
16474.e: The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission was created with the armistice agreement. Members of the Swiss armed forces are still stationed at Panmunjom today.
16474.m: Swiss officers have monitored the armistice in Korea since 1953.

16475.q: When did the GDR start building the Berlin Wall?
16475.e: In the night before 13 August 1961 the sector border was sealed off. Before that, hundreds of thousands had fled the GDR via Berlin.
16475.m: The Berlin Wall was built from 13 August 1961.

16476.q: Who said at a press conference on 15 June 1961: “No one has the intention of building a wall”?
16476.e: SED leader Walter Ulbricht made this statement just under two months before the Wall was built. The quotation is seen as an example of deliberate deception.
16476.m: Ulbricht denied plans for a wall shortly before the Wall was built.

16477.q: Which US President said “Ich bin ein Berliner” in West Berlin on 26 June 1963?
16477.e: Kennedy gave the speech in front of Schöneberg Town Hall. With it he confirmed the USA's solidarity with the enclosed city of West Berlin.
16477.m: In 1963 Kennedy's sentence “Ich bin ein Berliner” gave West Berlin support.

16478.q: Who demanded “Tear down this wall” at the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987?
16478.e: US President Reagan addressed the appeal to the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. Just over two years later, the Wall fell.
16478.m: In 1987 Reagan called on Gorbachev to tear down the Wall.

16479.q: Whose confusing statement at a press conference led to the opening of the Wall on the evening of 9 November 1989?
16479.e: SED Politburo member Schabowski announced that a new travel regulation applied “immediately, without delay”. Thousands then rushed to the border crossings.
16479.m: Schabowski's note and a misunderstanding opened the Wall in 1989.

16480.q: Which 18-year-old refugee bled to death after being shot in the death strip near Checkpoint Charlie on 17 August 1962?
16480.e: Fechter lay badly injured in the border strip for almost an hour without anyone helping him. His death caused great outrage in the West.
16480.m: Peter Fechter's death became a symbol of the brutality of the border regime.

16481.q: According to current research, at least how many deaths at the Berlin Wall are proven?
16481.e: The Centre for Contemporary History and the Berlin Wall Foundation count at least 140 deaths, including 101 people trying to escape. Other counts with a broader definition reach much higher figures.
16481.m: Well over a hundred people died at the Berlin Wall.

16482.q: Which discovery triggered the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962?
a: US spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites on Cuba
The Soviet Union set off an atomic bomb in the Caribbean
An American submarine was sunk off Cuba
16482.e: On 14 October 1962 a U-2 plane photographed launch sites for medium-range missiles. These could have reached large parts of the USA.
16482.m: Aerial photos of Soviet missiles on Cuba triggered the crisis in 1962.

16483.q: How did President Kennedy publicly respond to the missiles on Cuba on 22 October 1962?
a: He announced a naval blockade against Cuba, officially called a “quarantine”
He ordered an immediate invasion of Cuba
He declared war on the Soviet Union
He asked the UN to buy the missiles
16483.e: The blockade came into force on 24 October and was meant to stop further arms deliveries. The word “quarantine” was chosen because a blockade counts as an act of war under international law.
16483.m: In the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy relied on a naval blockade instead of an attack.

16484.q: When did Khrushchev announce the withdrawal of the Soviet missiles from Cuba?
16484.e: The announcement of 28 October 1962 ended the acute crisis. In those days the world was closer to nuclear war than ever before.
16484.m: The Cuban Missile Crisis ended after thirteen days on 28 October 1962.

16485.q: Which American concession was secretly agreed in the Cuban Missile Crisis?
a: The withdrawal of American Jupiter missiles from Turkey
The return of the Guantánamo base to Cuba
The withdrawal of US troops from West Berlin
16485.e: The USA also promised not to attack Cuba. The missiles were withdrawn from Turkey later and without publicity.
16485.m: In return for the withdrawal from Cuba, the USA secretly removed missiles from Turkey.

16486.q: What did the USA and the Soviet Union set up in 1963 as a lesson from the Cuban Missile Crisis?
a: A direct teleprinter link between Washington and Moscow, the “hotline”
A joint missile base on Cuba
A permanent military council at the UN
A demilitarised zone in the Caribbean
16486.e: The agreement of 20 June 1963 was meant to allow quick, direct communication in crises. In this way misunderstandings would no longer lead to nuclear war.
16486.m: Since 1963 the hotline has linked the leaders in Washington and Moscow.

16487.q: Which failed operation in April 1961 increased tensions between the USA and Cuba?
16487.e: Cuban exiles backed by the CIA tried to overthrow Fidel Castro and failed. Castro then sought even closer protection from the Soviet Union.
16487.m: The failed Bay of Pigs invasion drove Cuba closer to the Soviet Union.

16488.q: Who ruled Cuba at the time of the Cuban Missile Crisis?
16488.e: Castro had overthrown the dictator Batista in January 1959. He then leaned towards the Soviet Union.
16488.m: Fidel Castro led Cuba from the revolution of 1959.

16489.q: What role did Switzerland play during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
a: Its embassy in Havana represented the interests of the USA as protecting power
It negotiated the withdrawal of the missiles in Geneva
It provided troops for the naval blockade
It took Soviet missiles into safe keeping
16489.e: The USA had broken off diplomatic relations with Cuba. The Swiss embassy took over representing them and acted for the USA towards Cuba during the crisis.
16489.m: As protecting power, Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba.

16490.q: Along which parallel was Vietnam provisionally divided after the Geneva Conference on Indochina in 1954?
16490.e: The conference in Geneva set a ceasefire line and a demilitarised zone. Elections for the whole of Vietnam planned for 1956 never took place.
16490.m: The Geneva Conference of 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

16491.q: Which colonial power lost the Battle of Dien Bien Phu in 1954 and withdrew from Indochina?
16491.e: The defeat by the Viet Minh ended French rule in Indochina. After that the USA increasingly took France's place.
16491.m: After Dien Bien Phu, France left Indochina in 1954.

16492.q: What did the domino theory, which US governments used to justify intervening in Vietnam, say?
a: If one state falls to communism, its neighbours will follow like falling dominoes
Small states must join together in alliances
Every war in Asia automatically leads to a world war
Economic aid works better than military power
16492.e: President Eisenhower announced the image in 1954, and later US governments also referred to it. South Vietnam was therefore seen as a bulwark against the spread of communism in Southeast Asia.
16492.m: Out of fear of a domino effect, the USA intervened in Vietnam.

16493.q: Which event in August 1964 did the US government use to get Congress to grant it far-reaching war powers?
a: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu
16493.e: After a clash between North Vietnamese boats and the destroyer Maddox, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on 7 August 1964. A second reported attack later turned out not to have happened.
16493.m: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of 1964 opened the way to the big US war in Vietnam.

16494.q: What was the significance of the Tet Offensive of 1968 for the USA?
a: It shook the American public's belief in an early victory
It led to North Vietnam's unconditional surrender
It ended the war with a peace treaty
It was the first use of US ground troops
16494.e: Although the attackers suffered heavy military losses, the offensive showed that victory was not near. The anti-war movement gained strong momentum.
16494.m: In 1968 the Tet Offensive became the political turning point of the Vietnam War.

16495.q: What did the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 settle?
a: A ceasefire and the withdrawal of US troops from Vietnam
The reunification of Vietnam under South Vietnamese leadership
The division of Vietnam at the 17th parallel
16495.e: By 29 March 1973 the last US combat troops had left the country, and prisoners of war were released. But the fighting between North and South continued.
16495.m: With the Paris Peace Accords, the USA withdrew its troops from Vietnam in 1973.

16496.q: With which event did the Vietnam War end on 30 April 1975?
a: With the capture of Saigon by North Vietnamese troops
With the signing of a peace treaty in Geneva
With a referendum on Vietnamese unity
16496.e: The capture of the South Vietnamese capital meant the end of South Vietnam. In 1976 the country was united as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
16496.m: The fall of Saigon in 1975 ended the Vietnam War.

16497.q: What was “Agent Orange”, which the US army used in Vietnam?
a: A code name for a CIA secret agent
A radio code for air strikes
16497.e: The herbicide was used to strip forests of their leaves to reveal the enemy's hiding places and supply routes. The dioxin it contained caused serious and long-term damage to health.
16497.m: Agent Orange harmed people and nature in Vietnam for generations.

16498.q: What does the abbreviation MAD stand for in Cold War strategy?
a: Missile Attack Detection, early missile warning
16498.e: Each side could still destroy the other even after being attacked. This very certainty was meant to prevent a nuclear war.
16498.m: Mutual assured destruction deterred both superpowers from nuclear war.

16499.q: What is meant by second-strike capability?
a: The ability to strike back devastatingly even after an enemy nuclear attack
The ability to carry out a first strike twice in a row
An ally's right to attack second
The reserve of soldiers for a second war
16499.e: Submarines with nuclear missiles or hardened missile silos were meant to secure a counter-strike. This meant a first strike was not worth it for either side.
16499.m: Whoever can strike back will not be attacked: that was the logic of second-strike capability.

16500.q: Which treaties did Nixon and Brezhnev sign in Moscow on 26 May 1972?
a: SALT I and the ABM Treaty
The INF Treaty and START I
The Non-Proliferation Treaty and the Test Ban Treaty
The Paris Agreements and the Warsaw Treaty
16500.e: SALT I limited the number of strategic delivery systems, and the ABM Treaty limited missile defence. Multiple warheads, however, remained allowed.
16500.m: SALT I of 1972 was a first step towards limiting the nuclear arms race.

16501.q: Why did the SALT II Treaty, signed in Vienna in 1979, never formally come into force?
a: Because the US Senate did not ratify it after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
Because the Soviet Union cancelled it shortly after signing
Because Switzerland as host country objected
Because Great Britain and France blocked it
16501.e: Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT II on 18 June 1979. The invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 prevented ratification.
16501.m: The invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 brought down SALT II.

16502.q: What did NATO's Double-Track Decision of 1979 involve?
a: Stationing new intermediate-range weapons in Western Europe, combined with an offer of negotiations to the Soviet Union
Two states leaving NATO at the same time
Halving all nuclear weapons in Europe without conditions
Doubling the defence budget of all members
16502.e: NATO responded to Soviet SS-20 missiles with the threat to deploy Pershing II missiles and cruise missiles, while at the same time offering disarmament talks. The decision sparked large peace demonstrations.
16502.m: NATO's Double-Track Decision combined rearmament with an offer to negotiate.

16503.q: Which arms project did US President Reagan announce in 1983, which critics called “Star Wars”?
a: The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), a missile defence system in space
The Apollo programme for crewed flights to the Moon
16503.e: SDI was meant to make the USA invulnerable to Soviet nuclear missiles with defence systems. The project intensified the arms race and put the Soviet Union under economic pressure.
16503.m: Reagan's SDI programme was meant to intercept nuclear missiles while still in space.

16504.q: What was agreed in the INF Treaty of 8 December 1987?
a: The abolition of land-based nuclear missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 km
A complete ban on all nuclear weapons
Limiting nuclear submarines to ten each
A ban on missiles in space
16504.e: Reagan and Gorbachev signed the treaty in Washington. For the first time, a whole category of weapons was abolished.
16504.m: The INF Treaty of 1987 was the first to abolish a whole group of nuclear weapons.

16505.q: What did the term “missile gap” refer to at the end of the 1950s?
a: A feared, but in fact overestimated, Soviet superiority in missiles
A gap in NATO's defence belt in Norway
A lack of fuel for Soviet missiles
The time between the launch and impact of a missile
16505.e: After the Sputnik launch, the USA feared it was falling behind technologically. But the CIA had overestimated Soviet missile armament; the fear still drove the arms race.
16505.m: The supposed missile gap fuelled the arms race, even though it was overestimated.

16506.q: When did the Soviet Union set off its first atomic bomb, ending the USA's nuclear monopoly?
16506.e: The test came earlier than the West had expected. From then on both superpowers had nuclear weapons, which sped up the arms race.
16506.m: From 1949 the Soviet Union also had the atomic bomb.

16507.q: How did the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 differ?
a: The Hiroshima bomb used uranium, the Nagasaki bomb plutonium
The Hiroshima bomb was a hydrogen bomb, the Nagasaki bomb was not
The Nagasaki bomb was fired from a submarine
The Hiroshima bomb came from Great Britain, the Nagasaki bomb from the USA
16507.e: “Little Boy” over Hiroshima was a uranium bomb, “Fat Man” over Nagasaki a plutonium bomb. In Hiroshima an estimated 70,000 to 80,000 people died immediately, and many more from the after-effects.
16507.m: Hiroshima was destroyed by a uranium bomb, Nagasaki by a plutonium bomb.

16508.q: How does a hydrogen bomb basically differ from the Hiroshima bomb?
a: It uses nuclear fusion and is much more powerful
It works entirely without a nuclear reaction
It is weaker but more accurate
16508.e: The Hiroshima bomb was based on nuclear fission. Hydrogen bombs also fuse atomic nuclei and reach many times the explosive power; the USA tested the first in 1952.
16508.m: Hydrogen bombs are based on nuclear fusion and are much more powerful.

16509.q: What was the explosive power of the Soviet “Tsar Bomba”, set off on 30 October 1961?
16509.e: The Tsar Bomba was set off over the Novaya Zemlya islands. Soviet figures give 50 megatons, US estimates about 57; it is the most powerful nuclear weapon ever detonated.
16509.m: The Tsar Bomba of 1961 was the most powerful bomb of all time.

16510.q: Which state set off its first atomic bomb on 16 October 1964?
16510.e: China tested the bomb at Lop Nur. Great Britain had already tested in 1952, and France in 1960.
16510.m: In 1964 China became the fifth nuclear power.

16511.q: What did the Partial Test Ban Treaty, signed in August 1963, prohibit?
a: Nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water
All nuclear tests including underground tests
16511.e: The USA, the Soviet Union and Great Britain signed the treaty after the Cuban Missile Crisis. Underground tests remained allowed.
16511.m: Since the Test Ban Treaty of 1963, the great powers tested their bombs underground.

16512.q: What is the aim of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, signed on 1 July 1968?
a: To prevent nuclear weapons spreading to more states
To destroy all nuclear weapons by 1970
To ban nuclear power stations worldwide
To spread the superpowers' nuclear weapons evenly across Europe
16512.e: States without nuclear weapons commit themselves not to acquire any; the nuclear powers are supposed to disarm. The treaty came into force on 5 March 1970.
16512.m: The Non-Proliferation Treaty is meant to stop more and more states getting the bomb.

16513.q: What is true of Switzerland and nuclear weapons in the Cold War?
a: It looked into nuclear weapons of its own but finally gave up the programme in 1988
From 1965 it had its own operational atomic bombs
It stored American nuclear weapons in the Alps
It carried out its own nuclear test in 1964
16513.e: From 1945 the Confederation had nuclear armament examined; popular initiatives against nuclear weapons failed at the ballot box in 1962 and 1963. In 1969 Switzerland signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and in 1988 the last responsible body was dissolved.
16513.m: Switzerland considered nuclear weapons of its own but never built a bomb.

16514.q: When did the Soviet Union launch the first artificial Earth satellite, Sputnik 1?
16514.e: Sputnik 1 was launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome. This began the space age.
16514.m: On 4 October 1957, Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth.

16515.e: The sphere weighed 83.6 kg, had a diameter of 58 cm and sent out radio signals. After about 92 days it burned up in the atmosphere.
16515.m: Sputnik 1 was a beeping metal ball of just over 80 kilograms.

16516.q: What does the term “Sputnik shock” refer to?
a: The dismay in the West at the Soviet Union's technological lead
An accident during the launch of Sputnik 1
Panic in the Soviet Union about American satellites
A power cut caused by the satellite's radio signals
16516.e: The West had believed it was clearly superior technologically. The Soviet Union's success led to calls for more education and research.
16516.m: The Sputnik shock showed the West that the Soviet Union had caught up technologically.

16517.q: Why was the launch of Sputnik 1 also worrying in military terms?
a: The rocket showed that the Soviet Union could carry nuclear warheads as far as the USA
Sputnik 1 itself carried an atomic bomb
The satellite could shoot down American aircraft
The satellite jammed all Western radio stations
16517.e: The R-7 rocket that took Sputnik into space had been developed as an intercontinental missile. For the first time, the USA felt directly vulnerable.
16517.m: Whoever could launch satellites into space could also carry nuclear weapons across continents.

16518.q: Which agency did the USA found in 1958 in response to the Sputnik shock?
16518.e: The law founding NASA was signed on 29 July 1958, and it began work on 1 October 1958. It brought together the USA's civilian space programme.
16518.m: NASA was created in 1958 as a response to Sputnik.

16519.q: Which living creature did the Soviet Union put into Earth orbit with Sputnik 2 on 3 November 1957?
16519.e: Laika was the first animal in Earth orbit. She died a few hours after launch from overheating and stress.
16519.m: In 1957 the dog Laika was the first animal to orbit the Earth, but she did not survive the flight.

16520.q: Which further triumph did the Soviet Union celebrate in the space race on 12 April 1961?
a: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space
The first landing of a probe on Mars
The first spacewalk by a woman
The first crewed flight around the Moon
16520.e: Gagarin orbited the Earth once in Vostok 1, and the flight lasted about 108 minutes. The USA was behind once again.
16520.m: In 1961 Yuri Gagarin was the first human in space.

16521.q: Which goal did President Kennedy announce to Congress on 25 May 1961?
a: Landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out
Building a space station on Mars by 1965
Launching the first satellite before the Soviet Union
Flying to the Moon together with the Soviet Union
16521.e: In doing so, Kennedy was also reacting to Gagarin's flight and the Sputnik shock. In 1962 he confirmed the goal in a speech at Rice University.
16521.m: In 1961 Kennedy made the Moon landing a national goal of the USA.

16522.q: When did the Apollo 11 lunar module land on the Moon?
16522.e: Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969 and landed on the Moon on 20 July. On 24 July the capsule splashed down in the Pacific.
16522.m: On 20 July 1969, humans landed on the Moon for the first time.

16523.q: Which Apollo 11 crew member did not walk on the Moon but stayed in the command module in lunar orbit?
16523.e: Collins flew the command module “Columbia”. Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the lunar module and walked on the surface.
16523.m: Michael Collins waited in orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon.

16524.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module?
16524.e: After landing, Armstrong reported “The Eagle has landed”. Columbia was the name of the command module.
16524.m: The lunar module Eagle took Armstrong and Aldrin to the Moon.

16525.q: In which area of the Moon did Apollo 11 land?
a: In the Sea of Tranquillity (Mare Tranquillitatis)
In the Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum)
16525.e: The landing site was a fairly flat plain that was considered safe. The Moon's “seas” are dark basalt plains, not water.
16525.m: Apollo 11 landed in the Sea of Tranquillity.

16526.q: Which Swiss experiment did the Apollo 11 astronauts set up on the Moon?
a: A solar wind sail from the University of Bern
A Swiss watch for measuring time on the Moon
A Swiss flag made of aluminium
16526.e: The solar wind sail caught particles of the solar wind and was then brought back to Earth, where it was analysed in Bern.
16526.m: With the Bern solar wind sail, Swiss research was part of the first Moon landing.

16527.q: What was the significance of the Moon landing in the Cold War space race?
a: The USA overtook the Soviet Union, which never managed a crewed Moon landing
The Soviet Union had already put people on the Moon before
It ended the Cold War at once
It was a joint project of both superpowers
16527.e: After Sputnik and Gagarin, the Soviet Union had been ahead for a long time. With Apollo 11, the USA reached the most prestigious goal first.
16527.m: With the Moon landing, the USA won the race to the Moon.

16528.q: What consequence did the great uprising of 1857 in India have for British rule?
a: The British Crown took over rule from the East India Company
Great Britain withdrew completely from India
India immediately got an elected parliament
The East India Company received even more rights
16528.e: After the uprising of 1857 to 1859, the East India Company lost its power. From 1858 the British Crown ruled India directly (British India, the “Raj”).
16528.m: After 1857 the British Crown ruled India directly.

16529.q: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded in Bombay?
16529.e: The Indian National Congress was founded in Bombay in 1885 with 72 delegates, prompted by the Briton Allan Octavian Hume. It became the most important party of the independence movement.
16529.m: The Indian National Congress was founded in Bombay in 1885.

16530.q: What did the “Swadeshi” movement, which arose after the partition of Bengal in 1905, mean?
a: Boycotting British goods in favour of local products
Emigration of Indian workers to Africa
16530.e: When Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, many Indians responded with Swadeshi, buying their own goods and boycotting British products. The partition was reversed in 1911.
16530.m: Swadeshi relied on home-made products instead of British goods.

16531.q: What was the aim of the All-India Muslim League, founded in 1906?
a: To represent the interests of Muslims in British India
To make Hinduism the state religion
16531.e: Many Muslims feared being dominated by the Hindu majority in an independent India. Under Jinnah, the Muslim League later demanded a separate state.
16531.m: The Muslim League represented Muslims and later demanded Pakistan.

16532.q: What happened in the Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919?
a: British troops fired on an unarmed crowd
Gandhi began his first hunger strike
The Muslim League demanded a separate state
16532.e: Troops under General Dyer fired on a gathering; according to the official British count 379 people died, other estimates are higher. The massacre radicalised the independence movement.
16532.m: The Amritsar massacre of 1919 drove many Indians into resistance.

16533.q: Why did the Rowlatt Act of 1919 cause major protests in India?
a: It introduced a new salt tax
It divided India into two states
16533.e: The Rowlatt Act extended emergency powers from the First World War, including detention without trial. The protests against it also led to the gathering in Amritsar.
16533.m: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial.

16534.q: Why did the Indian independence movement boycott the Simon Commission in 1928?
a: Because not a single Indian was a member
Because it was led by the Muslim League
Because it met in South Africa
16534.e: The Simon Commission was meant to review India's constitution but consisted only of British members of parliament. Many Indians felt this was humiliating.
16534.m: The Simon Commission was boycotted because no Indians took part.

16535.q: What did the Congress demand with the goal of “Purna Swaraj” from 1929/30?
a: Division into a Hindu and a Muslim state
The return of the Mughal rulers
16535.e: At its session in Lahore in 1929, the Congress adopted the goal of complete self-rule. 26 January 1930 was marked as Purna Swaraj Day.

16536.q: Why did the Congress governments in the Indian provinces resign in 1939?
a: The Viceroy declared India a party to the war without consulting them
Gandhi demanded that the Congress be dissolved
The Muslim League won all the elections
16536.e: In 1939 Viceroy Linlithgow declared India’s entry into the Second World War without asking elected representatives. In protest, the Congress ministers resigned from office.
16536.m: In 1939 the Congress protested with resignations against entering the war without having a say.

16537.q: What did the Muslim League demand in the Lahore Resolution of 1940?
a: Separate states for areas with a Muslim majority
A united India under Hindu leadership
India remaining in the British Empire
The return of Bengal to Great Britain
16537.e: Under Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the Muslim League demanded independent states for Muslims in 1940. This developed into the demand for Pakistan.
16537.m: The Lahore Resolution of 1940 was a step towards the founding of Pakistan.

16538.q: When did the “Quit India” movement, which demanded the immediate withdrawal of the British, begin?
16538.e: On 8 August 1942 the Congress launched the Quit India movement. Almost the entire Congress leadership, including Gandhi, was then arrested; Gandhi was only released in May 1944 for health reasons.
16538.m: With “Quit India” the Congress demanded the withdrawal of the British in 1942.

16539.q: Which Indian politician fought alongside Japan against Great Britain in the Second World War with the Indian National Army?
16539.e: Unlike Gandhi, Subhas Chandra Bose relied on military struggle. His Indian National Army surrendered in 1945; Bose died in August 1945 after a plane crash.
16539.m: Subhas Chandra Bose also sought independence by force of arms.

16540.q: Which last British Viceroy presented the plan to partition British India in 1947?
16540.e: The Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 provided for two dominions, India and Pakistan. It was agreed with Nehru and Jinnah.
16540.m: The Mountbatten Plan of 1947 divided British India into two states.

a: The 1947 border between India and Pakistan
A British railway line across India
The border between India and China
16541.e: In 1947 the London lawyer Cyril Radcliffe drew the border between India and Pakistan in a short time. Many people suddenly found themselves on the “wrong” side.
16541.m: The Radcliffe Line separated India and Pakistan in 1947.

16542.q: Which law passed by the British Parliament in July 1947 confirmed partition and independence?
16542.e: The Indian Independence Act was passed on 18 July 1947. It created the two independent dominions of India and Pakistan.
16542.m: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 ended British rule in India.

16543.q: Why do India and Pakistan celebrate their independence on different days?
a: Pakistan celebrates on 14 August, India on 15 August 1947
Both celebrate the day of their constitution
16543.e: The transfer of power took place at midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947. Pakistan marks the 14th, India the 15th of August as Independence Day.
16543.m: India and Pakistan became independent in August 1947.

16544.q: Roughly how many people left their homes as a result of the 1947 partition?
16544.e: Around 14.5 million people crossed the new borders, and some estimates suggest even more were displaced. Estimates say between 200,000 and two million people died in the violence.
16544.m: The partition of India caused one of the largest refugee movements of the 20th century.

16545.q: Which region triggered the first war between India and Pakistan as early as 1947?
16545.e: Kashmir had a Muslim majority but a Hindu ruler. The dispute over which country it belonged to led to war in 1947 and is still unresolved today.
16545.m: The Kashmir conflict began as early as 1947.

16546.q: Which present-day country emerged from East Pakistan in 1971?
16546.e: From 1947 Pakistan consisted of two parts of the country far apart from each other. East Pakistan won its independence as Bangladesh in 1971.

16547.q: Who became the first Prime Minister of independent India in 1947?
16547.e: Jawaharlal Nehru led India as Prime Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964. Gandhi never held a government office.
16547.m: Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister of India.

16548.q: Which international day is marked every year on 2 October, Gandhi’s birthday?
16548.e: Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar in what is now Gujarat. The UN declared his birthday the International Day of Non-Violence.
16548.m: Gandhi’s birthday is the International Day of Non-Violence.

16549.q: What did Gandhi study in London from 1888?
16549.e: Gandhi studied law at the Inner Temple in London and was called to the bar as a barrister in 1891. He later used this knowledge in his political struggle.

16550.q: Which experience in Pietermaritzburg in 1893 is seen as a turning point in Gandhi’s life?
a: He was thrown out of a train compartment because of the colour of his skin
He was arrested for the first time
16550.e: On the journey from Durban to Pretoria, Gandhi was put off the train in Pietermaritzburg. The experience of racism made him decide to stand up for the rights of Indians in South Africa.
16550.m: The humiliation on the train turned Gandhi into a civil rights campaigner.

16551.q: Roughly how long did Gandhi live and work in South Africa?
16551.e: Gandhi came to Durban in 1893 and left South Africa in July 1914. There he developed his method of non-violent resistance.
16551.m: Gandhi developed his methods over more than 20 years in South Africa.

16552.q: What does the term “Satyagraha”, coined by Gandhi, roughly mean?
16552.e: Satyagraha combines the Sanskrit words for truth and holding firmly. Gandhi used it to describe the non-violent resistance he developed in South Africa from 1906.
16552.m: Satyagraha is non-violent resistance drawing on the power of truth.

16553.q: What was Gandhi’s first big Satyagraha campaign in the Transvaal from 1906 directed against?
a: A law requiring Indians to register
16553.e: The registration rules in the Transvaal (1906 and 1907) required Indians to register and give fingerprints. Gandhi called for non-violent disobedience against them.
16553.m: Gandhi’s first big Satyagraha was directed against a discriminatory registration law.

16554.q: Why did Gandhi found the newspaper “Indian Opinion” in South Africa in 1903?
a: To spread his ideas among Indians in South Africa
To recruit soldiers for the British army
16554.e: From the end of 1904 “Indian Opinion” was printed at the Phoenix Settlement near Durban. It spread Gandhi’s ideas among Indians in South Africa.
16554.m: With Indian Opinion, Gandhi spread his ideas in South Africa.

16555.q: After which Russian writer did Gandhi name a community settlement in South Africa in 1910?
16555.e: In 1910 the architect Hermann Kallenbach provided land on which Tolstoy Farm was built. Gandhi corresponded with Tolstoy and valued his ideas on non-violence.
16555.m: Tolstoy Farm shows Gandhi’s connection to Leo Tolstoy.

16556.q: What did Gandhi criticise in his 1909 work “Hind Swaraj”?
a: Modern Western civilisation with its industry and materialism
The teachings of the writer Tolstoy
16556.e: In “Hind Swaraj” (Indian Home Rule), written on a sea voyage in 1909, Gandhi set down his idea of a free India. In it he criticised industrialisation and materialism.
16556.m: In Hind Swaraj, Gandhi described his vision of self-rule.

16557.q: What does the honorary title “Mahatma” mean?
16557.e: Mahatma comes from Sanskrit and means “great soul”. He was given the title from about 1914; it is often credited to the poet Rabindranath Tagore, but this is not certain.

16558.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
a: Because demonstrators killed policemen in Chauri Chaura
Because the Muslim League took over the movement
16558.e: In Chauri Chaura demonstrators set fire to a police station and policemen were killed. For Gandhi, violence went against the principle of the movement, so he stopped it.
16558.m: Gandhi stopped non-cooperation because it had turned violent.

16559.q: What was Gandhi protesting against with the Salt March of 1930?
a: The British salt monopoly and the salt tax
16559.e: Only the colonial administration was allowed to produce and tax salt. By making salt himself by the sea, Gandhi broke the law symbolically and without violence.
16559.m: The Salt March was civil disobedience against the salt tax.

16560.q: Where did the Salt March, which Gandhi began on 12 March 1930, lead?
a: From the Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on the Arabian Sea
From Calcutta to the Bay of Bengal
16560.e: Gandhi walked with 78 companions about 385 km from the Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad to Dandi, which he reached in April. Thousands joined along the way.
16560.m: The Salt March of 1930 covered about 385 km to Dandi.

16561.q: Which conference in London did Gandhi attend in 1931 as the representative of the National Congress?
16561.e: The Round Table Conferences were meant to discuss India’s constitution. After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Gandhi attended the second one in 1931, but it brought no breakthrough.
16561.m: In 1931 Gandhi negotiated in London at the Round Table Conference.

16562.q: Which French writer and biographer of Gandhi did Gandhi visit in Switzerland in 1931?
16562.e: Romain Rolland lived in Villeneuve on Lake Geneva and had published a book about Gandhi in the mid-1920s. Gandhi met him in 1931 on his way back from London.
16562.m: In 1931 Gandhi visited Romain Rolland on Lake Geneva.

16563.q: Who assassinated Gandhi in Delhi on 30 January 1948?
a: A supporter of the Muslim League
16563.e: Nathuram Godse was a member of the Hindu Mahasabha and accused Gandhi of being too soft on Muslims and Pakistan. He was executed in 1949.
16563.m: Gandhi was shot by a Hindu nationalist in 1948.

16564.q: What does the term “Ahimsa”, central to Gandhi’s thinking, mean?
16564.e: Ahimsa is a principle from Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism. Gandhi made it the basis of his political struggle.
16564.m: Ahimsa means doing no violence to any living being.

16565.q: What did the spinning wheel, which Gandhi made a symbol of the movement, stand for?
16565.e: Gandhi called on people to wear home-spun cloth (khadi) instead of British factory goods. The spinning wheel thus became a sign of swadeshi and self-determination.
16565.m: The spinning wheel symbolised India’s economic independence.

16566.q: Which American civil rights leader was strongly influenced by Gandhi’s non-violent resistance?
16566.e: Martin Luther King studied Gandhi’s methods and travelled to India in 1959. He applied non-violent resistance to the civil rights movement in the USA.
16566.m: Gandhi’s non-violence also shaped Martin Luther King.

16567.q: What was unusual by today’s standards about Gandhi’s marriage in 1883?
a: He married against his parents’ wishes
16567.e: In May 1883, at the age of 13, Gandhi was married to 14-year-old Kasturba, as was usual at the time. Kasturba supported his struggle and died in British custody in 1944.
16567.m: Gandhi was married to Kasturba when he was only 13.

16568.q: What was decided at the Berlin Conference of 1884/85?
a: Rules for dividing Africa among European powers
The independence of the African colonies
The ban on slavery in America
The founding of the League of Nations
16568.e: Chaired by Bismarck, European states agreed on their claims in Africa without involving Africans. Many arbitrary borders from that time still exist today.
16568.m: At the Berlin Conference, Europeans divided up Africa without Africans.

16569.q: Which congress in Manchester demanded an end to colonialism in 1945?
16569.e: W. E. B. Du Bois, George Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah, among others, took part in the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester. It is seen as an important push towards decolonisation.
16569.m: The Pan-African Congress of 1945 demanded freedom for Africa.

16570.q: Which colony is considered the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to become independent, in 1957?
16570.e: On 6 March 1957 the British colony of the Gold Coast became independent as Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah. Sudan (1956) is usually counted as part of North Africa. Ghana’s example encouraged many other colonies.
16570.m: In 1957 Ghana led the way to independence south of the Sahara.

16571.q: What idea did Kwame Nkrumah express with the term “neo-colonialism”?
a: Even after independence, Africa remained economically dependent
Africa should found new colonies in Asia
16571.e: In his 1965 book Nkrumah argued that foreign companies continued to exploit the raw materials. Formal independence did not yet mean real freedom.
16571.m: Neo-colonialism means economic dependence despite formal independence.

16572.q: Which French colony was the only one to vote against remaining in the French Community in 1958?
16572.e: Under Sékou Touré, Guinea rejected the French Community in the referendum of 28 September 1958. It became independent immediately on 2 October 1958, and France withdrew abruptly.
16572.m: In 1958 Guinea was the only colony to say no to France.

16573.q: Why is 1960 called the “Year of Africa”?
a: Because the African Union was founded
Because the Olympic Games took place in Africa
16573.e: In 1960 alone 17 colonies became independent, including Nigeria, Congo and Somalia as well as many French colonies. Colonialism in Africa collapsed on a large scale.
16573.m: In the Year of Africa, 1960, 17 states became independent.

16574.q: What did British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan announce in February 1960 with his “Wind of Change” speech in South Africa?
a: That Great Britain recognised African nationalism
That Great Britain wanted to acquire new colonies
That South Africa would be expelled from the Commonwealth
16574.e: Macmillan spoke of a “wind of change” blowing through Africa. Afterwards Great Britain quickly pushed ahead with granting independence to its colonies.
16574.m: Macmillan’s 1960 speech stood for Britain’s rapid withdrawal from Africa.

16575.q: From which colonial power did Congo become independent on 30 June 1960?
16575.e: The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960. Soon afterwards mutinies and breakaways such as that of Katanga led to the Congo Crisis.
16575.m: Congo became independent from Belgium in 1960.

16576.q: What fate befell Patrice Lumumba, the first Prime Minister of Congo?
a: He was murdered in Katanga in January 1961
He ruled until his death in 1997
