He fled into exile in Belgium
He became Secretary-General of the UN
16576.e: Lumumba was removed from office in September 1960, captured and executed in Katanga in January 1961. In 2002 Belgium apologised for its share of the responsibility.
16576.m: Lumumba became a symbol of the anti-colonial struggle.

16577.q: Which movement led the war of independence in Algeria from 1954 to 1962?
16577.e: The FLN fought against France, which regarded Algeria as part of its own territory. The war was marked by great brutality on both sides.
16577.m: In the Algerian War the FLN fought against France.

16578.q: What role did Switzerland play in the Évian Accords of 1962?
a: It mediated and organised secret preliminary talks
16578.e: At the request of the Algerian side, the Swiss diplomat Olivier Long mediated from 1961. The Algerian delegation stayed in the canton of Vaud and was flown to Évian in army helicopters.
16578.m: In 1961/62 Switzerland helped make the negotiations on Algeria possible.

16579.q: On which day did Algeria declare its independence from France?
16579.e: After the Évian ceasefire (March 1962), more than 99 percent of Algerians voted for independence on 1 July. It was declared on 5 July 1962.

16580.q: In which British colony did the Mau Mau movement fight in the 1950s?
16580.e: The Mau Mau uprising was mainly directed against the seizure of land by white settlers. The British crushed it harshly; Kenya became independent in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta.
16580.m: The Mau Mau uprising paved Kenya’s way to independence in 1963.

16581.q: Which politician led Tanganyika to independence in 1961?
16581.e: Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 under Julius Nyerere. After uniting with Zanzibar, Tanzania was formed in 1964.
16581.m: Julius Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence in 1961.

16582.q: Where was the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) founded in 1963?
16582.e: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963. It supported the liberation movements and was replaced by the African Union in 2002.
16582.m: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963.

16583.q: What happened in the British colony of Rhodesia in 1965?
a: The white minority declared independence unilaterally
The black majority took power peacefully
The colony was handed over to Portugal
16583.e: Under Ian Smith, the white minority government declared independence unilaterally in 1965 to prevent majority rule. Only in 1980, after a civil war, did independent Zimbabwe come into being.
16583.m: After a long struggle, Rhodesia became Zimbabwe in 1980.

16584.q: Which event in Europe made the independence of Angola and Mozambique possible in 1975?
a: The Carnation Revolution in Portugal in 1974
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The end of the Spanish Civil War
16584.e: In 1974 the Carnation Revolution overthrew the dictatorship in Portugal, which had fought long colonial wars. The new government granted the colonies independence in 1975.
16584.m: The Carnation Revolution ended Portugal’s colonial empire in Africa.

16585.q: From which state did Namibia become independent in 1990?
16585.e: The former German South West Africa was administered by South Africa after the First World War. Namibia only gained independence in 1990.
16585.m: Namibia became independent from South Africa in 1990.

16586.q: Which African state became independent most recently, in 2011?
16586.e: South Sudan broke away from Sudan in 2011 after a referendum. Eritrea had already become independent from Ethiopia in 1993.
16586.m: Since 2011 South Sudan has been Africa’s youngest state.

16587.q: Which three North African countries became independent in 1956?
16587.e: Sudan became independent on 1 January, Morocco in March and Tunisia on 20 March 1956. Algeria, on the other hand, had to keep fighting until 1962.
16587.m: In 1956 Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia became independent.

16588.q: What does the Afrikaans word “apartheid” literally mean?
16588.e: In Afrikaans apartheid means roughly “separateness” or “segregation”. The word refers to the state-imposed racial segregation in South Africa.

16589.q: Which party began the systematic policy of apartheid after its election victory in 1948?
a: The National Party under Daniel François Malan
The United Party under Jan Smuts
The Communist Party of South Africa
16589.e: The National Party won the majority of seats in 1948, even though its opponents had more votes. Prime Minister Malan extended racial segregation by law.
16589.m: Apartheid began with the National Party’s election victory in 1948.

16590.q: What did the first apartheid law of 1949 ban?
16590.e: The Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act of 1949 banned mixed marriages. In 1950 a ban on relationships between the groups followed.
16590.m: The first apartheid law of 1949 banned mixed marriages.

16591.q: Which law of 1950 officially assigned every person in South Africa to a “race”?
16591.e: Under the Population Registration Act, every person was registered as “white”, “coloured”, “Indian” or “black”. This classification was the basis of all further apartheid laws.
16591.m: The Population Registration Act was the foundation of apartheid.

16592.q: What did the Group Areas Act of 1950 regulate?
a: Separate residential areas for each population group
16592.e: The law assigned separate residential areas to the population groups. Many non-white people were driven out of city districts, for example from Sophiatown in Johannesburg from 1955.
16592.m: The Group Areas Act separated residential areas by skin colour.

16593.q: What was the aim of the Bantu Education Act of 1953?
a: State-controlled, inferior schooling for black people
Teaching in English for all children
Abolishing compulsory schooling for white people
16593.e: Bantu education was meant to prepare black people only for simple work. The ANC then called for a school boycott.
16593.m: Bantu education was designed to put black people at a disadvantage.

16594.q: What happened in Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
a: Police shot dead 69 people at a protest against the pass laws
Pupils protested against Afrikaans as the language of teaching
16594.e: In the Sharpeville massacre the police fired on demonstrators and 69 people died. Afterwards the government banned the ANC and the PAC.
16594.m: After Sharpeville in 1960 the ANC and PAC were banned.

16595.q: What was the purpose of the pass laws in the apartheid state?
a: They controlled where black people could stay and work
They regulated travel abroad for everyone
They set the taxes for white people
They allowed black people to move freely into the cities
16595.e: Black people had to carry a pass book; without permission they could only stay briefly in “white” cities. In 1956 around 20,000 women marched in Pretoria against the pass laws.
16595.m: The pass laws severely restricted black people’s freedom of movement.

16596.q: Which politician is considered the “architect of apartheid” and was stabbed to death in parliament in 1966?
16596.e: As a minister and, from 1958, as Prime Minister, Hendrik Verwoerd shaped the homeland policy. He was murdered on 6 September 1966.
16596.m: Hendrik Verwoerd shaped apartheid like no one else.

16597.q: What was the aim of the homeland policy (Bantustans)?
a: To take South African citizenship away from black people
To give black people the best land
To unite the colony with Namibia
To resettle white people in reserves
16597.e: Black people were to become citizens of small, dependent “homelands”. Four of them, such as the Transkei in 1976, became nominally independent but were not recognised internationally; in the course of apartheid around 3.5 million people in total were forcibly resettled.
16597.m: The homelands were meant to make black people foreigners in their own country.

16598.q: What were pupils protesting against in the Soweto uprising on 16 June 1976?
a: Afrikaans as the language of teaching
16598.e: The government wanted to impose Afrikaans as the language of teaching. The police fired on the young people; officially 23 died, though the figure 176 is often given.
16598.m: The Soweto uprising of 1976 was a protest by school pupils.

16599.q: Which member of the “Black Consciousness Movement” died in 1977 as a result of ill-treatment in police custody?
16599.e: Steve Biko was arrested in August 1977 and died in custody after severe ill-treatment. His death caused outrage around the world.
16599.m: Steve Biko’s death made the brutality of the regime known worldwide.

16600.q: Since when was South Africa excluded from the Olympic Games because of apartheid?
16600.e: The International Olympic Committee excluded South Africa from the 1964 Games in Tokyo. The country was only allowed to take part again in 1992.
16600.m: The sports boycott isolated South Africa from 1964.

16601.q: Who was not represented in the Tricameral Parliament of 1984?
a: The black majority of the population
16601.e: The Tricameral Parliament had one chamber each for white, “coloured” and Indian people. The black majority remained excluded, which led to new unrest.
16601.m: The Tricameral Parliament continued to exclude the black majority.

16602.q: How did Switzerland respond to the economic sanctions imposed on South Africa by the USA, the EC and Japan in 1986?
a: It did not join the sanctions
It adopted the sanctions in full
16602.e: According to the National Research Programme NRP 42+ (final report 2005), Switzerland did not adopt the sanctions. Swiss companies also frequently got around the UN arms embargo.
16602.m: Switzerland did not take part in the 1986 sanctions.

16603.q: What did President Frederik Willem de Klerk announce on 2 February 1990?
a: The lifting of the ban on the ANC and other organisations
16603.e: In his speech to parliament, de Klerk legalised the ANC and other banned parties. A few days later Nelson Mandela was released.
16603.m: De Klerk’s 1990 speech marked the beginning of the end of apartheid.

16604.q: How did white voters vote in the referendum of 17 March 1992?
a: A good two thirds voted to continue the reforms
Almost all voted to keep apartheid
16604.e: Only white people were allowed to vote. More than two thirds supported the negotiations to end apartheid.
16604.m: In 1992 most white South Africans voted for reforms.

16605.q: What was special about the elections in South Africa in April 1994?
a: For the first time all adults could vote, regardless of skin colour
For the first time women could vote
They were the first elections after independence from Great Britain
Only the homelands were allowed to vote
16605.e: The elections in April 1994 were the first without racial barriers. The ANC won and Nelson Mandela became President.
16605.m: In 1994 South Africa held its first free elections for everyone.

16606.q: Under what condition could perpetrators receive amnesty from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
a: If they fully disclosed a politically motivated act
If they paid a large fine
If they emigrated from South Africa
If they were members of the ANC
16606.e: The commission under Archbishop Desmond Tutu began its work in 1996. Amnesty was only granted for politically motivated, proportionate acts and in return for the whole truth.
16606.m: The Truth Commission exchanged amnesty for the whole truth.

16607.q: When did South Africa leave the Commonwealth and become a republic?
16607.e: On 31 May 1961 South Africa became a republic and left the Commonwealth. Criticism of apartheid by other members played an important part in this.
16607.m: South Africa became a republic in 1961 and left the Commonwealth.

16608.q: What was Nelson Mandela’s profession before his long imprisonment?
16608.e: Mandela studied law and opened a law firm in Johannesburg with Oliver Tambo. It helped many black people who suffered under the apartheid laws.
16608.m: Mandela worked as a lawyer before he was arrested.

16609.q: What does the term “apartheid”, which Mandela fought against, refer to?
a: The state-imposed racial segregation in South Africa
South Africa’s independence from Great Britain
The distribution of land to black farmers
16609.e: In Afrikaans apartheid means roughly “separateness”. From 1948 the state separated people by skin colour and disadvantaged the black majority.
16609.m: Apartheid was state racial segregation in South Africa.

16610.q: What does “Madiba”, as Mandela is often called in South Africa, mean?
a: It is his underground code name
It is an honorary title from the UN
It is the name of his birthplace
16610.e: Madiba is the name of his clan. In South Africa it is used as a respectful form of address.

16611.q: Which organisation did Mandela help to found in 1944?
16611.e: In 1944 Mandela joined the ANC and helped found the ANC Youth League. It called for a more determined struggle against racial discrimination.
16611.m: Mandela co-founded the ANC Youth League in 1944.

16612.q: With whom did Mandela run South Africa’s only African-run law firm at the time in Johannesburg in the 1950s?
16612.e: The firm “Mandela & Tambo” helped many black people who suffered under the apartheid laws. Oliver Tambo later led the ANC in exile.
16612.m: Mandela and Tambo ran a pioneering law firm together.

16613.q: How did the South African government react in 1960 to the Sharpeville massacre and the protests that followed?
a: It introduced free elections for everyone
16613.e: After the Sharpeville massacre the government banned the ANC in 1960. Mandela then abandoned the purely non-violent approach.
16613.m: After Sharpeville the ANC was banned in 1960.

16614.q: What was “Umkhonto we Sizwe”, which Mandela led from 1961?
a: The armed wing of the ANC
A youth newspaper of the ANC
The police force of the homelands
16614.e: After the ANC was banned in 1960, Mandela gave up the purely non-violent approach. “Spear of the Nation” carried out acts of sabotage from December 1961.
16614.m: Umkhonto we Sizwe was the armed wing of the ANC.

16615.q: What sentence did Mandela receive at the Rivonia Trial in 1964?
16615.e: On 12 June 1964 Mandela and other ANC leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment. In his defence speech he said he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free society.
16615.m: At the Rivonia Trial in 1964 Mandela was given a life sentence.

16616.q: On which prison island did Mandela spend most of his imprisonment?
16616.e: From 1964 Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island off Cape Town. In 1982 he was moved to Pollsmoor Prison and in 1988 to Victor Verster Prison.
16616.m: Robben Island became a symbol of Mandela’s long imprisonment.

16617.q: How many years in total did Mandela spend in prison?
16617.e: Mandela was arrested in August 1962 and only released in 1990. That is about 27 years.
16617.m: Mandela was in prison for about 27 years.

16618.q: In which year was Mandela released from prison?
16618.e: After President de Klerk’s speech, Mandela left prison on 11 February 1990. The pictures went around the world.

16619.q: With whom did Mandela receive the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993?
16619.e: Mandela and de Klerk were honoured for peacefully ending apartheid. Desmond Tutu had already received the prize in 1984.
16619.m: Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

16620.q: When was Mandela sworn in as South Africa’s first black President?
16620.e: After the first free elections, Mandela was sworn in on 10 May 1994. He served one term until 1999.
16620.m: Mandela became President of South Africa in 1994.

16621.q: Who succeeded Mandela as President of South Africa in 1999?
16621.e: Mandela chose not to serve a second term. His successor in 1999 was Thabo Mbeki of the ANC.

16622.q: Which office did Frederik Willem de Klerk hold in Mandela’s Government of National Unity?
16622.e: De Klerk was one of the Deputy Presidents from 1994 to 1996. In 1996 he withdrew his National Party from the coalition.
16622.m: De Klerk served under Mandela as Deputy President.

16623.q: What is the title of Mandela’s autobiography, published in 1994?
16623.e: “Long Walk to Freedom” tells Mandela’s life up to his presidency. He wrote parts of it in secret on Robben Island.
16623.m: Mandela’s autobiography is called “Long Walk to Freedom”.

16624.q: What symbolic gesture did Mandela make at the 1995 Rugby World Cup?
a: He wore the shirt of the Springboks, seen as the team of white people
He played in the opening match himself
16624.e: Rugby was regarded as the sport of the white minority. By wearing the Springbok shirt, Mandela promoted reconciliation between black and white.
16624.m: With the Springbok shirt, Mandela made a gesture of reconciliation.

16625.e: Mandela died in Johannesburg on 5 December 2013 at the age of 95. Heads of state and government from all over the world attended the memorial service.

16626.q: What did the UN General Assembly declare International Nelson Mandela Day in 2009?
a: 11 February, the day of his release
27 April, the day of the first free elections
5 December, the day of his death
16626.e: Mandela Day on 18 July is meant to encourage people to help others. The UN decided on it in 2009, while Mandela was still alive.
16626.m: Nelson Mandela Day is on 18 July.

16627.q: What task did Archbishop Desmond Tutu take on after the end of apartheid?
a: He chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission
He became President of South Africa
He led the armed wing of the ANC
He became Secretary-General of the UN
16627.e: From 1996 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission investigated the crimes of the apartheid era. Victims and perpetrators were to be heard in public.
16627.m: Desmond Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

16628.q: Which principle had the Supreme Court confirmed in 1896 in the ruling Plessy v. Ferguson?
16628.e: In 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson declared racial segregation lawful as long as the separate facilities were supposedly equal. This principle justified segregation for decades.
16628.m: The 1896 ruling Plessy v. Ferguson made “separate but equal” a legal principle.

16629.q: Which Supreme Court ruling declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional in 1954?
16629.e: On 17 May 1954 the court ruled that separate public schools violated the 14th Amendment. This overturned the principle of Plessy v. Ferguson for education.
16629.m: With Brown v. Board of Education, segregation in schools fell legally in 1954.

16630.q: Which lawyer represented the plaintiffs in Brown v. Board of Education and later became the first African American justice on the Supreme Court?
16630.e: Thurgood Marshall led the lawsuits against school segregation for the NAACP. In 1967 he became the first African American justice on the Supreme Court.
16630.m: Thurgood Marshall won Brown v. Board of Education and later became a Supreme Court justice.

16631.q: What was the verdict of the nine justices in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954?
16631.e: Chief Justice Earl Warren made sure the court ruled as one. Separate educational facilities, it said, were inherently unequal.
16631.m: The Brown ruling was made jointly by all nine justices.

16632.q: Which organisation was founded in 1909 and fought racial discrimination mainly through lawsuits?
16632.e: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People relied heavily on legal action. Among other things, it developed the strategy that led to the Brown ruling.
16632.m: The NAACP is the oldest major civil rights organisation in the USA.

16633.q: What triggered the bus boycott in Montgomery (Alabama) on 1 December 1955?
a: A bomb attack on a church
16633.e: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger and was arrested. African Americans then boycotted the city’s buses.
16633.m: The arrest of Rosa Parks was the spark for the Montgomery bus boycott.

16634.q: What happened in Greensboro (North Carolina) on 1 February 1960?
a: Four students sat down at a “whites only” lunch counter
Rosa Parks was arrested on a bus
The first Freedom Ride set off
Malcolm X gave his last speech
16634.e: The students stayed seated at the Woolworth counter even though they were refused service. The sit-ins quickly spread to many cities in the South.
16634.m: The Greensboro sit-ins of 1960 made non-violent protest at lunch counters famous.

16635.q: What was the aim of the Freedom Rides from May 1961?
a: To test the end of segregation on long-distance buses
To register voters in the North
To protest against the Vietnam War
To raise money for the NAACP
16635.e: Mixed groups travelled south on long-distance buses to check whether rulings against segregated waiting rooms and buses were being enforced. Some were brutally attacked.
16635.m: In 1961 the Freedom Riders used bus journeys to check whether segregation had really been abolished.

16636.q: From which role model did Martin Luther King take the idea of non-violent resistance?
16636.e: Gandhi had fought British colonial rule in India with non-violent resistance. King applied this method to boycotts, sit-ins and marches in the USA.
16636.m: Martin Luther King learnt non-violent resistance from Gandhi.

16637.q: Which US President signed the Civil Rights Act on 2 July 1964?
16637.e: Kennedy had started the law; after his assassination, Johnson got it through Congress. He signed it on 2 July 1964.
16637.m: Lyndon B. Johnson put the Civil Rights Act into force in 1964.

16638.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 ban in the USA?
a: Discrimination because of skin colour in public places and at work
16638.e: The law banned racial segregation in restaurants, hotels and other public places as well as discrimination at work. It is seen as the civil rights movement’s most important success.
16638.m: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned racial segregation in public places.

16639.q: What happened on 7 March 1965, known as “Bloody Sunday”?
a: Police attacked demonstrators on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma
Martin Luther King was shot in Memphis
A bomb destroyed a church in Birmingham
Police stormed the headquarters of the Black Panthers
16639.e: A march for voting rights from Selma to Montgomery was stopped by force on the bridge. The pictures shocked the public and sped up the Voting Rights Act.
16639.m: “Bloody Sunday” on the Edmund Pettus Bridge became a turning point in the fight for voting rights in 1965.

16640.q: Which civil rights activist suffered a fractured skull on “Bloody Sunday” in 1965 and later became a member of Congress?
16640.e: As chairman of SNCC, John Lewis helped lead the march. Later he represented Georgia in the House of Representatives for decades.
16640.m: John Lewis marched in Selma and later became a member of Congress.

16641.q: Which law was signed on 6 August 1965 to prevent discrimination in elections?
16641.e: The Voting Rights Act banned discriminatory hurdles such as literacy tests for voter registration. The number of registered African American voters in the South then rose sharply.
16641.m: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 secured African Americans in the South the right to vote in practice.

16642.q: Which civil rights activist was murdered in New York on 21 February 1965?
16642.e: Malcolm X was for a long time a spokesman for the Nation of Islam and took a more radical line than King. After leaving the organisation in 1964, he was shot while giving a speech.
16642.m: Malcolm X was murdered in New York in 1965.

16643.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in 1967 in Loving v. Virginia?
a: Bans on marriage between people of different skin colour are unconstitutional
Poll taxes in elections are banned
16643.e: The married couple Loving had been convicted in Virginia because of their marriage. The court struck down all remaining bans on such marriages in the individual states.
16643.m: Since Loving v. Virginia in 1967, no one in the USA may be prevented from marrying because of skin colour.

a: Laws on racial segregation in the Southern states
16644.e: After the end of Reconstruction, Southern states passed laws separating black and white people in schools, transport and public places. They remained in force until the 1960s.
16644.m: The Jim Crow laws regulated racial segregation in the southern USA.

16645.q: In which city was Martin Luther King Jr. born on 15 January 1929?
16645.e: King grew up in Atlanta (Georgia), where his father preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church. Later he became co-pastor there himself.
16645.m: Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta in 1929.

16646.q: What was Martin Luther King’s job in Montgomery from 1954?
16646.e: In 1954 King took over Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery. A year later he became the spokesman of the bus boycott.
16646.m: King was a pastor when he became leader of the civil rights movement.

16647.q: In which subject did Martin Luther King earn his doctorate in 1955?
16647.e: In 1955 King received his doctorate in systematic theology from Boston University. In 1991 it became known that parts of the thesis had been plagiarised.
16647.m: King held a doctorate in theology.

16648.q: Roughly how long did the Montgomery bus boycott led by King last?
16648.e: The boycott began on 5 December 1955 and ended on 20 December 1956, after about 380 days. Before that, the Supreme Court had declared segregation on Montgomery’s buses unconstitutional.
16648.m: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted more than a year.

16649.q: Which organisation was founded in January 1957 and led by King as its first president?
16649.e: The SCLC linked black churches and pastors in the South. It became King’s most important platform for non-violent campaigns.
16649.m: From 1957 King led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

16650.q: Which country did King travel through for about a month in 1959 to learn more about Mahatma Gandhi’s non-violent methods?
16650.e: In February and March 1959 King travelled through India with his wife Coretta and met companions of Gandhi. He combined Gandhi’s method with Christian love for one’s neighbour.
16650.m: King travelled to India in 1959 to study Gandhi’s non-violent resistance more closely.

16651.q: Which famous text did King write while in prison in April 1963?
16651.e: King had been arrested in Birmingham on 12 April 1963. In the letter he defended civil disobedience against criticism from clergymen who urged patience.
16651.m: In the Letter from Birmingham Jail, King explained the reasons for non-violent civil disobedience.

16652.q: At which event did King give his “I Have a Dream” speech on 28 August 1963?
a: The march from Selma to Montgomery
16652.e: The speech took place in front of the Lincoln Memorial. The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom is one of the largest rallies in US history.
16652.m: King gave “I Have a Dream” at the March on Washington in 1963.

16653.q: Roughly how many people took part in the March on Washington in 1963?
16653.e: Estimates are usually around 250,000 participants (between 200,000 and 300,000), including many white people. The march increased the pressure on Congress for a civil rights law.
16653.m: About a quarter of a million people came to the March on Washington in 1963.

16654.q: In which year did King receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
16654.e: King received the prize in 1964, aged 35, for his non-violent struggle against racial discrimination. He donated the prize money to the civil rights movement.
16654.m: King was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

16655.q: Which nationwide campaign against poverty was King preparing with the SCLC when he was murdered in 1968?
16655.e: The campaign was to bring poor people of all skin colours to Washington to demand economic justice. After King’s death, Ralph Abernathy carried it out in May and June 1968 with the protest camp “Resurrection City”.
16655.m: In the end King also fought against poverty with the Poor People’s Campaign.

16656.q: Why was King in Memphis in April 1968?
a: He was supporting a strike by refuse workers
He was leading a bus boycott
He was giving an election speech
16656.e: The mostly African American refuse workers had been on strike since February 1968 for better pay, working conditions and recognition of their union. After King’s murder the city quickly gave in.
16656.m: In 1968 King was in Memphis to support striking refuse workers.

16657.q: Where was King shot on 4 April 1968?
a: On the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis
In front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington
In Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta
On the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma
16657.e: King was hit on the balcony of the motel and died shortly afterwards. Today the National Civil Rights Museum is located there.
16657.m: King was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis in 1968.

16658.q: Who was convicted of murdering King?
16658.e: James Earl Ray confessed and was convicted, but withdrew his confession shortly afterwards. The case is still debated today.
16658.m: James Earl Ray was convicted of assassinating King.

16659.q: Which speech did King give the evening before his death?
16659.e: On 3 April 1968 in Memphis, King said he had seen the “Promised Land” and might not get there with his listeners. Looking back, the speech seems prophetic.
16659.m: King’s last speech was called “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop”.

16660.q: On which day is Martin Luther King Day celebrated in the USA?
a: On the third Monday in January
On the first Monday in February
16660.e: The holiday falls close to King’s birthday on 15 January. It has been observed since 1986.
16660.m: Martin Luther King Day falls on the third Monday in January.

16661.q: In which city did King preach in 1964 during a visit behind the Iron Curtain?
16661.e: In September 1964 King preached in St Mary’s Church and St Sophia’s Church in East Berlin. Before that he had spoken in West Berlin.
16661.m: In 1964 King also preached in divided Berlin, in both the East and the West.

16662.q: Which work did Mary Wollstonecraft publish in 1792?
a: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
16662.e: Above all, Wollstonecraft demanded equal education for girls. Her work is considered an early founding text of feminism.
16662.m: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft demanded equal education for women.

16663.q: Which document was adopted at the Seneca Falls Convention (USA) in 1848?
16663.e: The declaration was modelled on the Declaration of Independence and demanded, among other things, votes for women. About 100 of the roughly 300 people present signed it.
16663.m: The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 is seen as the start of the organised women’s movement in the USA.

16664.q: Which two women were among the main organisers of the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848?
a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott
Susan B. Anthony and Rosa Parks
16664.e: Stanton and Mott had met in 1840 when women were excluded from an anti-slavery convention in London. Together with three other women they called the convention.
16664.m: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organised the Seneca Falls Convention.

16665.q: Which country was the first to introduce general voting rights for women at national level, in 1893?
16665.e: New Zealand was then a self-governing British colony. Women only gained the right to stand for election there later.
16665.m: In 1893 New Zealand was the first country to give women the general right to vote.

16666.q: Which European country was the first to introduce votes for women, in 1906?
16666.e: Finland, then a grand duchy under Russian rule, gave women the right to vote and to stand for election in 1906. In 1907 the first women entered parliament.
16666.m: In 1906 Finland was the first European country with votes for women.

16667.q: What were the women’s rights campaigners around Emmeline Pankhurst called, who fought for the vote with spectacular actions from 1903?
16667.e: Pankhurst founded the Women’s Social and Political Union in 1903. Its members used sometimes militant actions such as smashing windows and hunger strikes, and were called suffragettes.
16667.m: Emmeline Pankhurst led the suffragettes in Great Britain.

16668.q: What restriction applied to votes for women in Britain in 1918?
a: Women had to be at least 30 years old
Only women in London could vote
Women could only vote for local councils
16668.e: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave women over 30 who met certain property requirements the vote. Only in 1928 were women over 21 put on an equal footing with men.
16668.m: In Great Britain women could only vote from the age of 30 from 1918, and on the same terms as men from 1928.

16669.q: Which amendment to the US Constitution has guaranteed votes for women since 1920?
16669.e: The 19th Amendment was ratified in August 1920 after Tennessee became the 36th state to approve it. It forbids denying the vote on account of sex.
16669.m: The 19th Amendment brought votes for women in the USA in 1920.

16670.q: Which book did Simone de Beauvoir publish in 1949?
16670.e: Beauvoir examined how society defines women as “the Other” of men. The sentence “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” is famous.
16670.m: Simone de Beauvoir wrote “The Second Sex” in 1949.

16671.q: Which book by Betty Friedan (1963) is seen as the spark for the second wave of the women’s movement in the USA?
16671.e: Friedan described the dissatisfaction of well-educated housewives in the suburbs. Besides formal rights, the second wave demanded equality in everyday life, at work and in the family.
16671.m: Betty Friedan’s “The Feminine Mystique” shaped the second wave of feminism in 1963.

16672.q: Which book by the Swiss lawyer Iris von Roten caused fierce debate in 1958?
16672.e: In it, Iris von Roten sharply criticised the disadvantages women faced in Switzerland. The book appeared shortly before the first federal vote on women’s suffrage.
16672.m: In 1958 Iris von Roten wrote the book “Frauen im Laufgitter” (Women in the Playpen).

16673.q: How clearly did Swiss men reject votes for women at federal level in 1959?
16673.e: In the first federal vote on 1 February 1959 only about 33 percent said yes, and most cantons also rejected it. However, some cantons in French-speaking Switzerland introduced the vote at cantonal level in the same year.
16673.m: Votes for women clearly failed at the ballot box in Switzerland in 1959.

16674.q: Which canton was the first to introduce votes for women at cantonal level, on 1 February 1959?
16674.e: Vaud adopted cantonal votes for women on the same day they were rejected at federal level. Neuchâtel (1959) and Geneva (1960) followed.
16674.m: In 1959 the canton of Vaud was the pioneer of votes for women in Switzerland.

16675.q: With what share of yes votes were federal votes for women adopted on 7 February 1971?
16675.e: About two thirds of the men who voted and 15½ of 22 cantons said yes. As early as autumn 1971, women could be elected to the National Council and the Council of States for the first time.
16675.m: Since 1971 Swiss women have had the right to vote and stand for election at federal level.

16676.q: How many women were elected to the National Council in the first elections after the introduction of votes for women in 1971?
16676.e: That was a share of 5.5 percent of the 200 seats. One woman, Lise Girardin from Geneva, was elected to the Council of States.
16676.m: The first National Council with women in 1971 had 11 female members.

16677.q: Which European country was the last to introduce votes for women at national level, in 1984?
16677.e: In Liechtenstein similar proposals had been rejected in 1971 and 1973. In 1984 votes for women were narrowly accepted.
16677.m: In 1984 Liechtenstein was the last country in Europe to introduce votes for women.

16678.q: When did the UN General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
16678.e: The declaration was adopted at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. Since then, 10 December has been marked as Human Rights Day.
16678.m: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights dates from 10 December 1948.

16679.q: How does Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights begin?
a: “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.”
“All people are equal before the law.”
16679.e: Article 1 stresses the inborn dignity and equality of all human beings. The phrase “Human dignity shall be inviolable” comes from the German Basic Law.
16679.m: Article 1 of the 1948 Declaration declares all human beings free and equal in dignity and rights.

16680.q: Who chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights that drafted the Universal Declaration?
16680.e: The widow of US President Franklin D. Roosevelt chaired the commission with diplomatic skill. René Cassin and Peng Chun Chang were among those who worked on it.
16680.m: Eleanor Roosevelt led the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

16682.q: What is the legal status of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: It is a resolution and as such not legally binding
It is a binding treaty with its own court
It is part of the Swiss Federal Constitution
It only applies to the founding states of the UN
16682.e: As a resolution of the General Assembly, it cannot be enforced in court. But its content was put into binding treaties such as the UN Covenants of 1966, and parts of it are regarded as customary law.
16682.m: The Universal Declaration is politically very important but not a binding treaty.

16683.q: Which two UN Covenants of 1966 made many rights of the Universal Declaration binding under international law?
a: The Civil and Political Covenant and the Social Covenant
The Geneva Convention and the Hague Convention
The Rome Statute and the UN Charter
The Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Refugee Convention
16683.e: The Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights came into force in 1976. Together with the Declaration they form the “International Bill of Human Rights”.
16683.m: The two Covenants of 1966 make human rights binding.

16684.q: Which document of the French Revolution was proclaimed on 26 August 1789?
a: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
16684.e: In it the National Assembly declared liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression to be natural rights. Women and slaves were excluded in practice.
16684.m: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 is a milestone in the history of human rights.

16686.q: Which organisation created the European Convention on Human Rights in 1950?
16686.e: The Council of Europe’s ECHR was signed in Rome in 1950 and came into force in 1953. It is binding and can be enforced before its own court in Strasbourg.
16686.m: The ECHR is a treaty of the Council of Europe from 1950.

16687.q: Where is the European Court of Human Rights based?
16687.e: The court monitors compliance with the ECHR. People from Switzerland can also lodge complaints there once all national legal remedies have been used.
16687.m: The European Court of Human Rights sits in Strasbourg.

16688.q: Which organisation did the British lawyer Peter Benenson found in 1961?
16688.e: It was triggered by a newspaper appeal for non-violent political prisoners. Amnesty International received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
16688.m: Peter Benenson founded Amnesty International in 1961.

16689.q: In which city is the UN Human Rights Council, founded in 2006, based?
16689.e: The Human Rights Council replaced the earlier Commission on Human Rights. Geneva is also home to the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
16689.m: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

16690.q: Which UN convention of 9 December 1948 makes genocide a punishable crime?
a: Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide
Convention on the Rights of the Child
16690.e: The convention was adopted one day before the Universal Declaration. The term genocide goes back to the lawyer Raphael Lemkin.
16690.m: The Genocide Convention was adopted in 1948, one day before the Declaration of Human Rights.

16691.q: In which year did the UN General Assembly adopt the Convention on the Rights of the Child?
16691.e: The convention protects, among other things, the right to education, protection from violence and having a say. It is one of the most widely ratified human rights treaties.
16691.m: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child dates from 1989.

16692.q: When was the article on equality between women and men added to the Swiss Federal Constitution?
16692.e: The people and the cantons adopted the article on 14 June 1981. It obliges the state to ensure equality between women and men, above all in the family, education and work.
16692.m: Since 1981 equality between women and men has been in the Federal Constitution.

16693.q: What was the reason for the nationwide women’s strike in Switzerland on 14 June 1991?
a: The slow implementation of the equality article
The rejection of votes for women
The election of the first female Federal Councillor
16693.e: The idea came from women watchmakers in the Vallée de Joux who were outraged by unequal pay; the strike fell on the tenth anniversary of the constitutional article. The motto was “When women want it, everything stands still”.
16693.m: The women’s strike of 1991 demanded that the equality article be put into practice.

16694.q: According to the organisers, how many people took part in the women’s strike on 14 June 2019?
16694.e: Switzerland’s second big women’s strike was one of the largest political rallies in the country. The main issues were equal pay and unpaid work.
16694.m: According to the organisers, more than half a million people took part in the 2019 women’s strike.

16695.q: When did the Swiss Gender Equality Act come into force?
16695.e: The law bans direct and indirect discrimination in working life. It also makes it easier for those affected to provide evidence.
16695.m: The Gender Equality Act has applied in Switzerland since 1996.

16696.q: Under the Swiss Gender Equality Act, how is sexual harassment at work treated?
a: It is only punishable if there are witnesses
It is not covered by the law
16696.e: Article 4 of the Act classifies sexual harassment as discriminatory behaviour. Employers must take measures to prevent it.
16696.m: In the Gender Equality Act, sexual harassment at work counts as discrimination.

16697.q: What does the “easing of the burden of proof” in the Swiss Gender Equality Act mean?
a: Discrimination is presumed if it is shown to be credible
The person affected must prove everything completely
A court may not demand evidence
16697.e: In important areas such as pay or promotion, the employer must then prove that there is no discrimination. The easing does not apply to sexual harassment or not being hired.
16697.m: Under the Gender Equality Act it is enough to show that discrimination is credible.

16698.q: Who was elected the first woman on the Swiss Federal Council in 1984?
16698.e: The FDP politician Elisabeth Kopp headed the Federal Department of Justice and Police. She resigned at the beginning of 1989.
16698.m: From 1984 Elisabeth Kopp was Switzerland’s first female Federal Councillor.

16699.q: What did the new Swiss marriage law, adopted in 1985 and in force from 1988, change?
a: The husband was no longer considered the “head of the family”
Divorce was allowed for the first time
16699.e: Before, for example, the husband decided where the family lived, and the wife in practice needed his consent to take paid work. The new law gave both spouses equal rights and duties.
16699.m: Since the new marriage law, wife and husband in Switzerland have had equal rights.

16700.q: With what share of yes votes did Swiss voters approve “marriage for all” on 26 September 2021?
16700.e: Same-sex marriage came into force on 1 July 2022. Before that, same-sex couples could only enter a registered partnership.
16700.m: Since 2022 same-sex couples in Switzerland can also marry.

16701.q: Since when have same-sex couples in Switzerland been able to enter a registered partnership?
16701.e: The Partnership Act had been approved in a popular vote in 2005 with about 58 percent yes. Since marriage for all, no new partnerships can be registered.
16701.m: Registered partnerships existed in Switzerland from 2007.

16702.q: What is the difference between formal equal rights and actual equality?
a: Equal rights in law do not automatically mean equal chances in everyday life
Formal equal rights only apply to men
Actual equality is forbidden by law
Both terms mean exactly the same
16702.e: Even with equal laws, there can be differences in pay, careers or unpaid work. That is why the Federal Constitution also requires actual equality.
16702.m: Equal rights on paper do not yet guarantee equal chances in life.

16703.q: What does Article 8 paragraph 3 of the Swiss Federal Constitution require, among other things?
a: Equal pay for men and women for work of equal value
A quota for women on the Federal Council
The same retirement age for all jobs
Equal numbers of men and women in every company
16703.e: The paragraph guarantees equal rights for men and women and the right to equal pay for work of equal value. The legislature must ensure actual equality.
16703.m: The Federal Constitution guarantees equal pay for work of equal value.

16704.q: What does the anti-racism criminal provision, approved by Swiss voters in 1994, make punishable?
a: Publicly inciting hatred against people because of their origin or religion
Unequal pay for women and men
16704.e: The anti-racism provision (Article 261bis of the Criminal Code) bans, among other things, public incitement to hatred and discrimination. In 2020 it was extended to sexual orientation.
16704.m: Since 1994 racial discrimination has been a criminal offence in Switzerland.

16705.q: Which US law of 1963 banned unequal pay for men and women doing the same work?
16705.e: The Equal Pay Act was signed by President Kennedy. A year later the Civil Rights Act also banned discrimination on the basis of sex in hiring.
16705.m: The Equal Pay Act of 1963 required equal pay for equal work in the USA.

16706.q: What is meant by the “gender pay gap”?
a: The average difference in pay between women and men
The number of women in leadership positions
The different life expectancy of the sexes
16706.e: Part of the difference can be explained by industry, working hours or position, another part cannot. The unexplained part can point to discrimination.
16706.m: The gender pay gap measures the difference in pay between women and men.

16707.q: Which UN convention of 1979 obliges states to eliminate discrimination against women?
a: Convention on the Rights of the Child
Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
16707.e: The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women is often called the “Women’s Rights Convention”. A UN committee regularly reviews the states’ reports.
16707.m: CEDAW of 1979 is the most important UN convention for women’s rights.

16708.q: In migration research, what are “push factors”?
a: Reasons that drive people away from their home country
Reasons that attract people to a destination country
16708.e: Push factors include war, persecution, poverty or environmental disasters. Pull factors such as work or safety attract people to a destination country.
16708.m: Push factors drive people away, pull factors attract them.

16709.q: Which principle of the 1951 Geneva Refugee Convention forbids sending people back to a state where they are persecuted?
16709.e: Under Article 33, refugees may not be returned to areas where their life or freedom is threatened. Today the principle is seen as a central rule of refugee protection.
16709.m: The principle of non-refoulement forbids sending people back to persecution.

16710.q: In which year did the UN General Assembly decide to create the Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)?
16710.e: The UNHCR was created on 14 December 1950 and began its work in Geneva on 1 January 1951. It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
16710.m: The UN refugee agency UNHCR, based in Geneva, was set up in 1950.

16711.q: What did the 1967 Protocol change about the Geneva Refugee Convention?
a: It removed the restriction to events before 1951
It created the seasonal worker statute
It introduced free movement of persons
It abolished the right of asylum
16711.e: Originally the convention only applied to reasons for flight before 1 January 1951 and mainly to Europe. The Protocol made it applicable worldwide and without a time limit.
16711.m: The 1967 Protocol made refugee protection unlimited in time and place.

16712.q: Which edict caused about 200,000 Huguenots to flee France in 1685?
16712.e: With it Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and banned the Reformed faith. Many Huguenots fled to Protestant areas, including Switzerland.
16712.m: The Edict of Fontainebleau drove the Huguenots into exile in 1685.

16713.q: What role did Geneva play in the flight of the Huguenots at the end of the 17th century?
a: At times the city took in more refugees than it had inhabitants
The city refused passage to all refugees
The city was the destination only of Catholic refugees
The city was conquered by Huguenots
16713.e: At times Geneva housed up to 28,000 refugees with only about 12,000 inhabitants. About 20,000 Huguenots stayed in Switzerland for good and helped develop banking and the textile trade, among other things.
16713.m: Geneva was an important place of refuge for the Huguenots.

16714.q: What did the Swiss seasonal worker statute, introduced in 1934, regulate?
a: Temporary stays of foreign workers without family reunification
Free choice of where to live and work
16714.e: Seasonal workers could only stay for part of the year and could not freely change job or canton of residence. Bringing their families was banned for a long time, which led to children living in hiding.
16714.m: The seasonal worker statute allowed work but no normal family life in Switzerland.

16715.q: What caused the seasonal worker statute to lose its validity for EU citizens in 2002?
a: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU
16715.e: The free movement agreement came into force on 1 June 2002. It gives EU citizens the right to live and work in Switzerland, and vice versa.
16715.m: With free movement of persons, the seasonal worker statute ended for EU citizens in 2002.

16716.q: What did the Schwarzenbach initiative, voted on on 7 June 1970, demand?
a: Limiting the share of foreigners to 10 percent
Votes for women at federal level
16716.e: The initiative of the National Action around James Schwarzenbach called for no more than 10 percent foreigners per canton (except Geneva) and would have meant expelling many people. It was rejected fairly narrowly with a very high turnout.
16716.m: In 1970 the Schwarzenbach initiative wanted to strictly limit the share of foreigners and was narrowly rejected.

16717.q: What happened on 30 August 1965 on the building site of the Mattmark dam in Valais?
a: A glacier collapse killed 88 workers, 56 of them from Italy
A strike by Italian workers brought the site to a standstill
The dam burst and flooded the valley
The first seasonal workers received settlement permits
16717.e: Ice and rubble from the Allalin Glacier buried the huts, which stood directly below the tongue of the glacier. The disaster revealed the difficult conditions of the guest workers.
16717.m: The Mattmark disaster of 1965 hit mainly Italian guest workers.

16718.q: Which popular initiative did Switzerland approve with 50.3 percent yes on 9 February 2014?
16718.e: The initiative added Article 121a to the Federal Constitution, which requires Switzerland to control immigration independently. Implementing it was difficult because of free movement of persons with the EU.
16718.m: The mass immigration initiative was approved very narrowly in 2014.

16719.q: Which protection status did Switzerland activate for the first time in March 2022 for refugees from Ukraine?
16719.e: Status S allows quick, collective admission without a regular asylum procedure. It had been in the law for a long time but was used for the first time in 2022.
16719.m: In 2022 protection status S was activated for the first time for refugees from Ukraine.

16720.q: Which island off New York was the main immigration station of the USA from 1892 to 1954?
16720.e: Millions of immigrants were examined and registered there. Today the island has an immigration museum.
16720.m: Ellis Island was the gateway to America for millions of immigrants.

16721.q: With which country did West Germany sign its first agreement to recruit guest workers in 1955?
16721.e: The agreement with Italy marked the start of recruiting foreign workers during the economic miracle. In 1961 an agreement with Turkey followed, among others.
16721.m: Germany’s first recruitment agreement was signed with Italy in 1955.

16722.q: Which sentence by Max Frisch from 1965 commented on Swiss guest worker policy?
a: “We asked for workers, and human beings came.”
“Whoever does not vote has already voted.”
“Home is not a place but a feeling.”
16722.e: Frisch criticised that guest workers were only seen as labour. Yet people came with families and needs.
16722.m: Max Frisch reminded people that guest workers are human beings and not just labour.

16723.q: Why did many people emigrate from Switzerland in the 19th century?
a: Because of poverty, famines and lack of work
Because Switzerland required emigration by law
Because of an occupation by Austria
16723.e: Bad harvests, population growth and crises in farming and cottage industry drove many to North and South America. This is how settlements such as New Glarus in Wisconsin came about.
16723.m: In the 19th century Switzerland was a country of emigration.

16724.q: According to UN estimates, roughly how many international migrants were there worldwide in 2020?
16724.e: That was about 3.6 percent of the world’s population. So the vast majority of people live in the country where they were born.
16724.m: In 2020 about 3.6 percent of the world’s population lived outside their country of birth.

16725.q: Apart from pensioners, who else receives AHV pensions?
16725.e: AHV stands for old-age and survivors’ insurance. Survivors are the widows, widowers and orphans of a person who has died. Unemployed people are covered by unemployment insurance.
16725.m: The AHV also pays pensions to widows, widowers and orphans.

16726.q: With what share of yes votes was the AHV Act accepted in 1947?
16726.e: The AHV Act received 80 per cent yes votes with a turnout of 79.7 per cent. That was a very clear result.
16726.m: The AHV was accepted in 1947 with about four fifths of the votes.

16728.q: Which vote in 1925 created the constitutional basis for the AHV?
a: A constitutional article on old-age and survivors’ insurance
The introduction of compulsory pension funds
The total revision of the Federal Constitution
16728.e: On 6 December 1925 the people and the cantons accepted, with about 65 per cent, a constitutional article that gave the federal government the task of creating the AHV. However, it then took more than twenty years until a valid AHV Act existed.
16728.m: The AHV was already in the constitution as a task in 1925.

16729.q: What happened to the first AHV Act in the vote of 6 December 1931?
a: It was rejected with about 40 per cent yes
It was overturned by the Federal Supreme Court
It was never put to the vote
16729.e: The so-called Lex Schulthess received only 39.7 per cent yes votes. The AHV was only successfully introduced after the Second World War.
16729.m: The first attempt at the AHV failed at the ballot box in 1931.

16730.q: Which Second World War scheme did the AHV develop from?
a: The Wage and Earnings Compensation Scheme for soldiers
16730.e: During the war, soldiers received compensation for lost wages through wage and earnings compensation funds. This system of funds became the basis of the AHV.
16730.m: The AHV built on the compensation funds of the war years.

16731.q: At which event in 1918 was old-age insurance already demanded?
a: The founding of the League of Nations
The introduction of women’s right to vote
16731.e: In the general strike of 1918, the Olten Action Committee demanded, among other things, old-age and disability insurance. It took another 30 years until the AHV was introduced.
16731.m: Old-age insurance was already demanded in the general strike of 1918.

16732.q: How is the AHV basically financed?
a: On a pay-as-you-go basis from current income
By capital funding with personal accounts
16732.e: The current contributions of workers and employers pay the current pensions. This is why even the first generation could receive pensions without having paid in for long.
16732.m: The AHV passes the contributions of people in work directly on to pensioners.

16733.q: How high were AHV contributions when it was introduced in 1948?
a: 4 per cent of income, half each from employer and employee
10 per cent, from the employee only
1 per cent, from the employer only
8 per cent, from the federal government only
16733.e: Contributions were 4 per cent of earned income. Employers and employees each paid half, and public subsidies were added.
16733.m: At first the AHV cost four per cent of wages, shared between both sides.

16734.q: In which year was the three-pillar principle of retirement provision laid down in the constitution?
16734.e: The people and the cantons accepted the three-pillar principle in 1972. It consists of the AHV, occupational pensions and private savings.
16734.m: Since 1972 retirement provision has rested on three pillars.

16735.q: What did the 10th AHV revision of 1995 decide about women’s retirement age?
16735.e: With the 10th AHV revision, women’s retirement age was raised step by step from 62 to 64. At the same time, credits for bringing up children were introduced.
16735.m: The 10th AHV revision raised women’s retirement age to 64.

16736.q: With what result was the AHV 21 reform accepted on 25 September 2022?
a: Narrowly, with about 50.5 per cent yes
Clearly, with about 70 per cent yes
16736.e: AHV 21 was accepted very narrowly with 50.5 per cent and came into force in 2024. It sets a single reference age of 65; for women it rises step by step from 64 to 65 from 2025.
16736.m: With AHV 21, women’s reference age rises step by step to 65.

16737.q: What was historic about the initiative for a 13th AHV pension on 3 March 2024?
a: For the first time a left-wing popular initiative on the welfare state was accepted
For the first time women voted on the AHV
For the first time the AHV was abolished
For the first time an initiative was valid without a majority of the cantons
16737.e: The initiative was accepted with 58.2 per cent yes and 15 of 23 cantonal votes. According to the media, this was the first time a left-wing initiative on social policy had been accepted.
16737.m: The 13th AHV pension in 2024 was a historic success for a left-wing initiative.

16738.q: Which period is usually called the post-war boom in Switzerland?
16738.e: After the Second World War, Switzerland experienced long, strong growth. It ended with the oil crisis of 1973 and the recession that followed.
16738.m: The boom lasted from about 1950 until the oil crisis of 1973.

16739.q: Which event ended the boom in Switzerland?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
16739.e: The sharp rise in the oil price in 1973 led to a worldwide economic crisis. Switzerland suffered a particularly deep slump in 1975.
16739.m: The oil crisis of 1973 ended the economic miracle.

16740.q: Roughly how much did Swiss economic output shrink in real terms in 1975?
16740.e: Real gross domestic product fell by about 7 per cent in 1975. That was one of the sharpest falls among the industrialised countries.
16740.m: In 1975 Switzerland suffered a very deep economic slump.

16741.q: Why did people speak of the “export of unemployment” after 1974?
a: Many foreign workers had to leave Switzerland when jobs were lost
Switzerland sent unemployed people to colonies
Unemployed people got money for trips abroad
16741.e: Many seasonal workers and residents no longer received a permit and returned home. As a result, official unemployment in Switzerland stayed low.
16741.m: In the crisis, foreign workers served as a buffer for the economy.

16742.q: Which major building project became a symbol of progress during the boom?
16742.e: In 1958 the federal government was given the power to build a national road network. From 1962 new sections of motorway were opened one after another.
16742.m: Motorway building became a symbol of the boom.

16743.q: Which motorway is the main route from Geneva via Bern and Zurich to St Gallen?
16743.e: The former national road N1 was built from 1962; the first section was the Grauholz motorway near Bern. It is still the most important east-west route today.
16743.m: The A1 links western and eastern Switzerland.

16744.q: Where did the national exhibition Expo 64 take place?
16744.e: Expo 64 took place in Lausanne and showed a modern Switzerland full of faith in the future. It came right in the middle of the boom years.
16744.m: Expo 64 in Lausanne presented a modern Switzerland.

16745.q: Which agreement of 1937 shaped the social partnership during the boom?
a: The Peace Agreement in the engineering and metal industry
16745.e: Employers and trade unions committed themselves to settling conflicts by negotiation instead of strikes. This industrial peace contributed to the stability of the post-war period.
16745.m: The industrial peace of 1937 made strikes rare in Switzerland.

16746.q: Which source of energy became cheap during the boom and increasingly pushed out coal?
16746.e: From about 1950 cheap oil caused energy use and environmental pollution to rise sharply. The historian Christian Pfister speaks of the “1950s syndrome”.
16746.m: Cheap oil drove the boom years.

16747.q: Which party make-up of the Federal Council was created in 1959 and lasted until 2003?
a: The magic formula with 2 seats each for the FDP, Catholic Conservatives and SP, and 1 seat for the BGB
A Federal Council made up only of the FDP
One seat for each language region
16747.e: In 1959 the SP was brought into government with two seats. This concordance fitted the culture of consensus of the boom years.
16747.m: The magic formula of 1959 brought all the major parties into the Federal Council.

16748.q: Which traditional Swiss export industry lost especially many jobs in the crisis of the 1970s because of new electronic competition from Japan and the USA?
16748.e: Cheap electronic quartz watches put heavy pressure on mechanical Swiss watches. This is called the quartz crisis, and it cost tens of thousands of jobs.
16748.m: The quartz crisis hit the Swiss watch industry hard in the 1970s.

16749.q: Which sector of the economy grew particularly strongly after the end of the boom?
16749.e: From the 1970s, employment shifted from industry to banks, insurance, trade and other services. This is called the shift to a service economy.
16749.m: After the boom, Switzerland became a service society.

16750.q: With which country did Switzerland conclude an agreement on recruiting workers in 1948?
16750.e: The 1948 agreement with Italy made Italians the largest group of foreign workers. Later Spain, Portugal, Yugoslavia and Turkey followed.
16750.m: The first guest workers of the post-war period came mainly from Italy.

16751.q: What was a central feature of the seasonal worker statute?
a: Bringing family members over was generally forbidden
Seasonal workers could only work in banks
Seasonal workers could freely change where they lived
16751.e: Seasonal workers were only allowed to work in Switzerland for part of the year and could not bring their families. Many children therefore lived in hiding or separated from their parents.
16751.m: The seasonal worker statute separated many families.

16752.q: From 1973, what was the longest time per year that seasonal workers could work in Switzerland?
16752.e: From 1973 a maximum of nine months per year applied. After that, the seasonal workers had to leave the country.
16752.m: Seasonal workers could stay for a maximum of nine months a year.

16753.q: When did the seasonal worker statute end for EU citizens?
a: With the free movement of persons on 1 June 2002
With the no to the EEA in 1992
With the new Federal Constitution of 2000
16753.e: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons from the Bilateral Agreements I came into force on 1 June 2002. With it, the seasonal worker statute was abolished for EU citizens.
16753.m: The free movement of persons ended the seasonal worker statute in 2002.

16754.q: Which party did James Schwarzenbach represent in the National Council when his initiative was put to the vote in 1970?
16754.e: James Schwarzenbach sat in the National Council for the National Action against the Foreign Domination of People and Homeland. The initiative was named after him.
16754.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative came from the National Action.

16755.q: What maximum share of foreigners in the cantons did the Schwarzenbach initiative want to allow?
a: 5 per cent in the whole of Switzerland
16755.e: The initiative demanded a limit of 10 per cent per canton, and 25 per cent for Geneva. At the time, the share of foreigners was just over 15 per cent.
16755.m: Schwarzenbach wanted to reduce the share of foreigners to 10 per cent.

16756.q: What was the result of the vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative on 7 June 1970?
a: It was rejected with about 54 per cent no
It was accepted with about 54 per cent yes
It was rejected with 90 per cent no
16756.e: The initiative received 46 per cent yes and was therefore rejected relatively narrowly. The turnout of 74.7 per cent was unusually high.
16756.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative failed only narrowly in 1970.

16757.q: Which disaster on 30 August 1965 killed mainly Italian construction workers?
a: The glacier collapse at the Mattmark building site
The collapse of the Gotthard Tunnel
The fire at Zurich main station
16757.e: During the building of the Mattmark dam in Valais, part of the Allalin Glacier fell on the workers’ huts. 88 people died, most of them Italians.
16757.m: The Mattmark disaster showed how dangerous the guest workers’ work was.

16758.q: Who wrote the well-known sentence “We asked for workers, and human beings came”?
16758.e: The writer Max Frisch wrote the sentence in 1965 in the foreword to a book about Italian guest workers. He criticised the fact that migrants were seen only as workers.
16758.m: Max Frisch reminded people that guest workers are human beings.

16759.q: Which group of refugees did Switzerland take in in large numbers in 1956?
16759.e: After the Hungarian uprising was crushed in 1956, Switzerland took in over 10,000 Hungarians. Taking them in was very popular during the Cold War.
16759.m: In 1956 Switzerland took in many refugees from Hungary.

16760.q: When was the mass immigration initiative accepted?
16760.e: The SVP’s initiative was accepted on 9 February 2014 with 50.3 per cent yes. 12 full and 5 half cantons agreed, that is 14.5 of 23 cantonal votes.
16760.m: The mass immigration initiative was accepted very narrowly in 2014.

16761.q: Which article of the constitution was created by the mass immigration initiative?
a: Article 8 on equality before the law
16761.e: The initiative added Article 121a to the Federal Constitution. It requires Switzerland to manage immigration independently.
16761.m: Since 2014 Article 121a has governed the management of immigration.

16762.q: How did parliament implement the mass immigration initiative in 2016?
a: With priority for local workers and a duty to report vacancies, without quotas
With fixed maximum numbers for all countries
By cancelling all the Bilateral Agreements
16762.e: In December 2016 parliament decided on the so-called “domestic priority light”. It does without maximum numbers, but in 2018 it introduced a duty to report job vacancies.
16762.m: The implementation of the initiative did without quotas.

16763.q: From which country did many people flee to Switzerland in 1968 after Warsaw Pact troops invaded?
16763.e: After the Prague Spring was crushed in 1968, Switzerland took in about 12,000 refugees from Czechoslovakia. As with Hungary in 1956, solidarity was strong during the Cold War.
16763.m: After the Prague Spring of 1968, many Czechs and Slovaks found refuge in Switzerland.

16764.q: With what result did Swiss men reject women’s right to vote on 1 February 1959?
a: With about two thirds voting no
With about 51 per cent voting no
With over 90 per cent voting no
16764.e: In 1959 only 33 per cent voted yes and 67 per cent no. Only a few French-speaking cantons said yes.
16764.m: In 1959 women’s right to vote failed clearly.

16765.q: Which canton was the first to introduce women’s right to vote at cantonal level, in 1959?
16765.e: The canton of Vaud introduced women’s right to vote at cantonal level on 1 February 1959, the same day as the defeat at federal level. Neuchâtel and Geneva soon followed.
16765.m: In 1959 Vaud was the first canton with women’s right to vote.

16766.q: When did Swiss men accept women’s right to vote at federal level?
16766.e: On 7 February 1971 women’s right to vote at federal level was accepted. After that, women were allowed to vote and stand in federal elections and votes.
16766.m: Since 1971 women in Switzerland have had the right to vote at federal level.

16767.q: What was the share of yes votes in the vote on women’s right to vote in 1971?
16767.e: There were 621,109 yes and 323,882 no votes, so about 65.7 per cent yes. The cantons also agreed, by 15.5 to 6.5.
16767.m: In 1971 almost two thirds of the men said yes to women’s right to vote.

16768.q: How many women were elected to the National Council in 1971?
16768.e: In the first elections in which women took part, in 1971, 11 women were elected to the National Council. That was 5.5 per cent of the 200 seats.
16768.m: In 1971 the first eleven women entered the National Council.

16769.q: How did women in Appenzell Innerrhoden get the right to vote at cantonal level?
a: Through a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court on 27 November 1990
Through a decision of the Landsgemeinde in 1971
Through a Federal Council decision in 1981
16769.e: The Landsgemeinde still rejected women’s right to vote in April 1990. The Federal Supreme Court then ruled that this violated the equality before the law guaranteed in the Federal Constitution.
16769.m: In Appenzell Innerrhoden, only the Federal Supreme Court brought in women’s right to vote, in 1990.

16770.q: In which year did the Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Ausserrhoden introduce women’s right to vote?
16770.e: Appenzell Ausserrhoden agreed at its Landsgemeinde in 1989. After that, only Innerrhoden was still without women’s right to vote at cantonal level.
16770.m: Appenzell Ausserrhoden introduced women’s right to vote in 1989.

a: The people and the cantons accepted the equality article
The first woman Federal Councillor was elected
Women’s right to vote was rejected
The first women’s strike took place
16771.e: On 14 June 1981 the principle of equal rights for men and women was added to the constitution. It also requires equal pay for work of equal value.
16771.m: Since 1981 equality between women and men has been in the constitution.

16772.q: What did the big women’s strike of 14 June 1991 draw attention to?
a: Ten years of the equality article without real equality
The founding of the federal state
16772.e: Ten years after the equality article was accepted, hundreds of thousands of women stopped work. They criticised the fact that equality was still missing in everyday life.
16772.m: The women’s strike of 1991 demanded that equality be put into practice.

16773.q: Which book by Iris von Roten caused a fierce debate about the role of women in 1958?
16773.e: In it, Iris von Roten sharply criticised the disadvantages women faced in marriage, work and politics. The book was fiercely attacked at the time and is now regarded as a feminist classic.
16773.m: In 1958 Iris von Roten radically demanded equal rights.

16774.q: What was the “March on Bern” of 1 March 1969?
a: A demonstration for women’s right to vote in front of the Federal Palace
A farmers’ protest against milk prices
A protest against the Schwarzenbach initiative
16774.e: Thousands of women and men demonstrated in Bern for women’s right to vote. The reason was the Federal Council’s plan to sign the European Convention on Human Rights with a reservation.
16774.m: The March on Bern in 1969 increased the pressure for women’s right to vote.

16775.q: Why did many people in the northern Jura want a canton of their own?
a: As a French-speaking minority, they felt disadvantaged by the canton of Bern
They no longer wanted to pay taxes to the federal government
They wanted to belong to the canton of Neuchâtel
16775.e: The northern Jura was French-speaking and Catholic, while the canton of Bern was mainly German-speaking and Protestant. Many people from the Jura therefore felt they were not represented as equals.
16775.m: The Jura question arose from the feeling of being disadvantaged by Bern.

16776.q: What was the name of the most important organisation of the Jura separatists from 1951?
16776.e: The Mouvement séparatiste jurassien, founded in 1947, renamed itself Rassemblement jurassien in 1951. It fought for a canton of its own.
16776.m: The Rassemblement jurassien fought for a canton of Jura.

16777.q: Through which event did the area of today’s canton of Jura become part of the canton of Bern in 1815?
16777.e: At the Congress of Vienna, most of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel was given to Bern. This was meant to compensate Bern for losing Vaud and Aargau.
16777.m: From the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the Jura belonged to Bern.

16778.q: What was the result of the first Jura plebiscite on 23 June 1974?
a: Just under 52 per cent voted for a new canton
Over 80 per cent voted against a new canton
16778.e: In the whole Bernese Jura, 51.9 per cent voted for a canton of their own, with a turnout of about 90 per cent. The northern districts said yes, the southern ones no.
16778.m: In 1974 the Jura narrowly said yes to a canton of its own.

16779.q: Which three districts formed the new canton of Jura?
16779.e: Delémont, Franches-Montagnes and Porrentruy voted for a canton of their own in 1974. After further votes in 1975, the southern districts stayed with Bern.
16779.m: The canton of Jura was formed from the three districts of the northern Jura.

16780.q: Who had to approve the founding of the canton of Jura in 1978 so that it could be created?
a: The people and the cantons of the whole of Switzerland
Only the voters in the Jura
Only the Grand Council of the canton of Bern
16780.e: A new canton requires a change to the Federal Constitution. On 24 September 1978 the people and the cantons said yes with over 82 per cent.
16780.m: The people and the cantons of the whole of Switzerland decide on a new canton.

16781.q: Since when has the canton of Jura officially existed?
16781.e: The canton of Jura began its work on 1 January 1979. It is the youngest canton in Switzerland.
16781.m: Since 1979 the Jura has been the youngest canton.

16782.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Jura?
16782.e: Delémont, Delsberg in German, is the capital and seat of the cantonal government. Porrentruy is another important town.
16782.m: Delémont is the capital of the canton of Jura.

16783.q: Which group knocked the soldiers’ monument “Le Fritz” on the Col des Rangiers off its base in 1984?
16783.e: The Béliers were the militant youth organisation of the separatists. With spectacular actions like this one, they drew attention to the Jura question.
16783.m: The Béliers were the militant youth of the Jura separatists.

16784.q: Which Bernese district moved to the canton of Basel-Landschaft in 1994?
16784.e: The German-speaking Laufental at first stayed with Bern in 1974. After a repeated vote in 1989, it moved to Basel-Landschaft in 1994.
16784.m: The Laufental has belonged to Basel-Landschaft since 1994.

16785.q: Why was Moutier’s vote of 18 June 2017 on changing canton later declared invalid?
a: Because of irregularities in the vote
Because too few people had voted
Because the Federal Council was against it
Because the canton of Jura rejected the change
16785.e: The Bernese authorities annulled the result in 2018 because of irregularities. On 28 March 2021 Moutier again voted for the change, with about 55 per cent.
16785.m: Moutier had to vote a second time on the change in 2021.

16786.q: Since when has the town of Moutier belonged to the canton of Jura?
16786.e: After the vote of 2021 and approval by the Federal Assembly, Moutier moved to the canton of Jura on 1 January 2026.
16786.m: Since 2026 Moutier has been a municipality of the Jura.

16787.q: On what date did Switzerland vote on joining the European Economic Area?
16787.e: The EEA vote of 6 December 1992 is considered one of the most important votes of the post-war period. It still shapes European policy today.
16787.m: On 6 December 1992 Switzerland said no to the EEA.

16788.q: How narrowly was joining the EEA rejected in 1992?
16788.e: Only 49.7 per cent voted yes and about 50.3 per cent no. The majority of the cantons, on the other hand, was clearly missed.
16788.m: Among the people, the no to the EEA in 1992 was wafer-thin.

16789.q: What was the turnout in the EEA vote of 1992?
16789.e: At about 78.7 per cent, turnout was historically high. This shows how strongly the question moved the population.
16789.m: The EEA vote mobilised almost four out of five voters.

16790.q: Which regions voted for the EEA in 1992?
a: All the French-speaking cantons and the two Basels
All the German-speaking cantons and Ticino
16790.e: French-speaking Switzerland (the Romandie) said yes as one, as did Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft. The rest of German-speaking Switzerland and Ticino said no.
16790.m: On the EEA, the Romandie and the two Basels voted yes.

16791.q: Which canton had the highest share of yes votes for the EEA in 1992?
16791.e: Neuchâtel agreed most clearly with about 80 per cent yes, just ahead of Vaud and Geneva. The whole of French-speaking Switzerland was clearly in favour of joining.
16791.m: In 1992 Neuchâtel was the most pro-European canton.

16792.q: Which term describes the language border that became especially visible in the EEA result?
16792.e: The Röstigraben (literally “rösti ditch”) refers to the different voting results between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. In the EEA vote the difference was especially large.
16792.m: In 1992 the Röstigraben divided German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.

16793.q: Which organisation led the campaign against joining the EEA?
a: The Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland
The Swiss Federation of Trade Unions
16793.e: The AUNS led the no campaign. It was supported by the SVP among others, especially the Zurich SVP under Christoph Blocher.
16793.m: The AUNS and Christoph Blocher shaped the no to the EEA.

16794.q: What step had the Federal Council taken in May 1992, before the EEA vote?
a: It applied to join the European Community
It cancelled the free trade agreement of 1972
It signed the Bilateral Agreements I
16794.e: The application to join the EC fuelled the debate even more. Many opponents therefore saw the EEA as a first step towards joining the EC.
16794.m: The 1992 application to join the EC sharpened the EEA debate.

16795.q: Which path did Switzerland choose for its relations with the EU after the no to the EEA?
a: The bilateral path with agreements in individual sectors
