16795.e: After the no, Switzerland negotiated individual agreements with the EU. The Bilateral Agreements I were accepted by the people on 21 May 2000.
16795.m: After the no to the EEA, Switzerland took the bilateral path.

16796.q: Which EFTA states belong to the EEA today?
16796.e: Austria, Sweden and Finland joined the EU in 1995. Today Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway form the EFTA pillar of the EEA.
16796.m: Without Switzerland, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway form the EFTA part of the EEA.

16797.q: What did Liechtenstein do after the Swiss no to the EEA?
a: It voted to join shortly afterwards and joined in 1995
It left the customs union with Switzerland
It also decided against the EEA
16797.e: A week after the Swiss no, the people of Liechtenstein said yes. After changes to the customs union with Switzerland, the agreement came into force for Liechtenstein in 1995.
16797.m: Despite the Swiss no, Liechtenstein has been in the EEA since 1995.

16798.q: Which canton rejected joining the EEA most clearly in 1992?
16798.e: In Uri only about 25 per cent voted yes, so about three quarters voted no. The cantons of Central Switzerland were especially sceptical about Europe.
16798.m: Uri said no to the EEA most clearly in 1992.

16799.q: When did the people and the cantons accept the new Federal Constitution?
16799.e: The totally revised Federal Constitution was accepted on 18 April 1999. It came into force on 1 January 2000.
16799.m: Today’s Federal Constitution was accepted in 1999.

16800.q: What was the popular vote on the new Federal Constitution in 1999?
a: A clear yes, with just under 60 per cent
A wafer-thin yes with 50.1 per cent
16800.e: 59.2 per cent of voters said yes. Among the people the result was clear, but among the cantons it was close.
16800.m: The Federal Constitution of 1999 received almost 60 per cent yes.

16801.q: What was striking about the majority of the cantons for the new Federal Constitution in 1999?
a: It was missed, but the constitution came into force anyway
It was not counted at all
16801.e: Only 13 of the 23 cantonal votes were in favour. Without a majority of the cantons the constitution would have failed, because constitutional changes need both the people and the cantons.
16801.m: Among the cantons, the new constitution was accepted only narrowly.

16802.q: Since when has today’s Federal Constitution been in force?
16802.e: The Federal Constitution came into force on 1 January 2000 and replaced the constitution of 1874.
16802.m: Today’s Federal Constitution has applied since 2000.

16803.q: Which constitution was replaced by the Federal Constitution of 1999?
16803.e: The constitution of 1874 was a total revision of the constitution of 1848. With many partial revisions, it applied until the end of 1999.
16803.m: The constitution of 1874 applied until the end of 1999.

16804.q: How did the Federal Council describe its draft constitution of 1996?
a: As an update of existing constitutional law
As a revolution in popular rights
As a treaty for joining the EU
16804.e: The main aim was to rewrite the existing law in a clear and orderly way. Unwritten constitutional law from court rulings was included.
16804.m: The constitution of 1999 was mainly an update.

16805.q: With which words does the preamble of the Federal Constitution begin?
16805.e: The preamble begins by calling on God, as earlier federal constitutions did. It was deliberately kept during the debate.
16805.m: The Federal Constitution begins by calling on God.

16806.q: What are the social goals in the Federal Constitution?
a: Goals for the federal government and the cantons, but not rights you can enforce in court
Rights to housing and work that you can enforce in court
Duties of citizens towards the state
Rules for wage negotiations between employers and unions
16806.e: The federal government and the cantons work for social security, health, education and housing, for example. However, you cannot claim a right in court directly from them.
16806.m: The social goals are goals, not rights you can enforce in court.

16807.q: What is an important new feature of the 1999 Federal Constitution compared with that of 1874?
a: A detailed, written list of fundamental rights
The founding of the federal state
16807.e: Many fundamental rights had previously only existed as unwritten constitutional law from the Federal Supreme Court. In 1999 they were written down systematically, for example human dignity.
16807.m: Since 1999 the fundamental rights have been set out in detail in the constitution.

16808.q: Which fundamental right is in Article 7, as the first fundamental right of the Federal Constitution?
16808.e: Article 7 says, in essence, that human dignity must be respected and protected. It deliberately comes at the start of the list of fundamental rights.
16808.m: Human dignity comes first among the fundamental rights.

16809.q: Which federal department led the work on the new Federal Constitution of 1999?
a: The Department of Justice and Police
16809.e: Constitutional questions belong to the Department of Justice and Police. There, Federal Councillor Arnold Koller pushed the reform forward until the vote in 1999.
16809.m: The constitutional reform of 1999 was led by the Department of Justice.

16810.q: When was the Swiss federal state founded with its first Federal Constitution?
16810.e: The Federal Constitution of 12 September 1848 turned Switzerland from a confederation of states into a federal state. Total revisions followed in 1874 and 1999.
16810.m: The constitution of 1999 is the third federal constitution since 1848.

16811.q: How clearly did the people reject joining the UN on 16 March 1986?
a: With about 75 per cent no and without a single canton in favour
With about 60 per cent no and 12 cantons
16811.e: Only 24.3 per cent voted yes in 1986, and no canton accepted the proposal. The Federal Council and parliament had recommended joining.
16811.m: In 1986 Switzerland overwhelmingly rejected joining the UN.

16812.q: When did the people and the cantons agree to join the UN?
16812.e: On 3 March 2002 the popular initiative for joining the UN was accepted. That was 16 years after the clear no of 1986.
16812.m: On 3 March 2002 Switzerland said yes to the UN.

16813.q: What was the share of yes votes in the UN vote of 2002?
16813.e: The proposal was accepted with 54.6 per cent yes. The popular majority was clear, but the majority of the cantons was very narrow.
16813.m: Joining the UN received about 55 per cent yes in 2002.

16814.q: How narrow was the majority of the cantons for joining the UN in 2002?
16814.e: A single cantonal vote made the difference. If one canton had voted differently, joining would have failed for lack of a majority of the cantons.
16814.m: The majority of the cantons for joining the UN was as narrow as it could be.

16815.q: What was special internationally about Switzerland’s way into the UN?
a: It was the only country to join as the result of a popular vote
It was forced to join by the USA
It joined NATO at the same time
It joined without a vote, by Federal Council decision
16815.e: Switzerland is the only country that joined the UN after a decision by the people. The vote was triggered by a popular initiative.
16815.m: Switzerland is the only country that joined the UN by popular vote.

16816.q: On what date was Switzerland admitted to the UN?
16816.e: The UN General Assembly in New York admitted Switzerland on 10 September 2002. East Timor followed shortly afterwards.
16816.m: Switzerland has been a UN member since 10 September 2002.

16817.q: As which number member did Switzerland join the UN?
16817.e: In 2002 Switzerland became the 190th member of the United Nations. East Timor followed a few weeks later as the 191st member.
16817.m: Switzerland is the 190th member of the UN.

16818.q: What status did Switzerland have at the UN before joining?
a: It was a permanent member of the Security Council
It had no contact at all with the UN
It was an associate member with voting rights
16818.e: Switzerland had observer status from 1948 and was active in many UN specialised agencies. It only got full voting rights in the General Assembly in 2002.
16818.m: Before 2002 Switzerland was only an observer at the UN.

16819.q: Which argument of the opponents played a central role in the UN vote of 1986?
a: The wish to join the EU
16819.e: Many feared that sanctions and decisions of the Security Council would not be compatible with neutrality. This argument strongly shaped the debate during the Cold War.
16819.m: Neutrality was the main argument against joining the UN in 1986.

16820.q: In which years was Switzerland a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the first time?
16820.e: Switzerland was elected by the General Assembly in 2022 and sat on the Security Council for the first time in 2023 and 2024. The candidacy was controversial at home.
16820.m: Switzerland sat on the Security Council for the first time in 2023 and 2024.

16821.q: Which city is the European headquarters of the UN?
16821.e: The Palais des Nations in Geneva was previously the seat of the League of Nations. After 1946 Geneva became the European seat of the United Nations.
16821.m: Geneva is the most important UN location in Europe.

16822.q: Which international organisation had Switzerland already joined in 1920?
16822.e: After a popular vote in May 1920, Switzerland joined the League of Nations, which had its seat in Geneva. The UN replaced the League of Nations in 1946.
16822.m: Switzerland was already a member of the League of Nations.

16823.q: In which year did Mikhail Gorbachev become General Secretary of the CPSU?
16823.e: Gorbachev took office on 11 March 1985, one day after the death of his predecessor. He was 54 years old at the time.
16823.m: Gorbachev became head of the Soviet party in 1985.

16824.q: Whom did Gorbachev succeed as General Secretary of the CPSU?
16824.e: Chernenko died after only just over a year in office. The Central Committee then chose the much younger Gorbachev.
16824.m: The ill Chernenko was followed by the young Gorbachev.

16825.q: Which top Soviet politician particularly promoted Gorbachev’s rise in the 1980s?
16825.e: The former KGB chief Yuri Andropov was regarded as Gorbachev’s important patron. Under him, Gorbachev became one of his closest allies in the Politburo.
16825.m: Yuri Andropov was an important patron of Gorbachev.

16826.q: Which region of the Soviet Union did Mikhail Gorbachev come from?
a: Stavropol region in the North Caucasus
16826.e: Gorbachev was born in 1931 in the village of Privolnoye in the Stavropol region. He also began his party career there.
16826.m: Gorbachev came from the Stavropol region in the North Caucasus.

16827.q: What does the Russian term “glasnost”, which Gorbachev made a political slogan, mean?
16827.e: Glasnost stood for more openness in the media and public life. Problems could now be talked about more openly.

16828.q: What does the term “perestroika” refer to?
a: The restructuring of the economy and society
The opening of the KGB archives
The rearmament of the Red Army
16828.e: Perestroika literally means restructuring. With it, Gorbachev wanted to reform the rigid planned economy and the political system.
16828.m: Perestroika stands for the restructuring of the Soviet system.

16829.q: In which Swiss city did Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan meet for the first time in November 1985?
16829.e: The Geneva summit took place from 19 to 21 November 1985, partly at the Villa Fleur d’Eau in Versoix. It was the first summit between the two superpowers in six years.
16829.m: The first meeting between Reagan and Gorbachev took place in Geneva in 1985.

16830.q: What was the most important result of the Geneva summit of 1985?
a: A new line of dialogue between the superpowers
A treaty to scrap all nuclear weapons
The dissolution of the Warsaw Pact
16830.e: No major disarmament agreement was signed in Geneva. But both sides agreed on further meetings, which noticeably improved the climate in the Cold War.
16830.m: The Geneva summit of 1985 brought above all trust and further talks.

16831.q: In which city did Reagan and Gorbachev meet in October 1986 and negotiate far-reaching disarmament?
16831.e: The Reykjavík summit on 11 and 12 October 1986 ended without a treaty. But it paved the way for later disarmament agreements.
16831.m: In Reykjavík in 1986 the superpowers came close on disarmament.

16832.q: Which weapons did the INF Treaty, signed by Reagan and Gorbachev in December 1987, ban?
16832.e: The INF Treaty of 8 December 1987 banned land-based missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometres. By 1991, 2,692 such missiles had been destroyed.
16832.m: The INF Treaty abolished an entire class of nuclear missiles.

16833.q: Where was the INF Treaty signed in December 1987?
a: In the White House in Washington
In the Palais des Nations in Geneva
16833.e: Gorbachev travelled to Washington for the signing. The treaty came into force on 1 June 1988.
16833.m: The INF Treaty was signed in Washington in 1987.

16834.q: When did the last Soviet troops leave Afghanistan?
16834.e: On 15 February 1989 the last Soviet column crossed the border. Gorbachev had recognised the costly war as a burden and decided to withdraw.
16834.m: Under Gorbachev the Soviet Union withdrew from Afghanistan by February 1989.

16835.q: Which disaster of 1986 put Gorbachev’s policy of openness to a hard test?
16835.e: On 26 April 1986 a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant. The hesitant information given to the public at first contradicted glasnost.
16835.m: Chernobyl in 1986 showed the limits of Soviet openness.

16836.q: What did the so-called “Sinatra Doctrine” of the late 1980s say?
a: The Eastern Bloc states could choose their own way
The Soviet Union would intervene militarily against reforms
The USSR adopted Western music as cultural policy
All Eastern Bloc states had to follow perestroika
16836.e: The joking name refers to Frank Sinatra’s song “My Way”. With it Moscow moved away from the Brezhnev Doctrine, which had justified interventions in “brother states”.
16836.m: The Sinatra Doctrine let the Eastern Bloc states go their own way.

16837.q: Which doctrine did Gorbachev effectively abandon with his new foreign policy?
16837.e: In 1968 the Brezhnev Doctrine justified the invasion of Czechoslovakia. Gorbachev gave up such interventions, which made the revolutions of 1989 possible in the first place.
16837.m: Gorbachev gave up the Brezhnev Doctrine of limited sovereignty.

16838.q: Which award did Gorbachev receive in 1990?
a: The Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought
16838.e: In October 1990 the Nobel Committee honoured his role in the peaceful end of the Cold War. In the Soviet Union itself he was already controversial at that time.
16838.m: Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

16839.q: Which office did Gorbachev take on in March 1990 in addition to leading the party?
16839.e: In March 1990 the Congress of People’s Deputies elected him the first and only President of the USSR. He remained in office until December 1991.
16839.m: Gorbachev was the first and only President of the Soviet Union.

16840.q: What did Article 6 of the Soviet constitution, amended in March 1990, lay down?
a: The leading role of the Communist Party
The right of the republics to leave
The planned economy as the economic system
Compulsory military service for all men
16840.e: Article 6 guaranteed the CPSU its monopoly on power. When it was amended at Gorbachev’s urging, other parties became possible.
16840.m: When Article 6 was struck out in 1990, the CPSU lost its monopoly on power.

16841.q: Who said of Gorbachev in December 1984 that one could “do business” with him?
16841.e: After Gorbachev’s visit to Britain in December 1984, the British Prime Minister said: “We can do business together.” He was not yet General Secretary at the time.
16841.m: Margaret Thatcher recognised early on that negotiations with Gorbachev were possible.

16842.q: With which US President did Gorbachev declare the end of the Cold War at the Malta summit in December 1989?
16842.e: At the summit on 2 and 3 December 1989, Bush and Gorbachev met on a ship off Malta. Because of the stormy weather, the media called it the “Seasick Summit”.
16842.m: In 1989 off Malta, Bush and Gorbachev declared the Cold War over.

16843.q: For what occasion did Gorbachev visit East Berlin in October 1989?
a: The opening of the Palace of the Republic
The signing of the Warsaw Pact
16843.e: On 7 October 1989 the GDR celebrated 40 years of its existence. During his visit many people chanted “Gorbi, Gorbi”, while Honecker rejected reforms.
16843.m: Gorbachev’s visit for the GDR’s 40th anniversary encouraged the reformers.

16844.q: Which sentence is attributed to Gorbachev in connection with his visit to the GDR in 1989, although it is not documented word for word?
a: “Life punishes those who come too late.”
16844.e: The sentence became a well-known saying, but it is a shortened version of remarks to journalists and the SED leadership. Seen critically, it is an exaggerated version of what was said.
16844.m: The sentence about coming too late is an exaggerated version, not a word-for-word quotation.

16845.q: How did Gorbachev do in the Russian presidential election of 1996?
a: He received less than one percent of the votes
He only lost to Yeltsin in the run-off
He was not allowed to stand because of illness
16845.e: In 1996 Gorbachev received only about half a percent of the votes. In Russia many people blamed him for the collapse of the Soviet Union and the economic crisis.
16845.m: Celebrated in the West, Gorbachev had no political chance in Russia in 1996.

16846.e: Gorbachev died in Moscow on 30 August 2022 at the age of 91. He was buried in Novodevichy Cemetery next to his wife Raisa.
16846.m: Mikhail Gorbachev died in Moscow in 2022.

16847.q: Which person, as Gorbachev’s wife, played an unusually public role for Soviet times?
16847.e: Raisa Gorbacheva accompanied her husband on trips abroad and appeared self-confident. Earlier wives of Soviet party leaders mostly stayed in the background.
16847.m: Raisa Gorbacheva was more in the public eye than earlier wives of Soviet leaders.

16848.q: On which date was the Berlin Wall opened?
16848.e: On the evening of 9 November 1989 the border crossings in Berlin opened under pressure from the crowds. The date is a symbol of the end of the division of Europe.
16848.m: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989.

16849.q: Which member of the SED Politburo announced the new travel rules at a press conference on 9 November 1989?
16849.e: Shortly before 7 p.m. Schabowski read out a regulation whose content he himself did not know exactly. His words set off the rush to the border that same evening.
16849.m: Günter Schabowski’s press conference triggered the fall of the Wall.

16850.q: What did Schabowski answer when asked from when the new travel rules applied?
16850.e: In fact the rules were only supposed to apply from the next day. Schabowski’s spontaneous answer was broadcast on Western television and brought thousands to the border crossings.
16850.m: Schabowski’s “immediately, without delay” set off the rush to the border.

16851.q: Which border crossing was the first to be opened on the evening of 9 November 1989?
16851.e: The officer on duty, Harald Jäger, had the Bornholmer Strasse crossing opened late in the evening because the crowd was getting too big. There were no orders from above to do so.
16851.m: The Wall opened first at Bornholmer Strasse.

16852.q: How did the famous cellist Mstislav Rostropovich celebrate the fall of the Wall on 11 November 1989?
a: He played Bach in front of the Wall at Checkpoint Charlie
He gave a concert in the Kremlin in Moscow
He played in the Bundestag in Bonn
He gave a concert in front of the White House
16852.e: The musician, who had been stripped of his Soviet citizenship, travelled to Berlin on the spur of the moment and played Bach in front of the Wall on 11 November 1989. The pictures went around the world.
16852.m: Mstislav Rostropovich celebrated the fall of the Wall with his cello at Checkpoint Charlie.

16853.q: Which country did the correspondent Riccardo Ehrman, who asked Schabowski about the travel law on 9 November 1989, come from?
16853.e: The Italian correspondent Riccardo Ehrman worked for the ANSA agency and asked about the travel law shortly before the end of the press conference. Exactly who then asked when it would apply has not been clearly established.
16853.m: A question from an Italian journalist brought the travel rules into the discussion.

16854.q: What happened on 19 August 1989 on the Hungarian-Austrian border near Sopron?
a: The signing of the Helsinki Final Act
The founding of the civic movement New Forum
The dismantling of the Berlin Wall
16854.e: At the Pan-European Picnic a border gate was opened for about three hours. Between 600 and 700 GDR citizens fled to Austria.
16854.m: The Pan-European Picnic of 1989 made a first hole in the Iron Curtain.

16855.q: What was the Pan-European Picnic of 19 August 1989 on the Hungarian-Austrian border originally meant to be?
a: A sign of a united Europe without borders
A celebration of the GDR’s 40th anniversary
A meeting of the Warsaw Pact heads of state
A celebration of the end of the Second World War
16855.e: The Paneuropean Union and the Hungarian Democratic Forum organised the picnic as a sign of a united Europe. A border gate was opened for about three hours, and hundreds of GDR citizens fled.
16855.m: The Pan-European Picnic was meant to be a sign of a united Europe.

16856.q: When did Hungary finally open its border to Austria for GDR citizens?
16856.e: Hungary had already begun dismantling the border fence in May 1989. From 11 September 1989 GDR citizens could officially leave, and tens of thousands did so.
16856.m: From 11 September 1989 there was a way out of the GDR to the West via Hungary.

16857.q: What did the foreign ministers of Hungary and Austria do in front of the cameras on 27 June 1989?
a: They symbolically cut through the border fence
They closed the border to GDR citizens
16857.e: Gyula Horn and Alois Mock cut the fence with wire cutters. The pictures gave many GDR citizens the courage to flee via Hungary.
16857.m: In 1989 Hungary and Austria symbolically cut through the Iron Curtain.

16858.q: What did Hans-Dietrich Genscher announce on 30 September 1989 from the balcony of the West German embassy in Prague?
a: That the refugees could leave for West Germany
The opening of the Berlin Wall
16858.e: Thousands of GDR citizens had fled into the embassy. Genscher’s sentence was drowned out by cheering and is seen as a key moment of autumn 1989.
16858.m: Genscher’s speech in Prague allowed thousands of embassy refugees to leave.

16859.q: Why is the Monday demonstration in Leipzig on 9 October 1989 seen as a turning point?
a: About 70,000 people demonstrated without the state using violence
The People’s Army fired on the demonstrators
Honecker spoke to the demonstrators in person
The demonstrators occupied the Stasi headquarters
16859.e: Many feared a violent crackdown. Because the security forces did not intervene, people lost their fear and the protests grew.
16859.m: On 9 October 1989 non-violence won in Leipzig.

16860.q: Which chant did the demonstrators first use in autumn 1989 to challenge the rule of the SED?
16860.e: With “We are the people” people demanded a democratic say. Later the chant changed to “We are one people”, and so became a demand for unity.
16860.m: “We are the people” became the motto of the Peaceful Revolution.

16861.q: Who succeeded Erich Honecker as SED General Secretary on 18 October 1989?
16861.e: Honecker was pushed to resign by the Politburo. Krenz promised a “turnaround”, but was seen as part of the old system and stayed in office only a few weeks.
16861.m: Egon Krenz succeeded Erich Honecker in October 1989.

16862.q: What took place on Alexanderplatz in East Berlin on 4 November 1989?
a: One of the largest demonstrations in GDR history
The celebration of the GDR’s 40th anniversary
The demolition of the first piece of the Wall
16862.e: Hundreds of thousands demanded freedom of opinion, of the press and of assembly. It was an approved rally organised partly by artists and writers.
16862.m: On 4 November 1989 Alexanderplatz loudly demanded freedom.

16863.q: When was the last person trying to escape shot dead by border guards at the Berlin Wall?
a: In February 1989, a few months before the fall of the Wall
In August 1961, shortly after the Wall was built
In June 1953 during the popular uprising
On 9 November 1989, the day the Wall fell
16863.e: Chris Gueffroy was shot at the beginning of February 1989 while trying to escape. A few weeks later Winfried Freudenberg died when his gas balloon crashed.
16863.m: In 1989 Chris Gueffroy was the last person trying to escape who was shot at the Wall.

16864.q: What is the minimum number of deaths at the Berlin Wall given by the study of the Centre for Contemporary History?
16864.e: Research counts at least 140 deaths between 1961 and 1989, including 101 people trying to escape. The exact number is disputed, depending on how it is counted.
16864.m: At least about 140 people died at the Berlin Wall.

16865.q: When was the Brandenburg Gate opened to pedestrians after the fall of the Wall?
16865.e: Chancellor Kohl walked through the gate and was greeted by the GDR Prime Minister Hans Modrow. The gate thus became a symbol of unity.
16865.m: The Brandenburg Gate opened on 22 December 1989.

16866.q: When did the official demolition of the Berlin Wall begin?
16866.e: GDR border troops began the demolition at places including Bernauer Strasse. Before that, many “wall woodpeckers” had already chipped off pieces.
16866.m: The official demolition of the Wall began in June 1990.

16867.q: Where was Chancellor Helmut Kohl when the Wall fell on 9 November 1989?
a: On a state visit to Poland
16867.e: Kohl was on a state visit to Warsaw. He interrupted the trip on 10 November to come to Berlin.
16867.m: Kohl heard about the fall of the Wall in Poland.

16868.q: How much was the welcome money that GDR citizens received when visiting West Germany?
16868.e: The welcome money existed before 1989, but after the fall of the Wall millions of people collected it. Long queues formed outside banks.
16868.m: Every visitor from the GDR could collect 100 Deutschmarks of welcome money.

16869.q: Which US President demanded in Berlin in 1987: “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!”?
16869.e: Reagan spoke in front of the Brandenburg Gate in 1987. The speech only became a much-quoted symbol after 1989.
16869.m: In 1987 Reagan called on Gorbachev to tear down the Wall.

16870.q: Since when had the Berlin Wall divided East and West Berlin?
16870.e: In the night before 13 August 1961 the GDR sealed off the sector border with barbed wire. From 15 August concrete sections were put up.

16871.q: Roughly how long were the Berlin Wall’s border fortifications around West Berlin?
16871.e: The Wall around West Berlin was about 168 kilometres long. Just over 45 kilometres of it ran between East and West Berlin.
16871.m: The Wall enclosed West Berlin over about 160 kilometres.

16872.q: Which GDR civic movement was founded in September 1989 and called for open dialogue?
16872.e: New Forum was founded in September 1989 by opposition figures such as Bärbel Bohley. It became one of the most important voices of the Peaceful Revolution.
16872.m: In 1989 New Forum gave the opposition in the GDR a voice.

16874.q: How did reunification take place in constitutional terms?
a: By accession under Article 23 of the Basic Law
Through a new constitution under Article 146
Through a referendum in both states
Through a decision of the United Nations
16874.e: The GDR joined the area covered by the Basic Law. The quicker route via Article 23 was preferred to drawing up a new all-German constitution.
16874.m: The GDR joined the Basic Law under Article 23.

16875.q: When did the first free Volkskammer election in the GDR take place?
16875.e: Turnout was 93.4 percent. It was the first and only free parliamentary election in the GDR.
16875.m: In March 1990 the GDR held its first free election.

16876.q: Which alliance of parties won the Volkskammer election of March 1990?
16876.e: The alliance led by the CDU aimed for quick unity. The CDU alone had 163 of the 400 members.
16876.m: In 1990 the Alliance for Germany won with the promise of quick unity.

16877.q: Who was the first and only freely elected Prime Minister of the GDR?
16877.e: The CDU politician was elected in April 1990. He led the GDR until accession and was one of the signatories of the Two Plus Four Treaty.
16877.m: Lothar de Maizière led the GDR into its final phase.

16878.q: When did the monetary, economic and social union between West Germany and the GDR come into force?
16878.e: From that day the Deutschmark was also valid in the GDR. Economic unity thus came before political unity.
16878.m: On 1 July 1990 the Deutschmark arrived in the GDR.

16879.q: At what rate were wages and pensions converted in the monetary union of 1990?
16879.e: Wages, salaries and pensions were converted 1 to 1. Savings were only converted 1 to 1 up to an age-dependent limit, and 2 to 1 above that.
16879.m: In 1990 wages and pensions were converted one to one into Deutschmarks.

16880.q: What economic consequence did the favourable exchange rate of 1990 have for many GDR companies?
a: They suddenly became too expensive and lost their markets
They were able to increase their exports greatly
They automatically received large Western orders
They were all taken over by the Soviet Union
16880.e: Costs rose overnight to Deutschmark levels, while productivity stayed low. In addition, the markets in Eastern Europe collapsed, which ruined many companies.
16880.m: The monetary union made many East German companies uncompetitive overnight.

16881.q: What was the task of the Treuhandanstalt (trust agency)?
16881.e: The Treuhand took over about 8,500 state-owned companies with more than four million employees. Its work is still controversial today because of the many closures.
16881.m: The Treuhandanstalt privatised the GDR’s economy.

16882.q: What did Chancellor Helmut Kohl present to the Bundestag in November 1989, shortly after the fall of the Wall?
a: A ten-point programme for German unity
16882.e: Kohl presented the programme on 28 November 1989 without informing the allies beforehand. At first it provided for a gradual coming together of the two German states.
16882.m: Kohl’s ten-point programme of 1989 put unity on the political agenda.

16883.q: Which states negotiated the external aspects of unity in the Two Plus Four Treaty?
a: West Germany, the GDR, the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France
West Germany, the GDR, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Austria and Switzerland
West Germany, the GDR and the four Scandinavian states
West Germany, the GDR, the USA, China, Japan and India
16883.e: The two German states negotiated with the four victorious powers of the Second World War. These gave up their rights with regard to Germany and Berlin.
16883.m: The Two Plus Four Treaty settled unity with the four victorious powers.

16884.q: Where and when was the Two Plus Four Treaty signed?
16884.e: The treaty was signed in Moscow. On 1 October 1990 the Four Powers declared that they would suspend their rights from the day of unification.
16884.m: The Two Plus Four Treaty was signed in Moscow in September 1990.

16885.q: What did united Germany expressly give up in the Two Plus Four Treaty?
16885.e: Germany confirmed that it renounced NBC weapons and limited its armed forces to 370,000 soldiers. But it was allowed to remain a member of NATO.
16885.m: United Germany renounced nuclear, biological and chemical weapons.

16886.q: What concession did Kohl obtain at his meeting with Gorbachev in the Caucasus in July 1990?
a: United Germany could belong to NATO
The GDR could stay in the Warsaw Pact
Germany got its eastern territories back
The Soviet Union paid reparations to Germany
16886.e: In the talks on 15 and 16 July 1990, Gorbachev agreed to the free choice of alliance. Kohl afterwards spoke of a breakthrough.
16886.m: In the Caucasus in 1990 Gorbachev accepted a united Germany in NATO.

16887.q: Which border did united Germany confirm as final in a treaty with Poland in 1990?
16887.e: The German-Polish Border Treaty of November 1990 confirmed the border along the Oder and Neisse. This was a condition of the neighbours and the victorious powers for unity.
16887.m: In 1990 Germany finally recognised the Oder-Neisse border with Poland.

16888.q: What did the Unification Treaty between West Germany and the GDR of August 1990 regulate?
a: The adoption of West German law in the territory of the GDR
The consent of the four victorious powers to unity
The introduction of the Deutschmark in the GDR
16888.e: With extensive annexes, the Unification Treaty set out how West German law would be introduced in the GDR. The victorious powers gave their consent in the Two Plus Four Treaty, and the Deutschmark had already arrived on 1 July 1990.
16888.m: The Unification Treaty of August 1990 set out the details of unity.

16889.q: Which parliament decided in August 1990 that the GDR would join West Germany on 3 October 1990?
16889.e: In a night session on 23 August 1990, the freely elected Volkskammer voted by a large majority for accession. This fixed the date of unity.
16889.m: The Volkskammer decided on accession in August 1990.

16890.q: Which of these federal states is one of the five “new” states of 1990?
16890.e: The five new states are Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. They were re-established in 1990 after the GDR had introduced districts in 1952.
16890.m: With unity, five new federal states were created in the east.

16891.q: When did the first all-German Bundestag election take place?
16891.e: The election confirmed Helmut Kohl as Chancellor. For this election the five percent hurdle applied separately to East and West.
16891.m: In December 1990 the whole of Germany voted together for the first time.

16892.q: What did the Bundestag decide in a close vote on 20 June 1991?
a: Berlin would become the seat of parliament and government
Bonn would remain the capital for good
The solidarity surcharge would be abolished
The Deutschmark would be replaced by the euro
16892.e: Berlin won against Bonn by 338 votes to 320. Parliament and parts of the government had moved by 1999.
16892.m: In 1991 the Bundestag narrowly chose Berlin as the seat of government.

16893.q: Which expression used by Helmut Kohl in 1990 stands for his optimistic promises about the development of eastern Germany?
16893.e: Kohl announced that eastern Germany would quickly develop into blooming landscapes. The high unemployment of the following years often made the expression sound ironic.
16893.m: Kohl’s “blooming landscapes” became a symbol of disappointed expectations.

16894.q: By when had the last Russian troops withdrawn from the territory of the former GDR?
16894.e: The withdrawal of the former Soviet forces was settled in the Two Plus Four Treaty. The last units were given a farewell in Berlin in August 1994.
16894.m: The Russian troops left eastern Germany by 1994.

16895.q: Which levy was introduced in 1991, partly to pay for the costs of unity?
16895.e: The “Soli” was charged as a surcharge on income tax and corporation tax. Among other things, it was meant to help fund the rebuilding of the east.
16895.m: The solidarity surcharge helped to cover the costs of German unity.

16896.q: Who was West Germany’s Foreign Minister during the negotiations on German unity?
16896.e: Genscher led the Two Plus Four negotiations for West Germany. Wolfgang Schäuble, as Interior Minister, negotiated the Unification Treaty.
16896.m: Hans-Dietrich Genscher shaped the foreign policy of unity.

16897.q: What was the initial attitude of Great Britain and France towards rapid German unity?
a: They had demanded it even before the fall of the Wall
They refused to have any say
16897.e: Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand feared a Germany that would be too strong in Europe. Being bound into NATO and the European Community helped to ease these worries.
16897.m: London and Paris at first met German unity with scepticism.

16898.q: How many union republics did the Soviet Union consist of before its collapse?
16898.e: The 15 union republics became independent states in 1991. The largest was the Russian Soviet Republic, the RSFSR.
16898.m: 15 independent states emerged from the Soviet Union.

16899.q: Which Soviet republic was the first to declare its independence, on 11 March 1990?
16899.e: Lithuania declared the restoration of its independence. Moscow responded with an economic blockade.
16899.m: In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

16900.q: What did the “Baltic Way” of 23 August 1989 commemorate?
a: The 50th anniversary of the Hitler-Stalin Pact
The building of the Berlin Wall
16900.e: About two million people formed a human chain 650 to 675 kilometres long from Tallinn via Riga to Vilnius. The 1939 pact had prepared the occupation of the Baltic states.
16900.m: The Baltic Way commemorated the Hitler-Stalin Pact.

16901.q: What happened in Vilnius on 13 January 1991?
a: Soviet troops attacked the TV tower and 14 people died
The Soviet Union was officially dissolved
16901.e: Forces loyal to Moscow tried to regain control by force. However, the violence strengthened the will for independence.
16901.m: The January events in Vilnius in 1991 showed Moscow’s violent resistance.

16902.q: What was the result of the referendum on preserving the Soviet Union on 17 March 1991?
a: About 76 percent voted for a renewed union
Only Russia took part and voted against
16902.e: In the participating republics a clear majority voted for a reformed union. The Baltic states, Georgia, Armenia and Moldova boycotted the vote.
16902.m: In March 1991 a majority still voted to keep a reformed union.

16903.q: When was Boris Yeltsin elected President of the Russian Soviet Republic?
16903.e: Yeltsin received about 58.6 percent of the votes in the first popular election. This gave him a democratic legitimacy that Gorbachev lacked.
16903.m: In June 1991 Yeltsin was elected Russian President by the people.

16904.q: Which agreement was to be signed on 20 August 1991 and was one of the triggers of the August coup?
16904.e: The new Union Treaty would have given the republics considerably more rights. Conservative officials wanted to prevent this with the coup.
16904.m: The coup was meant to prevent the new Union Treaty.

16905.q: Who was behind the August coup of 1991 in Moscow?
a: Conservative communists from the party, KGB and army
Independence movements from the Baltic states
16905.e: Conservative officials, including the head of the KGB and the defence minister, wanted to stop Gorbachev’s reforms. They formed a State Committee on the State of Emergency, but failed after three days.
16905.m: In 1991 hardliners from the party, KGB and army wanted to stop the reforms.

16906.q: Where was Gorbachev when the August coup began in 1991?
a: At his dacha in Foros in Crimea
On a state visit to Washington
16906.e: Gorbachev was held at his holiday home and cut off from the outside world. After the coup failed, he returned to Moscow weakened.
16906.m: During the coup, Gorbachev was stuck in Crimea.

16907.q: Which image became the symbol of resistance to the August coup?
a: Yeltsin speaking from a tank in front of the White House
Gorbachev giving a speech on television
Tanks crossing the border into Poland
Demonstrators tearing down the Berlin Wall
16907.e: Yeltsin climbed onto a tank in front of the Russian parliament building and called for resistance. Thousands of people defended the building.
16907.m: Yeltsin on the tank became the image of victory over the coup.

16908.q: When did the Ukrainian parliament adopt Ukraine’s declaration of independence?
16908.e: Only a few days after the coup, the Verkhovna Rada declared independence. It was confirmed by a referendum on 1 December 1991.
16908.m: Ukraine declared itself independent on 24 August 1991.

16909.q: What share of voters said yes to independence in the Ukrainian referendum on 1 December 1991?
16909.e: About 92.3 percent voted yes, with a turnout of about 84 percent. On the same day Leonid Kravchuk was elected the first President.
16909.m: In 1991 more than 90 percent of Ukrainians voted for independence.

16910.q: Which three republics signed the Belovezha Accords on 8 December 1991?
16910.e: Yeltsin, Kravchuk and Shushkevich declared that the Soviet Union no longer existed. At the same time they founded the Commonwealth of Independent States.
16910.m: In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus sealed the end of the USSR.

16911.q: How many former Soviet republics signed the Alma-Ata Declaration on the CIS on 21 December 1991?
16911.e: All successor states except the three Baltic states and Georgia signed, including the three founding states. The Soviet Union had thus effectively been replaced.
16911.m: With Alma-Ata, the CIS grew to eleven states in 1991.

16912.q: What happened in the Kremlin on 25 December 1991?
a: The Red Army held a victory parade
The new Union Treaty came into force
Lenin’s body was removed from the mausoleum
16912.e: On the evening after Gorbachev’s resignation, the red flag with the hammer and sickle was lowered. The Russian tricolour flew in its place.
16912.m: On 25 December 1991 the Soviet flag disappeared from the Kremlin.

16913.q: What did Gorbachev hand over to Boris Yeltsin when he resigned on 25 December 1991?
a: Control of the nuclear weapon codes
The presidency of the United Nations
The office of General Secretary of the CPSU
The leadership of the Warsaw Pact
16913.e: With the so-called nuclear briefcase, control of the nuclear weapons passed to the Russian President. The handover of power was peaceful.
16913.m: In 1991 Gorbachev handed the nuclear codes to Yeltsin.

16914.q: When was the Soviet Union formally dissolved?
16914.e: The Council of the Republics of the Supreme Soviet declared the dissolution with Declaration 142-N. Gorbachev had resigned the day before.
16914.m: The Soviet Union formally ceased to exist on 26 December 1991.

16915.q: Which Eastern Bloc economic organisation decided to dissolve itself in Budapest in June 1991?
a: The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance
16915.e: Founded in 1949, the CMEA, called Comecon in the West, coordinated the planned economies. At its last meeting on 28 June 1991 it decided to dissolve.
16915.m: With Comecon, the economic bond holding the Eastern Bloc together also disappeared in 1991.

16916.q: Which conflict over a territory in the Caucasus broke out between Armenia and Azerbaijan in 1988?
16916.e: In February 1988 the regional soviet of Nagorno-Karabakh voted to join Armenia. Violence and expulsions followed, which Moscow could not stop.
16916.m: The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict showed early on the USSR’s problems with its nationalities.

16917.q: Which present-day Russian holiday commemorates Russia’s declaration of sovereignty in 1990?
16917.e: On 12 June 1990 Russia declared its state sovereignty and placed its laws above those of the Union. Russia Day commemorates this today.
16917.m: Russia Day on 12 June commemorates the declaration of sovereignty of 1990.

16918.q: Which state took over the Soviet Union’s permanent seat on the UN Security Council after 1991?
16918.e: Russia was recognised as the continuing state of the Soviet Union. It thus also took over the right of veto in the Security Council.
16918.m: In 1991 Russia inherited the USSR’s seat on the Security Council.

16919.q: What assurance did Ukraine receive in the Budapest Memorandum of 1994 for giving up its nuclear weapons?
a: Respect for its borders and sovereignty
A permanent seat on the UN Security Council
16919.e: Russia, the USA and Great Britain assured Ukraine that they would respect its territorial integrity. In return, Ukraine handed over the Soviet nuclear weapons on its territory to Russia.
16919.m: In the Budapest Memorandum of 1994 Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in exchange for security assurances.

16920.q: Which Soviet republic was the last to declare its independence, in December 1991?
16920.e: Kazakhstan declared its independence on 16 December 1991, only a few days before the Alma-Ata conference. Alma-Ata was its capital at the time.
16920.m: Kazakhstan was the last Soviet republic to become independent, in 1991.

16921.q: Besides the nationalism of the republics, which factor contributed significantly to the collapse of the Soviet Union?
a: The severe economic crisis of the planned economy
A war with the People’s Republic of China
16921.e: Shortages, falling oil prices and expensive arms spending greatly weakened the economy. Gorbachev’s reforms could not stop the decline.
16921.m: Economic crisis and national movements together brought down the Soviet Union.

16922.q: Which organisation, founded by six states in 1951, is seen as the seed of today’s EU?
a: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe
16922.e: The ECSC was founded on 18 April 1951 by Belgium, West Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. It placed coal and steel under common supervision.
16922.m: The Coal and Steel Community of 1951 is seen as the beginning of European unification.

16923.q: Which treaties founded the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom in 1957?
16923.e: The Treaties of Rome were signed on 25 March 1957. They created the EEC and the European Atomic Energy Community.
16923.m: The EEC was created with the Treaties of Rome in 1957.

16924.q: Which treaty founded the European Union and came into force on 1 November 1993?
16924.e: The Maastricht Treaty was signed on 7 February 1992 and came into force in 1993. It founded the EU and set the path to monetary union.
16924.m: The Maastricht Treaty turned the Community into the European Union.

16925.q: How many states joined the EU in the eastern enlargement on 1 May 2004?
16925.e: On 1 May 2004 ten states joined, including Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the three Baltic states. It was the largest enlargement in EU history.
16925.m: The eastern enlargement of 2004 brought the EU ten new members.

16926.q: When was the euro introduced as cash, after already existing as book money from 1999?
16926.e: From 1999 the euro was used as book money for payments. Coins and banknotes came into circulation on 1 January 2002.
16926.m: Euro coins and banknotes have existed since 1 January 2002.

16927.q: On which day did the United Kingdom leave the EU after the 2016 referendum?
16927.e: In the referendum of 23 June 2016 a majority voted to leave. Brexit took place on 31 January 2020, followed by a transition period until the end of 2020.
16927.m: Brexit legally took place on 31 January 2020.

16928.q: How did Swiss voters decide on joining the European Economic Area (EEA) on 6 December 1992?
16928.e: The people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the EEA on 6 December 1992. Switzerland then chose the bilateral path with the EU.
16928.m: After the EEA no of 1992, Switzerland relied on bilateral agreements.

16929.q: When did the Bilateral Agreements I between Switzerland and the EU come into force?
16929.e: The seven agreements of the Bilaterals I were concluded in 1999 and approved by the people on 21 May 2000. They came into force on 1 June 2002.
16929.m: The Bilaterals I have applied since 2002 and include free movement of persons.

16930.q: In which city is the World Trade Organization (WTO) based?
16930.e: The WTO began its work on 1 January 1995 and is based in Geneva. It sets rules for international trade and settles trade disputes.
16930.m: The World Trade Organization is based in Geneva.

16931.q: Which agreement of 1947 was the forerunner of the World Trade Organization?
16931.e: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947 gradually lowered customs duties. After the Uruguay Round it became part of the WTO in 1995.
16931.m: The GATT of 1947 was the forerunner of the WTO.

16932.q: With which agreement, signed in April 1994, was the WTO founded?
16932.e: The Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO was signed in April 1994. It came into force on 1 January 1995.
16932.m: The Marrakesh Agreement created the World Trade Organization in 1994.

16933.q: Which highly populated country joined the WTO in December 2001?
16933.e: China became a member of the WTO in December 2001. Joining greatly strengthened China’s integration into world trade.
16933.m: By joining the WTO in 2001, China became a firm part of world trade.

16934.q: Which invention of the 1950s cut transport costs in world trade particularly sharply?
16934.e: The standard container, used by Malcolm McLean from 1956, made reloading faster and cheaper. It is seen as the technical basis of today’s globalisation.
16934.m: The container made transporting goods around the world cheap and fast.

16935.q: Where does the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum (WEF) traditionally take place?
16935.e: The WEF was founded by Klaus Schwab in 1971 and is based in Cologny near Geneva. Its annual meeting traditionally takes place in Davos.
16935.m: The World Economic Forum meets every year in Davos.

a: Moving parts of a company abroad
16936.e: In offshoring, companies move production or services to other countries, often because of lower costs. It is a typical feature of economic globalisation.
16936.m: Offshoring means that companies move work abroad.

16937.q: Which two republics declared their independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991?
16937.e: Slovenia and Croatia declared themselves independent on 25 June 1991. The Ten-Day War in Slovenia and the war in Croatia followed.
16937.m: The break-up of Yugoslavia began with the declarations of independence in 1991.

16938.q: Which long-serving head of state of Yugoslavia died in 1980?
16938.e: Josip Broz Tito led Yugoslavia from 1945 until his death on 4 May 1980. After that, tensions between the republics grew.
16938.m: After Tito’s death in 1980, tensions in Yugoslavia grew.

16939.q: How many Bosniak men and boys were killed in the Srebrenica massacre in July 1995?
16939.e: In July 1995 Bosnian Serb troops under Ratko Mladić killed more than 8,000 Bosniaks. International courts classified the crime as genocide.
16939.m: The Srebrenica massacre of 1995 was classified by courts as genocide.

16940.q: Which agreement ended the Bosnian War and was signed in Paris on 14 December 1995?
16940.e: The agreement was negotiated in Dayton (USA) in November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December 1995. It divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities.
16940.m: The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War in 1995.

16941.q: In which city was the UN tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) based?
16941.e: The UN Security Council created the tribunal in 1993. It sat in The Hague and, among others, sentenced Ratko Mladić to life imprisonment in 2017.
16941.m: War crimes in Yugoslavia were tried before the UN tribunal in The Hague.

16942.q: When did NATO carry out air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the Kosovo War?
16942.e: The NATO air strikes lasted from 24 March to 10 June 1999. They took place without an explicit mandate from the UN Security Council.
16942.m: In the Kosovo War in 1999 NATO carried out air strikes for about eleven weeks.

16943.q: When did Kosovo declare its independence from Serbia?
16943.e: Kosovo’s parliament declared independence on 17 February 2008. Serbia still does not recognise it (as of 2026); Switzerland recognised Kosovo in February 2008.

16944.q: What is the name of the Swiss Army contingent that has served in KFOR in Kosovo since 1999?
16944.e: Swisscoy has been part of the international Kosovo Force KFOR since 1999. It is a voluntary peace support mission of the Swiss Army.
16944.m: Since 1999 Swisscoy has helped to keep the peace in Kosovo.

16945.q: How many planes were hijacked by terrorists on 11 September 2001?
16945.e: The attackers hijacked four passenger planes. Two hit the World Trade Center, one hit the Pentagon and one crashed in Pennsylvania.
16945.m: Four planes were hijacked on 11 September 2001.

16946.q: Which terrorist organisation was responsible for the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16946.e: The attacks were planned by al-Qaeda under Osama bin Laden. The 19 attackers belonged to this network.
16946.m: Al-Qaeda was behind the attacks of 11 September.

16947.q: How many attackers took part in the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16947.e: Nineteen men hijacked the four planes. Fifteen of them were Saudi citizens.
16947.m: Nineteen attackers carried out the attacks of 11 September.

16948.q: Where did United Airlines Flight 93 crash after passengers had fought back against the hijackers?
16948.e: Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville in Pennsylvania. Its real target is not known for certain.
16948.m: Flight 93 did not reach its target and crashed in Pennsylvania.

16949.q: Which building near Washington was hit by American Airlines Flight 77?
16949.e: Flight 77 was steered into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. People died on the plane and in the building.
16949.m: The Pentagon was also hit on 11 September 2001.

16950.q: Which clause of the NATO treaty was applied for the first time in the alliance’s history after the attacks of 11 September 2001?
a: The mutual defence clause in Article 5
16950.e: On 12 September 2001 the NATO Council declared that Article 5 applied, provided the attack came from abroad. This was confirmed on 2 October 2001; it was the first use of the mutual defence clause.
16950.m: After 11 September, NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time.

16951.q: When and where was Osama bin Laden killed by a US special forces unit?
16951.e: Bin Laden was killed on 2 May 2011 in Operation Neptune Spear in Abbottabad. He had been hiding there for years.
16951.m: Osama bin Laden was killed in Pakistan in 2011.

16952.q: According to official figures, how many people died in total in the attacks of 11 September 2001?
16952.e: Officially 2,996 people died, including the 19 attackers. Most of the victims were in the World Trade Center in New York.
16952.m: The attacks of 11 September cost about 3,000 people their lives.

16953.q: On which day did the USA and its allies begin Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan?
16953.e: On 7 October 2001 attacks on Taliban and al-Qaeda positions began. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden.
16953.m: The war in Afghanistan began on 7 October 2001.

16954.q: Which international force was created by UN Resolution 1386 in December 2001?
16954.e: The International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) was at first meant to ensure security in Kabul. From 2003 it was under NATO command.
16954.m: ISAF was the international security force in Afghanistan.

16955.q: Who was chosen as head of the interim government at the Afghanistan conference on the Petersberg near Bonn at the end of 2001?
16955.e: The Petersberg conference formed an interim government at the end of 2001. Hamid Karzai was put at its head and later elected President.
16955.m: Hamid Karzai led Afghanistan after the fall of the Taliban.

16956.q: Which group took Kabul without a fight on 13 November 2001?
16956.e: The Afghan Northern Alliance entered Kabul in November 2001 after the Taliban had withdrawn. It was supported from the air by the USA.
16956.m: The Northern Alliance took over Kabul in November 2001.

16957.q: Between whom was the Doha Agreement concluded on 29 February 2020?
16957.e: The Doha Agreement set out the withdrawal of US troops. In return, the Taliban promised, among other things, not to give terrorist groups room to operate.
16957.m: In the Doha Agreement of 2020 the USA agreed the withdrawal with the Taliban.

16958.q: On which day did the Taliban take Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani flee?
16958.e: On 15 August 2021 the Taliban entered Kabul and Ghani left the country. This ended the government supported by Western states.
16958.m: On 15 August 2021 the Taliban took power in Kabul again.

16959.q: When did the last US soldiers leave Afghanistan?
16959.e: After an evacuation operation at Kabul airport, the last US soldiers flew out on 30 August 2021. This ended the mission of almost 20 years.
16959.m: The US military mission in Afghanistan ended in August 2021.

16960.q: What was the main task of NATO’s Resolute Support mission, which followed ISAF in Afghanistan in 2015?
a: Training and advising Afghan security forces
Guarding the border with Pakistan on its own
16960.e: After ISAF’s combat mission ended at the end of 2014, Resolute Support took over. It trained Afghan forces and ended in 2021.
16960.m: From 2015 Resolute Support was NATO’s training mission in Afghanistan.

16961.q: On which date did the Iraq War begin with attacks by the US-led coalition?
16961.e: The bombing began in the night between 19 and 20 March 2003. Ground troops then advanced quickly on Baghdad.
16961.m: The Iraq War began on 20 March 2003.

16962.q: What was the main reason the USA and Great Britain gave for attacking Iraq?
a: Its alleged possession of weapons of mass destruction
16962.e: The governments pointed above all to alleged weapons of mass destruction. Apart from old leftover stocks, no such weapons were found after the war.
16962.m: The claimed weapons of mass destruction were not found in Iraq.

16963.q: Which US Secretary of State presented alleged evidence against Iraq to the UN Security Council on 5 February 2003?
16963.e: Colin Powell presented material on alleged weapons programmes to the Security Council. Important parts of it later turned out to be false.
16963.m: Powell’s speech at the UN in 2003 is a well-known example of faulty intelligence.

16964.q: What happened to Saddam Hussein in December 2003?
a: He was captured by US troops near Tikrit
He fled into exile in Syria
He died in an air strike on Baghdad
16964.e: Saddam Hussein was captured on 13 December 2003 in a hiding place near Tikrit. He was then handed over to a special Iraqi court.
16964.m: Saddam Hussein was captured near Tikrit at the end of 2003.

16965.q: In which year was Saddam Hussein executed?
16965.e: After being sentenced on 5 November 2006, Saddam Hussein was executed on 30 December 2006.
16965.m: Saddam Hussein was executed at the end of 2006.

16966.q: Which two large EU states openly opposed the Iraq War in 2003?
16966.e: Germany and France spoke out against the war. Great Britain, Spain, Italy and Poland, on the other hand, supported the USA.
16966.m: The Iraq War divided the European states in 2003.

16967.q: In which year did the last US troops leave Iraq after the Iraq War?
16967.e: The US combat mission officially ended in August 2010. The last US soldiers left the country in December 2011 under President Obama.
16967.m: At the end of 2011 the last US troops left Iraq.

16968.q: Which terrorist militia proclaimed a “caliphate” in 2014 after conquests in Iraq and Syria?
16968.e: The so-called Islamic State conquered Mosul, among other places, in 2014 and proclaimed a caliphate. Its rise is closely linked to the instability after the Iraq War.
16968.m: Islamic State used the instability in Iraq for its rise.

16969.q: In which US market did the financial crisis begin from 2007?
a: The market for Greek government bonds
16969.e: Many home loans had been given to borrowers with poor creditworthiness. When house prices fell, the securities bundled from them lost much of their value.
16969.m: The financial crisis began with bad mortgage loans in the USA.

16970.q: Which US investment bank went bankrupt on 15 September 2008?
16970.e: Lehman Brothers filed for insolvency on 15 September 2008 after no government rescue came. Afterwards lending between banks almost collapsed worldwide.
16970.m: The collapse of Lehman Brothers made the financial crisis dramatically worse in 2008.

16971.q: How much money did the US rescue law of October 2008 provide for stabilising the banks?
16971.e: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 had a volume of 700 billion dollars. It funded the TARP programme.
16971.m: In 2008 the USA provided about 700 billion dollars to rescue the banks.

16972.q: Which major Swiss bank was supported by the Confederation and the National Bank in October 2008?
16972.e: On 16 October 2008 the Confederation and the SNB announced a rescue package for UBS. The Confederation subscribed to mandatory convertible notes worth 6 billion francs.
16972.m: The Confederation and the National Bank supported UBS in 2008.

16973.q: What did the National Bank’s stabilisation fund take over from UBS in 2008?
a: Risky securities that were hard to sell
16973.e: In 2008 the SNB set up the StabFund, which took over illiquid and risky securities from UBS. This relieved the bank’s balance sheet without the state taking over the bank.
16973.m: The National Bank’s StabFund took over risky securities from UBS in 2008.

16974.q: Which country was the first euro country to fall into a serious debt crisis from 2010 and receive rescue loans?
16974.e: In 2010 Greece received a first aid package from euro states and the IMF. The financial crisis thus turned into the euro crisis.
16974.m: The euro crisis began with Greece in 2010.

16975.q: Which President of the European Central Bank said in July 2012 that the ECB would do “whatever it takes” to preserve the euro?
16975.e: Mario Draghi made this promise in London in July 2012. Risk premiums on government bonds in the euro area then fell clearly.
16975.m: Draghi’s promise of 2012 calmed the markets in the euro crisis.

16976.q: What does the expression “too big to fail” mean in connection with the financial crisis?
a: A bank is so important that the state cannot let it collapse
A bank is too big to grow
A state is too big to go bankrupt
A stock exchange must never be closed
16976.e: If systemically important banks collapse, they can endanger the whole economy. That is why they were given stricter rules, in Switzerland for example through the too-big-to-fail legislation.
16976.m: Systemically important banks are so important that their collapse threatens the whole economy.

16977.q: Which event on 17 December 2010 in Sidi Bouzid is seen as the trigger of the Arab Spring?
a: The self-immolation of the vegetable seller Mohamed Bouazizi
The election of a new president
16977.e: Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in protest against arbitrary treatment by the authorities. Nationwide protests in Tunisia followed.
16977.m: Mohamed Bouazizi’s act sparked the protests in Tunisia.

16978.q: Which Tunisian President fled abroad on 14 January 2011?
16978.e: After weeks of protests, Ben Ali left Tunisia on 14 January 2011. He had ruled the country since 1987.
16978.m: Ben Ali was the first ruler to be overthrown in the Arab Spring.

16979.q: Which square in Cairo became the centre of the protests against President Hosni Mubarak in 2011?
16979.e: Hundreds of thousands gathered in Tahrir Square for weeks. On 11 February 2011 Mubarak resigned after about 30 years in power.
16979.m: Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after protests in Tahrir Square.

16980.q: What did UN Security Council Resolution 1973 of 17 March 2011 make possible?
16980.e: The resolution allowed measures to protect the civilian population in Libya, including a no-fly zone. Western states then intervened militarily.
16980.m: With Resolution 1973 the UN allowed intervention in Libya in 2011.

16981.q: When and where was Muammar al-Gaddafi killed?
16981.e: Gaddafi was killed near Sirte on 20 October 2011 after being captured. This ended his rule of more than 40 years.
16981.m: Gaddafi’s rule ended with his death in October 2011.

16982.q: Who was elected Egypt’s first freely elected President in 2012 and removed by the military in 2013?
16982.e: Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood won the presidential election of 2012. In July 2013 the military removed him.
16982.m: Mohamed Morsi was Egypt’s first freely elected President.

16983.q: Which group received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its contribution to democracy in Tunisia?
16983.e: The quartet of a trade union, an employers’ federation, a human rights league and the bar association mediated in a political crisis. For this it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.
16983.m: The Tunisian Dialogue Quartet received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.

16984.q: When did the rule of Bashar al-Assad in Syria, whose government had cracked down on protests from 2011, end?
16984.e: The protests of 2011 developed into a long civil war. On 8 December 2024 Assad fled to Russia after rebels had taken Damascus.
16984.m: Assad’s rule in Syria ended in December 2024.

16985.q: What is the name of the virus that causes the disease COVID-19?
16985.e: COVID-19 is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. The first known cases appeared at the end of 2019 in Wuhan in China.
16985.m: The SARS-CoV-2 virus causes the disease COVID-19.

16986.q: On which day did the World Health Organization (WHO) classify COVID-19 as a pandemic?
16986.e: On 30 January 2020 the WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern. On 11 March 2020 it spoke of a pandemic.
16986.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020.

16987.q: When and where was the first COVID-19 case confirmed in Switzerland?
16987.e: The first case was a man in the canton of Ticino. It was confirmed on 25 February 2020.
16987.m: The first Swiss COVID-19 case was confirmed in Ticino in February 2020.

16988.q: Which level under the Epidemics Act did the Federal Council declare on 16 March 2020?
a: A state of emergency under martial law
16988.e: The Epidemics Act has a normal, a special and an extraordinary situation. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation, and in June 2020 the special situation followed again.
16988.m: In March 2020 the extraordinary situation applied in Switzerland.

16989.q: Which vaccine did Swissmedic authorise on 19 December 2020 as the first COVID-19 vaccine, for a limited time?
16989.e: On 19 December 2020 Swissmedic granted temporary authorisation for the mRNA vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech. It was the first COVID-19 vaccine authorised in Switzerland.
16989.m: The first COVID-19 vaccine authorised in Switzerland came from Pfizer and BioNTech.

16990.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the Covid-19 Act on 13 June 2021?
16990.e: The Covid-19 Act was accepted with 60.2 percent yes. The amendments in November 2021 and the extension in June 2023 were also accepted.
16990.m: Voters said yes to the Covid-19 Act three times.

16991.q: For which basic research did Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023?
a: For work that made mRNA vaccines possible
16991.e: Karikó and Weissman found out how to change mRNA so that it does not cause strong inflammation. This was a basis for the COVID-19 vaccines.
16991.m: The research of Karikó and Weissman made mRNA vaccines possible.

16992.q: When did the WHO declare the end of the global health emergency due to COVID-19?
16992.e: On 5 May 2023 the WHO lifted the international emergency. However, it stressed that the virus was still circulating.
16992.m: The WHO ended the global COVID-19 emergency in May 2023.

16993.q: Which computer network of 1969 is considered the forerunner of the internet?
16993.e: ARPANET was built from 1969 on behalf of the US Department of Defense. At first it connected a few universities and research institutes.
16993.m: The ARPANET of 1969 is the forerunner of the internet.

16994.q: At which research institution did Tim Berners-Lee develop the World Wide Web from 1989?
16994.e: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the concept at CERN in March 1989, supported by Robert Cailliau. The first website went online in 1990.
16994.m: The World Wide Web was created at CERN near Geneva.

16995.q: What happened to the World Wide Web on 30 April 1993?
a: CERN released it for free use
It was sold to a company
It was banned in Europe for the first time
16995.e: On 30 April 1993 CERN made web technology available to the public free of licence fees. This helped it spread quickly around the world.
16995.m: Since 1993 the World Wide Web has been free for everyone to use.

16996.q: In which year did Apple present the first iPhone?
16996.e: Steve Jobs presented the iPhone in January 2007. With its touchscreen and mobile internet access, it greatly changed the way people use digital services.
16996.m: The triumph of smartphones began with the iPhone in 2007.

16997.q: Since when has the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applied?
16997.e: The GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018. It also applies to Swiss companies that process data of people in the EU.
16997.m: Since 2018 the GDPR has governed data protection in the EU.

16998.q: When did Switzerland’s revised Data Protection Act come into force?
16998.e: The fully revised Data Protection Act has applied since 1 September 2023. It brought Swiss data protection up to date with digital developments and European standards.
16998.m: The new Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.

16999.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the law on a state e-ID on 28 September 2025?
a: Narrowly accepted with about 50.4 percent yes
Clearly rejected with about 64 percent no
Clearly accepted with about 64 percent yes
Narrowly rejected with about 50.4 percent no
16999.e: A first e-ID proposal with private providers had been rejected on 7 March 2021 with about 64 percent no. The new proposal with a state e-ID was narrowly accepted on 28 September 2025 with 50.4 percent yes (as of 2026).
16999.m: In 2025 Switzerland narrowly said yes to a state e-ID.

17000.q: Under which name did Facebook start at Harvard University in February 2004?
17000.e: Mark Zuckerberg founded the network in 2004 with fellow students such as Eduardo Saverin and Dustin Moskovitz. At first it was called “Thefacebook”; in 2005 the name was shortened to “Facebook”.
17000.m: Facebook started in 2004 under the name “Thefacebook”.

17001.q: What has the Facebook company been called since it was renamed in October 2021?
17001.e: On 28 October 2021 the company announced it was changing its name to Meta. It owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, among others.
17001.m: The Facebook company has been called Meta since 2021.

17002.q: Which entrepreneur took over the short message service Twitter at the end of October 2022?
17002.e: Elon Musk took over Twitter at the end of October 2022. In July 2023 the service was renamed X.
17002.m: Twitter has belonged to Elon Musk since 2022 and is now called X.

17003.q: Which company bought the video platform YouTube in 2006?
17003.e: YouTube was founded in 2005 and taken over by Google as early as 2006. Today it belongs to Google’s parent company Alphabet.
17003.m: YouTube has belonged to Google since 2006.

17004.q: In which 2018 scandal was data from millions of Facebook users analysed for political advertising without their knowledge?
17004.e: The firm Cambridge Analytica had obtained data from many Facebook profiles without consent and used it for political campaigns. The case became known in 2018.
17004.m: In 2018 the Cambridge Analytica scandal showed the risks in handling user data.

17005.q: Which country was the first to ban children under 16 by law from having their own accounts on major social networks (from 10 December 2025)?
17005.e: In Australia, since 10 December 2025, platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and YouTube must prevent under-16s from having an account. Companies face large fines if they break the rule.
17005.m: In 2025 Australia introduced a minimum age of 16 for social networks.

17006.q: Which Chinese company developed the platform TikTok?
17006.e: TikTok comes from the Chinese company ByteDance, which runs the sister app Douyin in China. TikTok spread internationally from 2017; for the US business a separate joint venture was formed in 2026, in which ByteDance holds only a minority.
17006.m: TikTok was developed by the Chinese company ByteDance.

17008.q: With whom did the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change share the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007?
17008.e: The IPCC and the former US Vice President Al Gore received the Nobel Peace Prize together in 2007. They were honoured for their contributions to knowledge about climate change.
17008.m: In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.

17009.q: In which city was a protocol with binding reduction targets for industrialised countries agreed in 1997?
17009.e: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 set binding targets for cutting greenhouse gases for industrialised countries for the first time. It came into force in 2005.
17009.m: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 brought the first binding climate targets.

17010.q: Which temperature target does the Paris Agreement of 2015 set?
a: Warming well below 2 degrees, ideally 1.5 degrees
Warming of no more than 3 degrees
Warming of no more than 2.5 degrees
17010.e: The agreement adopted on 12 December 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees compared with pre-industrial times. The goal is 1.5 degrees.
17010.m: The Paris Agreement aims to limit warming to 1.5 degrees.

17011.q: When did the Paris Agreement come into force?
17011.e: The agreement came into force on 4 November 2016 after enough states had ratified it. For Switzerland it has applied since November 2017.
17011.m: The Paris climate agreement has been in force since November 2016.

17012.q: How has the USA’s participation in the Paris Agreement developed (as of 2026)?
a: Left in 2020, rejoined in 2021, left again in 2026
The USA never joined the agreement
The USA has been a member without a break since 2016
Left in 2017 and never a member since
17012.e: The first withdrawal took effect on 4 November 2020, and from 19 February 2021 the USA was a member again. After a new declaration of withdrawal on 20 January 2025, the USA has no longer been a party since 27 January 2026.
17012.m: The USA has left the Paris Agreement twice, most recently with effect in 2026.

17013.q: Which target is contained in the Climate and Innovation Act that Switzerland approved on 18 June 2023?
a: Net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050
A ban on all petrol cars by 2030
17013.e: The act was approved with 59.1 percent yes and has been in force since 1 January 2025. It states that Switzerland should reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 (as of 2026).
17013.m: Under the Climate Act, Switzerland aims to reach net zero by 2050.

17014.q: What did the European Court of Human Rights decide on 9 April 2024 in the case of the KlimaSeniorinnen (Senior Women for Climate Protection) against Switzerland?
a: Switzerland had violated the right to private and family life
Switzerland must adopt the EU climate targets
Switzerland must shut down its nuclear power stations
17014.e: The court found a violation of Article 8 of the ECHR because Switzerland had done too little against climate change. Article 6 was also judged to have been violated.
17014.m: In the KlimaSeniorinnen case in 2024, the Court of Human Rights ruled against Switzerland.

17015.q: Who proposed a test in 1950 to check whether a machine can think like a human?
17015.e: In 1950 Alan Turing described the so-called imitation game. It became known as the Turing test.
17015.m: The Turing test goes back to Alan Turing in 1950.

17016.q: At which conference in 1956 was the term “artificial intelligence” established as a field of research?
17016.e: The Dartmouth Conference of 1956 was co-organised by John McCarthy. The term “artificial intelligence” comes from the proposal for this conference.
17016.m: The Dartmouth Conference of 1956 is seen as the birth of AI research.

17017.q: Which computer beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997?
17017.e: In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue won a six-game match against Kasparov. It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost to a computer in this way.
17017.m: In 1997 Deep Blue beat a reigning world chess champion for the first time.

17018.q: Which DeepMind program won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol in March 2016?
17018.e: AlphaGo won the match in Seoul 4 to 1. Because of the huge number of possible moves, Go was considered especially difficult for computers.
17018.m: In 2016 AlphaGo beat one of the world’s best Go players.

17019.q: When did OpenAI release the chatbot ChatGPT to the general public?
17019.e: ChatGPT was made freely available on 30 November 2022. It is based on a large language model with a transformer architecture.
17019.m: ChatGPT has been available to the public since the end of 2022.

17020.q: On what principle does the EU’s AI Act (in force since 1 August 2024) classify AI systems?
a: By the risk to people and fundamental rights
17020.e: The regulation distinguishes between unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk. The higher the risk, the stricter the obligations.
17020.m: The EU’s AI Act regulates AI systems according to their risk.

17021.q: Which two researchers received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for the foundations of machine learning with neural networks?
17021.e: Hopfield and Hinton were honoured for fundamental discoveries about artificial neural networks. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Hassabis and Jumper, among others, for AlphaFold.
17021.m: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured pioneers of neural networks.

17022.e: Asia is the biggest continent. It has the most area.
17022.m: Asia is the biggest continent on Earth.

17023.e: Australia is the smallest continent. Most of it belongs to the country of Australia.

17024.e: A continent is a very large landmass. There are often many countries on it.
17024.m: A continent is a huge piece of land.

17025.e: The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean. Its name means “peaceful ocean”.
17025.m: The Pacific is the biggest ocean on Earth.

17026.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and America?
17026.e: The Atlantic separates Europe and Africa from America. Ships need many days to cross it.
17026.m: The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.

17027.q: What does the water in the ocean taste like?
17027.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. That is why you cannot drink it.
17027.m: The water in the ocean is salty.

17028.q: What colour are oceans usually on maps?
17028.e: On maps and globes, water is almost always drawn in blue. That way you recognise it at once.
17028.m: Oceans are usually blue on maps.

17029.q: Which country is the biggest in the world?
17029.e: Russia has the largest area of all countries. It lies in Europe and in Asia.
17029.m: Russia is the biggest country in the world by area.

17030.q: Which country is the smallest in the world?
17030.e: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre. The Pope lives there.
17030.m: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

17031.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is very small and lies to the east?
17031.e: Liechtenstein lies between Switzerland and Austria. It is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
17031.m: Liechtenstein is a small neighbouring country of Switzerland.

17032.q: What does the Swiss flag look like?
17032.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is square.
17032.m: The Swiss flag has a white cross on a red background.

17033.q: Which country has a white flag with a red circle?
