17783.q: Through which process are new body cells made as you grow?
17783.e: In cell division (mitosis), one cell becomes two identical daughter cells. That is how the body grows.
17783.m: The body grows through cell division.

17784.q: Which hormone is especially important for boys in puberty?
17784.e: Testosterone, for example, makes the beard grow, the voice get deeper and the muscles get stronger.
17784.m: Testosterone controls many changes in boys.

17785.q: What triggers the changes in the body during puberty?
17785.e: Hormones are messengers in the blood. In puberty the body makes more of them, and they control growth and many other changes.

17787.q: Why do boys' voices break during puberty?
a: Because the voice box and vocal cords grow
17787.e: Under the influence of hormones, the voice box and vocal cords grow. This makes the voice deeper.
17787.m: When the voice breaks, it gets deeper.

17788.q: Why do many teenagers get spots in puberty?
a: Because the oil glands make more oil
Because they drink too much water
Because the skin has fewer cells
17788.e: Hormones stimulate the oil glands. If the pores get blocked, spots can form.
17788.m: Hormones in puberty can cause spots.

17795.q: Which cell organelle is the main site of cellular respiration and ATP production?
17795.e: The citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain take place in the mitochondria. Most of the ATP is made there.
17795.m: Mitochondria are known as the power stations of the cell.

17796.q: Which structure do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
a: A cell wall made of cellulose
17796.e: In addition to the cell membrane, plant cells are surrounded by a firm cell wall made of cellulose. Animal cells only have the cell membrane.
17796.m: Only plant cells have a firm cell wall made of cellulose.

17797.q: What is the basic structure of a biological membrane made of?
17797.e: Phospholipids arrange themselves into a double layer, with their water-loving heads facing outwards and their water-repelling tails facing inwards. Proteins are embedded in it.
17797.m: Every biological membrane is based on a double layer of phospholipids.

17798.q: What do you call the passive movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane?
17798.e: In osmosis, water moves through a partially permeable membrane to the side with the higher concentration of dissolved particles. The cell needs no energy for this.
17798.m: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

17799.q: What fundamentally distinguishes prokaryotes such as bacteria from eukaryotes?
17799.e: In prokaryotes, the DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm; there is no nucleus surrounded by an envelope. They certainly do have ribosomes, DNA and a cell membrane.
17799.m: Prokaryotes are cells without a true nucleus.

17801.q: Who published the double helix model of DNA in 1953?
17801.e: Watson and Crick presented the double helix model in 1953, based on X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin. They received the Nobel Prize for it in 1962.
17801.m: Watson and Crick described the double helix of DNA in 1953.

17802.q: Which researcher from Basel discovered nucleic acid in 1869 and called it “nuclein”?
17802.e: In 1869 in Tübingen, the Basel doctor Friedrich Miescher isolated a phosphorus-rich substance from the nuclei of pus cells. Today we know it was DNA.
17802.m: Friedrich Miescher from Basel was the first to discover DNA.

17803.q: What three components make up a DNA nucleotide?
a: Amino acid, sugar and a base
17803.e: A DNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and one of the four bases A, T, G or C. Ribose is the sugar of RNA.
17803.m: A DNA building block consists of phosphate, deoxyribose and a base.

17804.q: How many hydrogen bonds join guanine and cytosine?
17804.e: Guanine and cytosine are joined by three hydrogen bonds, adenine and thymine by only two. DNA rich in GC is therefore more stable.
17804.m: There are three hydrogen bonds between guanine and cytosine.

17805.q: What do you call the copying of DNA before a cell divides?
17805.e: In replication, each strand serves as a template for a new strand. Each daughter DNA contains one old and one new strand (semi-conservative).
17805.m: Before every cell division, DNA is copied by replication.

17806.q: What do you call rewriting a gene into mRNA?
17806.e: In transcription, RNA polymerase reads a DNA strand and builds a matching mRNA. This carries the information out of the nucleus.
17806.m: In transcription, a gene is rewritten into mRNA.

17807.q: Where does translation, that is protein synthesis, take place?
17807.e: Ribosomes read the mRNA and link the matching amino acids into a chain. They lie freely in the cytoplasm or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
17807.m: Proteins are assembled at the ribosomes.

17808.q: How many bases make up a codon?
17808.e: A codon is a triplet of bases on the mRNA. It specifies a particular amino acid or a stop signal.
17808.m: A codon always consists of three bases.

17809.q: How many different codons are there in the genetic code?
17809.e: With four bases and three positions, there are 4 to the power of 3, that is 64, combinations. They code for 20 amino acids and stop signals, so the code is redundant (degenerate): many amino acids have several codons.
17809.m: The genetic code has 64 different codons.

17810.q: What are the non-coding sections of a gene called that are removed during splicing?
17810.e: During splicing, the introns are cut out of the precursor mRNA. The exons are joined to form the mature mRNA.
17810.m: Introns are removed from the mRNA during splicing.

17811.q: According to current knowledge, roughly how many protein-coding genes do humans have?
17811.e: The Human Genome Project and later analyses found only about 20,000 protein-coding genes. That is far fewer than had been expected earlier.
17811.m: Humans have only about 20,000 genes for proteins.

17812.q: How many chromosomes does a normal human body cell have?
17812.e: Body cells are diploid, which means they contain two sets of chromosomes. These include 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes.

17813.q: What is the ordered display of all the chromosomes of a cell by size and shape called?
17813.e: For a karyogram, chromosomes in metaphase are stained, photographed and arranged in pairs by size and shape. This makes it possible to spot differences in the number and structure of the chromosomes.
17813.m: A karyogram shows all the chromosomes of a cell arranged in pairs.

17814.q: What is the point called where the two chromatids of a chromosome are joined?
17814.e: The sister chromatids are joined at the centromere. That is where the spindle fibres attach during cell division.
17814.m: The two chromatids are held together at the centromere.

17815.q: Which chromosome change underlies Down syndrome?
17815.e: In Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice. The cause is usually a faulty division during meiosis.
17815.m: In Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is present three times.

17816.q: What are the end sections of chromosomes called that get a little shorter with every cell division?
17816.e: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes. Because they get shorter with every division, they are seen as a kind of cell ageing clock.
17816.m: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes.

17817.q: How many chromosomes does a mature human egg cell contain?
17817.e: Meiosis produces haploid germ cells with a single set of chromosomes. At fertilisation, a diploid set is formed again.
17817.m: Germ cells contain only a single set of chromosomes.

17818.q: Who is seen as the founder of genetics thanks to cross-breeding experiments with peas?
17818.e: The Augustinian monk Gregor Mendel published his rules of inheritance in 1866. They were only rediscovered around 1900.
17818.m: Gregor Mendel discovered the basic rules of inheritance.

17819.q: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. In what ratio do the dominant and recessive traits appear?
17819.e: The possible combinations are AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Three of them show the dominant trait, one the recessive.
17819.m: When two heterozygous parents are crossed, the traits split in a ratio of 3 to 1.

17820.q: In the cross Aa × aa, what percentage of the offspring are homozygous recessive?
17820.e: The aa parent always passes on a, and the Aa parent passes on A or a half the time each. So half of the offspring are Aa and half are aa.
17820.m: A test cross with aa gives half Aa and half aa.

17821.q: Why are males more often affected by X-linked recessive traits such as red-green colour blindness?
a: They have only one X chromosome
Their Y chromosome carries the allele
17821.e: Males have only one X chromosome, so a recessive allele on it is always expressed. Females usually have a second, healthy X chromosome to make up for it.
17821.m: Males show recessive traits on the X chromosome more often.

17822.q: What do you call it when two alleles are both fully expressed in the phenotype at the same time?
17822.e: In codominance, both alleles show side by side, for example in blood group AB. In intermediate inheritance, by contrast, a blend is produced.
17822.m: In codominance, both alleles show at the same time.

17823.q: In what ratio do the phenotypes split in the F2 generation in a dihybrid dominant-recessive cross?
17823.e: If two independent traits are inherited, they combine freely (Mendel's third law). 3 to 1 times 3 to 1 gives 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
17823.m: A dihybrid cross splits in a ratio of 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 in the F2.

17824.q: Which gland is connected to the hypothalamus and controls many other hormone glands?
17824.e: The pituitary gland receives signals from the hypothalamus. It releases control hormones that stimulate the thyroid and the gonads, for example.
17824.m: The pituitary gland is the control centre for many hormone glands.

17825.q: What does negative feedback do in the hormone system?
a: A high hormone level inhibits further release
A high hormone level increases release
Hormones are broken down in the blood immediately
17825.e: When the amount of hormone in the blood rises, the gland above it is slowed down. This keeps the hormone level within a stable range.
17825.m: Negative feedback keeps the hormone level in balance.

17826.q: Which element does the thyroid gland need for its hormones, which is why it has been added to table salt in Switzerland since 1922?
17826.e: Thyroid hormones contain iodine. Because Swiss soils are low in iodine and goitre was widespread, iodised table salt has been available since 1922.
17826.m: The thyroid gland needs iodine, which is why there is iodised salt in Switzerland.

17827.q: In which organ are the islets of Langerhans found?
17827.e: The islets of Langerhans are small groups of cells in the pancreas. They make hormones that regulate blood sugar.
17827.m: The islets of Langerhans are in the pancreas.

17828.q: Which gland lies behind the breastbone and is important, especially in childhood, for the maturing of T lymphocytes?
17828.e: In the thymus, T lymphocytes learn to tell foreign structures from the body's own. After puberty it gradually shrinks.
17828.m: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus.

17829.q: What do you call glands that release their hormones directly into the blood?
17829.e: Endocrine glands have no duct and release their substances into the blood. Exocrine glands such as sweat glands release their secretion to the outside or into hollow organs.
17829.m: Endocrine glands release their hormones directly into the blood.

17830.q: Which hormone lowers the blood sugar level?
17830.e: Insulin makes body cells take up glucose from the blood and makes the liver and muscles store it. It is the only hormone that lowers blood sugar.
17830.m: Insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood sugar.

17831.q: Which hormone from the pineal gland controls the sleep-wake rhythm?
17831.e: The pineal gland releases melatonin mainly in the dark. It makes you tired and helps control the day-night rhythm.
17831.m: Melatonin is made in the dark and makes you tired.

17832.q: Which hormone from the pituitary gland promotes growth in height in children and young people?
17832.e: The pituitary gland releases growth hormone mainly during sleep. It stimulates the growth of bones and muscles.
17832.m: Growth hormone from the pituitary gland makes us grow.

17833.q: Which hormone from the kidney stimulates the production of red blood cells?
17833.e: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more erythropoietin (EPO). It stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells and is also known as a doping substance.
17833.m: EPO from the kidney promotes the production of red blood cells.

17834.q: Which hormone from the adrenal medulla raises pulse and blood pressure within seconds during stress?
17834.e: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight. It raises the heartbeat, blood pressure and blood sugar and widens the bronchi.
17834.m: Adrenaline puts the body on alert during stress.

17835.q: Which hormone is often called the “bonding hormone” because it promotes trust and closeness between people?
17835.e: Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released via the pituitary gland. It is released during hugs, for example, and strengthens social bonds.

17836.q: Which end products are formed in the complete cellular respiration of glucose?
17836.e: Glucose is completely broken down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. Energy is gained in the form of ATP.
17836.m: Cellular respiration produces carbon dioxide, water and energy.

17837.q: Which substance is formed in muscle from pyruvate by fermentation when oxygen is short?
17837.e: When oxygen is lacking, the muscle turns pyruvate into lactate (lactic acid). This lets glycolysis carry on, but it supplies only a little ATP.
17837.m: When oxygen is short, the muscle makes lactate.

17838.q: In what form do humans store glucose in the liver and muscles?
17838.e: Glycogen is a highly branched polysaccharide made of glucose. Starch, on the other hand, is the storage substance of plants.

17839.q: What do you call the amount of energy the body needs at complete rest for vital functions?
17839.e: The basal metabolic rate covers breathing, heartbeat, body temperature and organ functions at rest. Any extra activity counts towards the active metabolic rate.
17839.m: The basal metabolic rate is the body's energy need at complete rest.

17840.q: In which organ is poisonous ammonia from the breakdown of protein turned into urea?
17840.e: In the urea cycle, the liver turns ammonia into urea, which is less poisonous. The kidneys then excrete it in the urine.
17840.m: The liver makes urea, and the kidneys excrete it.

17841.q: A snack contains 10 g of fat and 20 g of carbohydrate. About how many kilocalories does it supply if fat supplies 9 kcal/g and carbohydrate 4 kcal/g?
17841.e: Fat supplies 10 times 9, that is 90 kcal. Carbohydrate supplies 20 times 4, that is 80 kcal, making 170 kcal together.
17841.m: Per gram, fat supplies more than twice as much energy as carbohydrate.

17842.q: What is the part of an enzyme called to which the substrate binds?
17842.e: The substrate attaches at the active site, where the chemical reaction takes place. The product is then released and the enzyme stays unchanged.
17842.m: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.

17843.q: Which model describes how only a matching substrate fits a particular enzyme?
17843.e: In 1894, Emil Fischer compared enzyme and substrate to a lock and key. This explains the substrate specificity of enzymes.
17843.m: Enzyme and substrate fit together like a lock and key.

17844.q: What happens to most human enzymes at temperatures well above 40 °C?
17844.e: Enzymes are proteins whose three-dimensional structure is destroyed by heat. That is why a very high fever can be dangerous.
17844.m: Heat destroys the structure of enzymes.

17845.q: Which enzyme in saliva starts the digestion of starch?
17845.e: Salivary amylase splits starch into smaller sugar units. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet after you chew it for a long time.
17845.m: Amylase in saliva starts digesting starch.

17846.q: At what pH does the stomach enzyme pepsin work best?
17846.e: Pepsin is adapted to the hydrochloric acid in the stomach and works best at about pH 2. In the neutral to slightly alkaline small intestine it becomes inactive.
17846.m: Pepsin works best in the acidic stomach.

17847.q: What is the inhibition called in which an inhibitor competes with the substrate for the same binding site?
17847.e: The inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the binding site. A higher substrate concentration can push it out again.
17847.m: In competitive inhibition, inhibitor and substrate compete for the binding site.

17848.q: Which extension of a nerve cell carries signals away from the cell body?
17848.e: The axon carries action potentials from the cell body to the terminal buttons. Dendrites, on the other hand, receive signals.
17848.m: The axon carries signals away from the cell body.

17849.q: Roughly what is the resting potential of a typical nerve cell?
17849.e: At rest, the inside of the cell is negatively charged compared with the outside, usually by about -70 millivolts. The cause is unevenly distributed ions, especially potassium.
17849.m: A resting nerve cell is negatively charged on the inside.

17850.q: Which ions flow into the nerve cell during the depolarisation of an action potential?
17850.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions flow in. This makes the inside of the cell positive for a short time.
17850.m: In an action potential, sodium flows into the cell first.

17851.q: What effect does the myelin sheath around an axon have?
a: It speeds up the conduction of impulses
It supplies the axon with blood
17851.e: The myelin sheath insulates the axon electrically. The impulse therefore jumps from gap to gap (saltatory conduction) and is much faster.
17851.m: Myelin makes nerve conduction much faster.

17852.q: Which neurotransmitter passes the signal from the nerve to the skeletal muscle at the motor end plate?
17852.e: At the motor end plate, acetylcholine is released and binds to receptors on the muscle fibre. The enzyme acetylcholinesterase then breaks it down quickly.
17852.m: Acetylcholine passes signals from the nerve to the muscle.

17853.q: What are the uninsulated gaps between the myelin segments of an axon called?
17853.e: The nodes are named after the French anatomist Louis-Antoine Ranvier. In myelinated fibres, action potentials arise only there.
17853.m: Action potentials arise at the nodes of Ranvier.

17854.q: Which cells of the innate immune system take in pathogens and digest them?
17854.e: Macrophages are phagocytes that take in pathogens by phagocytosis. Afterwards they present parts of them to other immune cells.
17854.m: Macrophages are the eating cells of the immune system.

17855.q: Which cells specifically kill body cells infected with a virus?
17855.e: Cytotoxic T cells (killer cells) recognise foreign antigens on the surface of infected cells. They trigger the death of those cells.
17855.m: Killer T cells destroy infected body cells.

17856.q: Where do B lymphocytes mature in humans?
17856.e: B lymphocytes form and mature in the bone marrow. Afterwards they move to lymphatic organs such as the lymph nodes and spleen.
17856.m: B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow.

17857.q: What do you receive in an active vaccination?
a: Weakened pathogens or parts of pathogens
White blood cells from a donor
17857.e: The vaccination imitates an infection without making you ill. The body makes its own antibodies and memory cells and is often protected for years.
17857.m: In an active vaccination the body builds up its own protection.

17858.q: What is an excessive immune reaction to actually harmless substances such as pollen called?
17858.e: In an allergy the immune system reacts to harmless substances such as pollen or house dust. Typical results are hay fever, itching or asthma.
17858.m: An allergy is an overreaction to harmless substances.

17859.q: In which disease does the immune system destroy the insulin-producing beta cells?
17859.e: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease that usually begins in childhood or adolescence. People affected must take insulin for life.
17859.m: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease.

17860.q: Which cells make and secrete antibodies?
17860.e: Activated B lymphocytes develop into plasma cells. These release large amounts of antibodies into the blood.
17860.m: Plasma cells are the body's antibody factories.

17861.q: What basic shape does a typical antibody molecule have?
17861.e: An antibody looks like a Y. The binding sites for the antigen are at the tips of the two arms.
17861.m: Antibodies are shaped like a Y.

17862.q: How many polypeptide chains make up a single antibody molecule in its basic form?
17862.e: An antibody consists of two heavy and two light chains. They are joined by disulphide bridges.
17862.m: An antibody consists of two heavy and two light chains.

17863.q: Which class of antibody can cross the placenta and so protect the newborn baby?
17863.e: Only immunoglobulin G is actively transported across the placenta to the baby. It protects the baby in the first months of life (maternal immunity).
17863.m: The mother's IgG antibodies give the baby early protection.

17864.q: Which class of antibody is mainly involved in immediate allergic reactions?
17864.e: IgE binds to mast cells. When the allergen meets it, these cells release histamine and trigger the allergic symptoms.
17864.m: IgE antibodies play the main role in allergies.

17865.q: What is the part of an antigen called to which an antibody binds specifically?
17865.e: An epitope is a small section on the surface of the antigen. One antigen can carry several different epitopes.
17865.m: Antibodies recognise a particular epitope on the antigen.

17866.q: Who discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901?
17866.e: The Viennese doctor Karl Landsteiner described the blood groups A, B and O in 1901. He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for this in 1930.
17866.m: Karl Landsteiner discovered the blood groups.

17867.q: Which antibodies are found in the blood plasma of a person with blood group A?
17867.e: People with blood group A carry antigen A on their red blood cells. In their plasma they have antibodies against the foreign antigen B.
17867.m: With blood group A, the plasma contains antibodies against B.

17868.q: Which blood group counts as the universal donor for red cell concentrates?
17868.e: Red blood cells of group O negative carry neither A nor B antigens nor the Rhesus antigen D. That is why they are used in emergencies.
17868.m: In an emergency, O negative blood can be given to almost everyone.

17869.q: The mother has the genotype AO and the father BO. Which blood groups can their children have?
17869.e: The mother passes on A or O, the father B or O. AB, AO, BO and OO are possible, so all four blood groups.
17869.m: Two heterozygous parents can have children with all four ABO blood groups.

17870.q: What risk exists when a Rhesus-negative mother is expecting a Rhesus-positive baby?
a: The mother makes antibodies against the baby's blood cells
The baby later becomes Rhesus negative
The mother loses her own blood group
The baby makes antibodies against the mother
17870.e: If the baby's blood reaches the mother, she can make anti-D antibodies. In a later pregnancy these can destroy the baby's blood cells, which is why anti-D prophylaxis is given.
17870.m: Anti-D prophylaxis protects the babies of Rhesus-negative mothers.

17871.q: Which ABO blood group can receive red blood cells from all ABO groups?
17871.e: People with blood group AB have neither anti-A nor anti-B in their plasma. That is why they count as universal recipients for red blood cells.
17871.m: People with blood group AB are universal recipients.

17872.q: What is the narrowing of arteries by deposits in the vessel wall called?
17872.e: In arteriosclerosis, fat, calcium and connective tissue build up in the artery wall. The vessels become narrower and stiffer.
17872.m: Arteriosclerosis is a narrowing of the arteries by deposits.

17873.q: What happens in a heart attack?
a: Heart muscle tissue dies because a coronary artery is blocked
The heart valves suddenly become inflamed
17873.e: Usually a blood clot blocks a narrowed coronary artery. The heart muscle behind it no longer gets oxygen and dies.
17873.m: In a heart attack, heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen.

17874.q: From what value measured at the doctor's surgery do European guidelines and the WHO speak of high blood pressure?
17874.e: According to the WHO and the European Society of Cardiology, high blood pressure is present from 140 mmHg systolic or 90 mmHg diastolic. In the long term it damages vessels, heart and kidneys.
17874.m: Blood pressure of 140 over 90 or more counts as too high.

17875.q: Which risk factor for heart and circulation diseases can be influenced by your own behaviour?
17875.e: Smoking damages the walls of the blood vessels and encourages hardening of the arteries. Age, sex and family history, on the other hand, cannot be changed.
17875.m: Not smoking lowers your risk of heart and circulation diseases.

17876.q: Where do cardiovascular diseases rank among the causes of death in Switzerland (as of 2022)?
a: They are the most common cause of death
They are the third most common cause of death
They are the fifth most common cause of death
They are the tenth most common cause of death
17876.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, cardiovascular diseases caused 27.5 per cent of deaths in 2022, making them the most common cause of death in Switzerland, ahead of cancer with 23.1 per cent. They mainly affect older people.
17876.m: Cardiovascular diseases are the most common cause of death in Switzerland.

17877.q: What is the most common cause of a stroke?
a: Blockage of an artery in the brain
17877.e: Around 80 per cent of strokes are ischaemic, that is, caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain. Quick treatment saves brain tissue.
17877.m: Most strokes are caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain.

17878.q: Why do antibiotics not help against flu?
17878.e: Antibiotics attack structures of bacteria, such as the cell wall. Influenza viruses do not have such structures.
17878.m: Antibiotics only work against bacteria, not against viruses.

17879.q: What kind of pathogen causes tuberculosis?
17879.e: Robert Koch discovered the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis in 1882. Tuberculosis is treated with a combination of antibiotics.
17879.m: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium.

17880.q: Which virus can lead to the disease AIDS if untreated?
17880.e: The human immunodeficiency virus mainly attacks helper T cells and so weakens the immune system. Modern medicines can prevent AIDS from developing.
17880.m: HIV weakens the immune system and can lead to AIDS.

17881.e: Plasmodia are single-celled parasites carried by Anopheles mosquitoes. They multiply in the liver and in red blood cells.
17881.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled plasmodia.

17882.q: Which tick-borne disease can be prevented by vaccination in Switzerland?
17882.e: There is a vaccine against viral TBE, and the Federal Office of Public Health recommends it for almost all of Switzerland. There is no vaccine against bacterial Lyme disease.
17882.m: A vaccine protects against TBE, but not against Lyme disease.

17883.q: What is meant by a point mutation?
a: A change in a single base
17883.e: In a point mutation a single base is swapped, inserted or removed. One example is sickle cell anaemia.
17883.m: A point mutation affects only a single base.

17884.q: What is the exchange of sections between homologous chromosomes during meiosis called?
17884.e: In crossing over, paired homologous chromosomes swap pieces. This creates new combinations of alleles.
17884.m: Crossing over reshuffles the genes in meiosis.

17885.q: Which genetic engineering tool uses a guide RNA to find a particular spot in the DNA and cut it precisely?
17885.e: CRISPR/Cas9 is known as “gene scissors”. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 2020.
17885.m: The gene scissors CRISPR/Cas9 can change DNA precisely.

17886.q: Which method is used in the lab to copy particular sections of DNA many times?
17886.e: In the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), DNA is heated, cooled and copied by a heat-stable polymerase in cycles. This makes millions of copies in a short time.
17886.m: PCR copies DNA in the lab.

17887.q: Roughly how many base pairs does a single human set of chromosomes contain?
17887.e: The haploid human genome contains about 3.1 billion base pairs. Only about 1 to 2 per cent of it codes for proteins.
17887.m: The human genome has about three billion base pairs.

17888.q: In a population, 1 per cent show a recessive trait (aa). According to the Hardy-Weinberg law, how common is the allele a?
17888.e: The frequency of aa is q times q, so 0.01. It follows that q is the square root of 0.01, which is 0.1 or 10 per cent.
17888.m: The allele frequency is the square root of the share of homozygous recessives.

17889.q: What is the famous partial skeleton of an Australopithecus afarensis found in Ethiopia in 1974 called?
17889.e: The skeleton, about 3.2 million years old, was named after the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”. It shows that Lucy already walked upright.
17889.m: Lucy is one of the best-known fossils of early humans.

17890.q: On which continent did Homo sapiens originate, according to current knowledge?
17890.e: Fossils and genetic data show that modern humans originated in Africa. From there they spread across the world (“Out of Africa”).

17891.q: Roughly how old are the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco?
17891.e: The finds from Jebel Irhoud were dated to about 300,000 years in 2017. They are considered the oldest known remains of our species.
17891.m: Our species is about 300,000 years old.

17892.q: Which human species died out about 40,000 years ago and left traces in the genes of people today?
17892.e: People outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA. Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022 for this research.
17892.m: Many people today carry some Neanderthal genes.

17893.q: Which feature was one of the earliest to develop in human evolution?
17893.e: Even early hominins such as the australopithecines walked upright but still had small brains. The brain only grew much larger later.
17893.m: Walking upright came long before the large brain.

17894.q: What is the thick main part of a tree between the roots and the crown called?
17894.e: The trunk carries the crown and carries water up from the roots.
17894.m: The trunk holds up the whole tree.

17895.q: What is the outer protective layer of a tree trunk called?
17895.e: The bark wraps around the trunk and protects it from cold, heat and animals.
17895.m: Bark protects the tree like skin.

17896.q: What can you count on a felled tree trunk to estimate its age?
17896.e: A tree forms a new ring in its wood every year. If you count the rings, you know roughly how old it is.
17896.m: Each annual ring stands for one year.

17897.q: What is the top part of a tree with the branches and leaves called?
17897.e: The crown is made of branches, twigs and leaves. It catches the sunlight.
17897.m: The crown is the top part of the tree.

17898.q: Which gas do trees give off into the air that we need to breathe?
17898.e: Using sunlight, trees make food and give off oxygen as they do so.
17898.m: Trees give us oxygen to breathe.

17899.q: What does a flower in a pot need so that it does not wilt?
17899.e: Without water, flowers go limp and wilt. That is why you have to water them regularly.

17900.q: Which white flower often peeps out of the snow in late winter?
17900.e: The snowdrop flowers very early in the year, often while there is still snow on the ground. Its white flowers hang like little bells.
17900.m: The snowdrop is one of the first flowers of the year.

17901.q: Which flower often has sharp prickles on its stem?
17901.e: Roses have sharp prickles on their stems, often called thorns. They protect the plant from animals.
17901.m: With a rose you have to watch out for the prickles.

17902.q: Which white mountain flower feels like felt and is very well known in Switzerland?
17902.e: Edelweiss grows in the Alps. Its flowers are covered in fine white hairs, which is why they feel like felt.
17902.m: Edelweiss is a famous alpine flower.

17903.q: What does a tulip grow back from every spring?
17903.e: The tulip stores nutrients in a bulb in the ground. In spring it grows again from it.

17904.q: Which of these plants is a grass?
17904.e: Wheat is a cereal, and all cereals are grasses. Potatoes, peas and carrots are not grasses.

17905.q: Which very tall plant is also a grass?
17905.e: Bamboo is a grass, even though it can grow as tall as a tree.

17906.q: What is dried grass that farmers store as winter food called?
17906.e: Grass is cut and dried in the sun. That makes hay, which animals eat in winter.
17906.m: Hay is dried grass for the animals.

17907.q: From the grains of which grass plant is popcorn made?
17907.e: Like wheat, maize is a grass. Its grains burst open when heated, and that makes popcorn.
17907.m: Maize is a grass, and popcorn is made from its grains.

17908.q: What makes a shrub different from a tree?
17908.e: A shrub usually has many thin stems growing straight out of the ground. A tree usually has just one thick trunk.
17908.m: A shrub has many stems instead of one.

17910.q: Which berries grow on a bush?
17910.e: Redcurrants grow on a bush. Cherries and plums grow on trees, and strawberries on low plants on the ground.

17911.q: What is a row of shrubs that marks the edge of a garden called?
17911.e: A hedge is made of many shrubs side by side. Birds and hedgehogs find shelter in it.
17911.m: A hedge is a fence made of shrubs.

17912.q: What does a plant take in from the soil with its roots?
17912.e: The roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil. Light, on the other hand, is caught by the leaves.
17912.m: Roots drink water from the soil.

17913.q: Where are a plant’s roots usually found?
17913.e: Most roots grow under the ground. There they find water and support.
17913.m: Roots usually grow under the ground.

17914.q: Which vegetable is a root that we eat?
17914.e: The carrot is a thickened root. Cucumbers and tomatoes are fruits, and with lettuce we eat the leaves.
17914.m: With a carrot we eat the root.

17915.q: Apart from drinking, what are roots for?
17915.e: Roots hold the plant firmly in the ground. That way it does not fall over in the wind.
17915.m: Roots hold the plant firmly in the ground.

17916.q: What colour are most leaves in summer?
17916.e: Leaves contain a green pigment. It helps the plant make food with sunlight.
17916.m: In summer most leaves are green.

17917.q: What do leaves need to make food for the plant?
17917.e: With sunlight, water and air the leaves make sugar as food.
17917.m: Leaves need sunlight to make food.

17918.q: What are the fine lines on a leaf that water flows through called?
17918.e: The leaf veins spread water through the whole leaf. They also make the leaf sturdy.
17918.m: Leaf veins bring water into the leaf.

17919.q: What is the thin part by which a leaf hangs from the twig called?
17919.e: The leaf stalk connects the leaf to the twig.
17919.m: A leaf hangs from the twig by its leaf stalk.

17920.q: What do the leaves of many plants do when they get too little water?
17920.e: Without water the leaves lose their firmness and hang down. After watering they often stand up again.
17920.m: Drooping leaves show that the plant is thirsty.

17921.q: Which animal flies from flower to flower and makes honey?
17921.e: Bees fly from flower to flower. They make honey from the sweet juice.

17922.q: What is the sweet juice in many flowers called?
17922.e: Nectar is a sweet juice in flowers. It attracts insects.
17922.m: Nectar is the sweet juice of flowers.

17923.q: What is the fine yellow dust in many flowers called?
17923.e: Pollen is also called flower dust. Insects carry it from one flower to the next.

17924.q: What does a flower turn into after it has been pollinated?
17924.e: After pollination, a fruit with seeds grows from the flower.
17924.m: A pollinated flower becomes a fruit.

17925.q: What grows from a seed when it gets water and warmth?
17925.e: Inside the seed there is a tiny plant. With water and warmth it starts to grow.
17925.m: A new plant grows from a seed.

17926.q: What is it called when a seed starts to grow?
17926.e: When a seed bursts open and a little shoot grows out, we say the seed is germinating.
17926.m: A seed germinates when it starts to grow.

17927.q: Which animal hides nuts and seeds as a store for the winter?
17927.e: Squirrels bury nuts and seeds. Some they never find again, and new plants grow from them.

17928.q: What is the job called when you put seeds into the soil?
17928.e: When sowing, you put seeds into the soil. Weeding means pulling out weeds.
17928.m: Putting seeds into the soil is called sowing.

17929.q: Which fruit grows on a tree?
17929.e: Cherries grow on the cherry tree. Strawberries, pumpkins and melons grow on plants on the ground.

17930.q: What do you find inside a cherry?
17930.e: Inside the cherry there is a hard pip, also called a stone. The seed is inside it.
17930.m: Inside a cherry there is a hard stone.

17931.q: What colour is a ripe banana?
17931.e: Bananas are green at first. When they are ripe, their skin turns yellow.

17932.q: What is it called when you pick and gather ripe fruit?
17932.e: At harvest time, ripe fruit, vegetables or grain are brought in from the field or the tree.
17932.m: The harvest is gathering in the ripe fruit.

17933.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland’s area is covered by forest (as of 2025)?
17933.e: About a third of Switzerland is forest (Swiss Forest Report 2025). The south side of the Alps has the most forest in relation to its area.
17933.m: About a third of Switzerland is forest.

17934.q: Which forest animal has large antlers?
17934.e: The male red deer has antlers. It sheds them every year and grows new ones.

17935.q: Which soft green cushion often grows on stones and tree trunks in the forest?
17935.e: Moss likes damp, shady places. It stores a lot of water like a sponge.
17935.m: Moss is soft and stores water.

17936.q: Where are you allowed to make a fire in the forest?
17936.e: Fire belongs only in a fireplace. Otherwise a dangerous forest fire can start.
17936.m: Only make fires at a fireplace.

17937.q: Which bird knocks holes in tree trunks with its beak?
17937.e: The woodpecker hammers into the wood with its strong beak. This is how it looks for insects and builds nest holes.
17937.m: The woodpecker knocks holes in wood.

17938.q: Which small white flower with a yellow centre often grows in lawns and meadows?
17938.e: The daisy is very common and flowers almost all year. It has white petals and a yellow centre.
17938.m: The daisy grows in the grass almost everywhere.

17939.q: What is a meadow where cows graze called?
17939.e: In a pasture, animals like cows, sheep or horses eat the grass straight from the ground.

17940.q: Which insect chirps loudly in the meadow in summer?
17940.e: Grasshoppers and crickets chirp by rubbing their legs or wings together.
17940.m: Grasshoppers chirp in the meadow in summer.

17941.q: Which animal digs tunnels under the meadow and makes mounds of earth?
17941.e: The mole lives underground. It pushes the earth from its tunnels upwards, which makes molehills.
17941.m: The mole digs tunnels under the meadow.

17942.q: What is a patch of soil in the garden where you plant vegetables called?
17942.e: A bed is a prepared area in the garden. There you plant vegetables, herbs or flowers.

17943.q: What do you water plants in the garden with?
17943.e: You fill the watering can with water. It flows gently onto the plants through the rose.
17943.m: You water plants with a watering can.

17944.q: Which animal is useful in the garden because it loosens the soil?
17944.e: Earthworms dig tunnels and eat old leaves. This makes the soil loose and fertile.

17945.q: Which vegetable grows as a tuber under the ground?
17945.e: The potato forms tubers under the ground. These are dug up and eaten.

17946.q: What do vegetable peelings and leaves turn into over time in the compost?
17946.e: Small creatures and fungi break down the waste in the compost. New, good soil is made from it.
17946.m: In the compost, waste turns into good soil.

17947.q: What do most broadleaf trees here do in autumn?
17947.e: In winter there is little water and light. That is why most broadleaf trees drop their leaves beforehand.
17947.m: Broadleaf trees lose their leaves in autumn.

17948.q: Which of these trees is a broadleaf tree?
17948.e: The lime has broad, heart-shaped leaves and is a broadleaf tree. Fir, spruce and pine have needles.
17948.m: The lime is a broadleaf tree with heart-shaped leaves.

17949.q: What colours do many leaves turn in autumn?
17949.e: In autumn the tree breaks down the green pigment. Then yellow and red colours become visible.
17949.m: In autumn the leaves turn yellow and red.

17950.q: Which broadleaf tree has winged fruits that spin like propellers as they fall?
17950.e: Maple fruits have flat wings. As they fall they spin and so fly further away.
17950.m: Maple fruits fly like little propellers.

17951.q: Which conifer loses its needles in autumn?
17951.e: The larch is a special conifer. Its needles turn golden yellow in autumn and then fall off.
17951.m: The larch sheds its needles in autumn.

17952.q: On which conifer do the long needles always grow in pairs?
17952.e: On the Scots pine, two long needles always grow together. On fir, spruce and yew the needles grow singly.
17952.m: The Scots pine has needles in pairs.

17953.q: Which sticky sap often oozes from the bark of conifers?
17953.e: Resin is sticky and has a strong smell. It seals wounds in the bark.
17953.m: Resin protects the conifer when it is injured.

17954.q: Which conifer grows high up in the Swiss Alps and has edible little nuts?
17954.e: The Swiss stone pine grows up to the tree line in the Alps. Its cones contain edible little nuts.
17954.m: The Swiss stone pine grows high up in the mountains.

17955.q: In which season does the apple tree flower here?
17955.e: Apple trees flower in April and May. After that the apples grow until autumn.
17955.m: The apple tree flowers in spring.

17956.e: Apple blossoms are white and often tinged with pink, especially as buds.
17956.m: Apple blossoms glow white and pink.

17959.q: What are the fruits of the oak called?
17959.e: Acorns are nuts sitting in a little cup. They grow on the oak.

17960.q: How old can an oak tree get?
17960.e: Oaks grow slowly and can live for many hundreds of years. Some are even said to be around a thousand years old.

17961.q: What does the edge of an oak leaf look like?
17961.e: The oak leaf has rounded bulges along its edge, called lobes. They make the oak easy to recognise.

17962.q: Which forest animal likes to eat the fruits of the oak?
17962.e: In autumn, wild boar search the forest floor for the fruits of the oak and love to eat them.
17962.m: Wild boar love the fruits of the oak.

17963.q: What are the fruits of the beech called?
17963.e: Beechnuts are small, three-sided nuts. They sit in a prickly husk.
17963.m: Beechnuts are the fruits of the beech.

17964.q: What does the bark of a beech look like?
17964.e: The beech has smooth, silver-grey bark. That makes it easy to recognise in the forest.
17964.m: The beech has smooth grey bark.

17965.q: Which broadleaf tree is the most common in Swiss forests?
17965.e: The beech is the most common broadleaf tree in Switzerland. It grows mainly in the Central Plateau and the Jura.
17965.m: The beech is the most common broadleaf tree in Switzerland.

17967.q: How do fir cones sit on the branch?
17967.e: Fir cones stand upright on the branches. They fall apart on the tree, which is why you rarely find whole fir cones on the ground.
17967.m: Fir cones stand upright like candles.

17968.q: Which tree is often decorated as a Christmas tree?
17968.e: At Christmas a fir is often decorated with candles and baubles. It stays green in winter too.
17968.m: The fir is a popular Christmas tree.

17969.q: What is the fir that grows wild in Swiss forests called?
17969.e: The silver fir grows in our forests. Its bark is light grey, almost whitish.
17969.m: The silver fir grows in our forests.

17970.q: What can you see on the underside of fir needles?
17970.e: Fir needles have two light stripes underneath. They make the fir easy to recognise.
17970.m: Fir needles have two white stripes underneath.

17971.q: How do spruce cones hang on the tree?
17971.e: Spruce cones hang downwards. They fall to the ground whole, which is why you often find them in the forest.

17972.q: Which tree species is the most common overall in Swiss forests?
17972.e: The spruce is the most common tree species in Switzerland; more than a third of all trees are spruces (Forest Report 2025). Its wood is often used for building.
17972.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Switzerland.

17974.q: What do spruce needles feel like?
17974.e: Spruce needles are sharp and prick you when you touch them. They grow all round the twig.

17975.q: What colour are the petals of a sunflower?
17975.e: The sunflower has bright yellow petals around a large brown centre.

17976.q: Which part of the sunflower do people and birds like to eat?
17976.e: Lots of seeds ripen in the centre of the sunflower. You can eat them roasted, and birds love them.
17976.m: Sunflower seeds are a healthy snack.

17977.q: What is made from sunflower seeds?
17977.e: Sunflower oil is pressed from the seeds. It is used for cooking and frying.
17977.m: Oil is made from sunflower seeds.

17978.q: Which way do young sunflowers turn their heads during the day?
17978.e: Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west. Fully grown flowers mostly face east.

17979.q: What does a dandelion form after it has finished flowering?
17979.e: After flowering, the dandelion forms a white ball of seeds with little parachutes. The wind carries them away.
17979.m: A dandelion turns into a dandelion clock.

17980.q: What colour is a dandelion flower?
17980.e: The dandelion has a bright yellow flower. In spring it turns many meadows yellow.

17981.q: What comes out of the stem when you snap a dandelion?
17981.e: A dandelion contains a white, milky sap. It can leave stains on your clothes.
17981.m: The dandelion has white, milky sap.

17982.q: Where does the dandelion get its name from?
17982.e: The leaves of the dandelion have sharp, jagged points. They remind people of a lion’s teeth, and the name comes from the French “dent de lion”, lion’s tooth.
17982.m: The dandelion’s leaves look like teeth.

17983.q: Which pet likes to eat dandelion leaves?
17983.e: Rabbits eat plants and really like fresh dandelion leaves.

17984.q: Where in Switzerland can you have mushrooms you have picked checked?
17984.e: Many municipalities have a mushroom inspection office. There, experts check whether the mushrooms are edible or poisonous.
17984.m: Take mushrooms you have picked to the mushroom inspection office.

17985.q: Which poisonous mushroom has a red cap with white spots?
17985.e: The fly agaric is easy to recognise and poisonous. You must not eat it.
17985.m: The red fly agaric is poisonous.

17987.q: What is the top part of a mushroom called?
17987.e: A typical mushroom has a stalk and a cap on top. Under the cap there are often gills or tubes.
17987.m: A mushroom has a stalk and a cap.

17988.q: What are the fine threads of a fungus in the soil called?
17988.e: Most of a fungus lives invisibly in the soil as a fine network. What we see is only the fruiting body.
17988.m: Most of a fungus lives hidden in the soil.

17990.q: In which season do many plants rest and it may snow?
17990.e: In winter it is cold, and many plants do not grow. They wait for spring.

17991.e: The order is spring, summer, autumn and winter.

17992.q: In which season are many nuts and apples ripe here?
17992.e: In autumn many fruits and nuts are ripe. Then you can pick and gather them.
17992.m: In autumn many fruits are ripe.

17993.q: Which three basic organs does a typical flowering plant have?
17993.e: The body of a seed plant is made of root, shoot axis and leaves. Flowers are modified parts of the shoot.
17993.m: Root, shoot axis and leaf form the basic plan of a flowering plant.

17994.q: In which vessels is water carried up from the root?
17994.e: The xylem (woody tissue) carries water and minerals from the root into the leaves. The phloem, on the other hand, transports dissolved sugars.
17994.m: In the xylem, water rises from the root to the leaves.

17995.q: On most broad leaves, where are most of the stomata?
a: On the underside of the leaf
On the upper side of the leaf
17995.e: Less water evaporates on the cooler, shady underside. That is why most leaves have most of their stomata there.
17995.m: Most stomata are protected on the underside of the leaf.

17996.q: What can you read from the annual rings of a felled tree?
17996.e: Every year the tree forms a new layer of wood with light early wood and dark late wood. If you count the rings, you get its approximate age.
17996.m: Each annual ring stands for one year of the tree’s life.

17997.q: Which part of the flower is the male organ that produces pollen?
17997.e: The stamens carry anthers in which the pollen grains form. The pistil with the ovary is the female part.
17997.m: The stamens are the male parts of the flower.

17998.q: What job do root hairs do?
17998.e: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area of the root. This lets the plant take in more water and dissolved minerals from the soil.
17998.m: Root hairs increase the surface area for taking in water.

17999.q: Which two raw materials does a plant need for photosynthesis?
17999.e: Using light energy, plants build glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released in the process.
17999.m: With light, the plant makes sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

18001.q: In which parts of the cell does photosynthesis take place?
18001.e: The chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which captures light energy. That is why the steps of photosynthesis take place there.
18001.m: Photosynthesis takes place in the green chloroplasts.

a: The cell walls are dyed green
18002.e: Chlorophyll mainly absorbs red and blue light. Green light is mostly reflected and reaches our eyes.
18002.m: Leaves are green because chlorophyll reflects green light.

18003.q: What does a plant make from carbon dioxide and water in photosynthesis?
18003.e: Using light energy, the plant builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released in the process.

18004.q: In what form do many plants store the sugar from photosynthesis, for example in the potato?
18004.e: Glucose is linked together into starch, which is easy to store. Potato tubers and cereal grains contain especially large amounts of starch.
18004.m: Plants store extra sugar as starch.

18005.e: In pollination, pollen is transferred to the stigma of a flower. Only after that can fertilisation take place.
18005.m: In pollination, pollen lands on the stigma.

18006.q: Which plant is pollinated mainly by the wind?
18006.e: Hazel flowers as early as late winter and releases huge amounts of light pollen from its catkins into the wind. That is why many people with allergies suffer early in the year.
18006.m: Wind-pollinated plants produce a lot of light pollen.

18007.q: What do many flowers use to attract bees?
18007.e: Nectar is a sugary liquid and an important food for insects. Colours and scents show the bees the way to the flower.
18007.m: Flowers attract pollinators with nectar, scent and colours.

18008.q: What is it called when pollen reaches the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species?
18008.e: In cross-pollination the pollen comes from another plant. This gives the offspring more variety in their genes.
18008.m: Cross-pollination mixes the genes of different plants.

18009.q: After pollination, what grows from the pollen grain through the style to the ovule?
18009.e: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube. Through it the male sex cell reaches the egg cell in the ovule.
18009.m: The pollen tube carries the male sex cell to the egg cell.

18010.q: What does a seed NOT necessarily need to germinate?
18010.e: Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate. Cress, for example, also germinates on damp cotton wool without soil.
18010.m: To germinate, a seed needs water, air and warmth.

18011.q: What is the first step of germination called, when the seed takes in water and swells?
18011.e: In imbibition the dry seed soaks up water and gets bigger. This makes the chemical processes in the seed active again.
18011.m: Germination begins with the seed swelling up with water.

18012.q: Which part of the seedling usually comes out of the seed coat first?
18012.e: First the root breaks through the seed coat. This lets the seedling anchor itself early and take in water.
18012.m: During germination the root usually comes out first.

18013.q: What does a bean seedling live on before it has green leaves?
a: The nutrients in its seed leaves
18013.e: The thick seed leaves of the bean contain starch and protein as a store. The seedling lives on this until it can carry out photosynthesis itself.
18013.m: Seed leaves supply the young seedling with nutrients.

18014.q: How many seed leaves do grasses like maize or wheat have?
18014.e: Grasses are monocots. Beans and peas, on the other hand, are dicots.
18014.m: Grasses like maize and wheat have only one seed leaf.

18015.q: How does the strawberry reproduce asexually?
18015.e: The strawberry forms runners above ground that put down roots at their ends. This creates new plants with the same genes.

18016.q: Which part of the flower develops into the fruit after fertilisation?
18016.e: After fertilisation the ovary grows into the fruit. The ovules inside it become seeds.
18016.m: The fruit develops from the ovary.

18017.q: Which invention did the burrs of the burdock inspire?
18017.e: The Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed that burrs with tiny hooks got caught in his dog’s fur. From this he developed Velcro.
18017.m: Burdock spreads its fruits with little hooks in animals’ fur.

a: By the wind, spinning as they fly
18018.e: The winged maple fruits spin like a propeller as they fall. This lets the wind carry them further from the parent tree.
18018.m: Maple fruits fly through the air like little propellers.

18019.q: What is the most important difference between sexual and asexual reproduction in plants?
a: Only in sexual reproduction are genes mixed
Only sexual reproduction works without seeds
18019.e: In sexual reproduction sex cells fuse and the genes of two parents are mixed. Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring.
18019.m: Sexual reproduction mixes genes; asexual reproduction produces clones.

18020.q: What is the cell wall of a plant cell mainly made of?
18020.e: The cell wall is mainly made of cellulose, a long sugar molecule. It gives the cell strength and shape.
18020.m: The plant cell wall is mainly made of cellulose.

18021.q: Which cell part do plant cells have, but animal cells do not?
18021.e: Only plant cells have chloroplasts, a cell wall and usually a large vacuole. The nucleus, membrane and mitochondria are found in both cell types.
18021.m: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, not in animal cells.

18022.q: What job does the large vacuole do in a plant cell?
a: It stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm
18022.e: The vacuole is filled with cell sap and presses the cell contents against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called turgor and keeps plants upright.
18022.m: The vacuole keeps the plant cell firm with its cell sap.

18023.q: Which scientist was the first to describe “cells”, in 1665, when he looked at cork under a microscope?
18023.e: Robert Hooke saw small chambers in cork and called them “cells”. He published this in 1665 in his book “Micrographia”.
18023.m: Robert Hooke coined the term cell while looking at cork.

18024.q: What happens to a plant cell placed in strong salt water?
a: It takes in water and bursts
It does not change at all
18024.e: The salt water draws water out of the vacuole, and the cell contents pull away from the cell wall. This process is called plasmolysis.
18024.m: In salt water a plant cell loses water.

18025.q: Which broadleaf tree is the most common in Swiss forests?
18025.e: The common beech is the most common broadleaf tree in Switzerland and shapes many forests in the Central Plateau and the Jura. Its fruits are called beechnuts.
18025.m: The beech is the most common broadleaf tree in Switzerland.

18026.q: Why do broadleaf trees drop their leaves in autumn?
a: So that they do not dry out in winter
Because the leaves get too heavy
Because they need more light in winter
18026.e: When the ground is frozen, the tree can hardly take in water. But it would keep losing water through its large leaves and dry out.
18026.m: Broadleaf trees drop their leaves to save water in winter.

18027.q: Why do many leaves turn yellow in autumn?
a: Chlorophyll is broken down and yellow pigments become visible
The leaves absorb the colour of the sun
The rain washes out the green
18027.e: The tree breaks down the valuable chlorophyll and takes back its building blocks. The yellow carotenoids were already in the leaf and now become visible.
18027.m: In autumn the green disappears and the yellow pigments show through.

18028.q: Why do early-flowering plants like the wood anemone flower so early in the year in broadleaf woods?
a: Before the trees come into leaf, lots of light reaches the ground
There are no insects in spring
The ground is too wet in summer
18028.e: While the trees are still bare, lots of light falls on the forest floor. The early-flowering plants use this time before the canopy shades the ground.
18028.m: Early-flowering plants use the light before the canopy closes.

18029.q: Which tree species is the most common overall in Swiss forests?
18029.e: According to the National Forest Inventory, the spruce is the most common tree species in Swiss forests. It used to be planted a lot because it grows quickly.
18029.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.

18030.q: How do the cones of the silver fir and the spruce differ?
a: Fir cones stand upright, spruce cones hang down
Fir cones hang down, spruce cones stand upright
18030.e: Silver fir cones stand upright and fall apart on the tree. So the hanging cones you find on the forest floor almost always come from spruces.
18030.m: Whole cones lying on the ground usually come from the spruce.

18031.q: Which native conifer loses its needles in autumn?
18031.e: In autumn the larch turns its needles golden yellow and sheds them. This helps it survive the harsh mountain winters better.
18031.m: The larch is the conifer that is bare in winter.

18032.q: How many needles grow together in a bunch on the Swiss stone pine?
18032.e: The Swiss stone pine carries its needles in bunches of five, whereas the Scots pine has them in pairs. Swiss stone pines grow in the Alps up to near the tree line.
18032.m: The Swiss stone pine carries its needles in bunches of five.

18033.q: What is the huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of Russia, Scandinavia and Canada called?
18033.e: The taiga is the largest forest area on Earth and consists mainly of conifers. It lies in the cold north.
18033.m: The taiga is the great belt of coniferous forest in the north.

18034.q: Why can conifers keep their needles in winter too?
a: A waxy layer protects against water loss
18034.e: Needles are narrow and covered with a thick layer of wax. As a result they lose very little water in winter.
18034.m: The waxy layer protects the needles from drying out.

a: A forest of broadleaf and coniferous trees
A forest of young trees only
18035.e: In a mixed forest broadleaf and coniferous trees grow side by side. It provides a habitat for many different animals and plants.
18035.m: In a mixed forest broadleaf and coniferous trees grow together.

18036.q: In the layers of a forest, which layer lies directly above the moss layer?
18036.e: From bottom to top come the moss layer, herb layer, shrub layer and tree layer. Each storey has its own inhabitants.
18036.m: A forest is divided into several layers from the ground up to the treetops.

18037.q: Why are mixed forests considered more resilient than pure spruce forests?
a: Pests and storms do not affect all the trees in the same way
They grow faster than all other forests
18037.e: A pest such as the bark beetle mainly attacks certain tree species. In a mixed forest other species are spared, and deep-rooted trees withstand storms better.
18037.m: Variety makes a forest more resilient.

18038.q: Which hurricane-force storm caused very great damage in Swiss forests on 26 December 1999?
18038.e: Storm Lothar blew down millions of trees in Switzerland on St Stephen’s Day 1999. Afterwards, mixed forests suited to their location were promoted more.
18038.m: Storm Lothar destroyed large areas of forest in Switzerland in 1999.

18039.q: In the Emmental there are forests where only single trees are ever cut down. What does such a forest look like?
a: Young and old trees stand side by side
All the trees are the same age
18039.e: Because only single trees are harvested, young trees keep growing in the gaps. Such a forest is called a selection forest.
18039.m: In a selection forest young and old trees grow side by side.

18040.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland’s area is covered by forest?
18040.e: According to the 2025 Forest Report, forest covers about 32 per cent of Switzerland’s land area. The share is especially high on the south side of the Alps and in the Jura.
18040.m: About a third of Switzerland is forested.

18041.q: What is the most important job of a protection forest in the mountains?
18041.e: Protection forests hold back snow, stones and soil. In this way they protect villages, roads and railway lines in the mountains.
18041.m: Protection forests guard mountain villages against avalanches and rockfall.

18042.q: In Switzerland, what must in principle happen if forest may exceptionally be cleared for a building project?
a: Replacement forest must be created in the same area
Only a small fee has to be paid
The wood must be sold abroad
Nothing at all has to happen
18042.e: The Forest Act generally bans clearing forest. If an exception is granted, a replacement must be provided in the same area, usually by planting new forest.
18042.m: Anyone who clears forest in Switzerland must in principle replace it.

18043.q: Which field does the idea of “sustainability” originally come from?
18043.e: In 1713 Hans Carl von Carlowitz called for only as much wood to be cut as can grow back. This gave rise to the principle of sustainability.
18043.m: Sustainable means not using more than can grow back.

18044.q: In Switzerland, are you generally allowed to enter any forest, even if it belongs to a private person?
a: Yes, the Civil Code allows it
Only forest owners may go in
18044.e: The Swiss Civil Code allows everyone access to forest and pasture to the extent customary in the area. You must respect nature and property.
18044.m: In Switzerland forests are open to everyone.

18045.q: What does a typical food chain on land begin with?
18045.e: Green plants make their own food using sunlight. They are called producers and stand at the start of the food chain.
18045.m: Every food chain starts with the producers.

18046.q: In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, stork: which animal is the secondary consumer?
18046.e: The grasshopper eats the grass and is the primary consumer. The frog eats the grasshopper and is therefore the secondary consumer.

18047.q: Plants in a meadow store 10,000 kilojoules of energy. Roughly how much of it reaches the secondary consumers if only 10 per cent is passed on at each level?
18047.e: Of the 10,000 kJ, 10 per cent reaches the plant-eaters, so 1,000 kJ. Of that, 10 per cent again reaches the secondary consumers, so 100 kJ.
18047.m: At each level of the food chain most of the energy is lost.

18048.q: What are living things that break down dead animals and plants called?
18048.e: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead material. This closes the cycle of materials.
18048.m: Decomposers break down dead material and close the nutrient cycle.

18049.q: What do you call several food chains linked together?
18049.e: Most animals eat different foods and are eaten by different animals. That is why the chains join up into a web.
18049.m: In nature food chains are linked into a web.

18050.q: How does a raised bog get its water?
18050.e: Raised bogs are cut off from the groundwater and get only rainwater. That is why they are very poor in nutrients.
18050.m: Raised bogs are fed only by rain and are poor in nutrients.

18051.q: Since a popular vote in 1987, what does the Swiss Federal Constitution especially protect?
18051.e: The trigger was a planned army training ground in the moorland of Rothenthurm. Since the initiative was accepted, beautiful moors have been protected in the Constitution.
18051.m: Switzerland’s moors have been protected by the Constitution since 1987.

18052.q: What is the altitude zone in the Alps above the tree line, with alpine pastures and dwarf shrubs, called?
18052.e: Above the subalpine zone comes the alpine zone, without closed forest. Higher still is the nival zone with snow and ice.
18052.m: The alpine zone begins above the tree line.

18053.q: How is the cactus adapted to its dry habitat?
a: It stores water in its thick stem
It loses especially large amounts of water
18053.e: Cacti store water in their fleshy stems. Their leaves have turned into spines, so little water evaporates.
18053.m: Cacti store water and have spines instead of leaves.

18054.q: Why are hedges between fields important habitats?
a: They give animals food, nesting sites and hiding places
They keep all animals off the field
They only serve as a fence
18054.e: Birds, hedgehogs, insects and weasels find shelter and food in hedges. They also connect other habitats with each other.
18054.m: Hedges are valuable habitats in farmland.

18055.q: What is the underground network of threads of a fungus called?
18055.e: The actual fungus lives as a fine network of fungal threads in the soil or in wood. What we gather is only the fruiting body.
18055.m: Most of a fungus is the invisible mycelium in the soil.

18056.q: Which mushroom is responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings in Europe?
18056.e: The death cap contains poisons that destroy the liver. Even a single mushroom can be fatal for a person.
18056.m: The death cap is the most dangerous poisonous mushroom in Europe.

a: A partnership between fungi and plant roots
A kind of fungus on bread
A poison of the fly agaric
18057.e: Fungal threads wrap around the roots of trees and help them take in water and minerals. In return the fungus receives sugar from the tree.
18057.m: In mycorrhiza, fungus and tree help each other.

18058.q: From which fungus did Alexander Fleming discover the first antibiotic in 1928?
18058.e: Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria in his dish. Penicillin was obtained from it.

18059.q: Why does bread dough with yeast rise?
a: The yeast melts in the oven
18059.e: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that breaks down sugar. This produces gas bubbles of carbon dioxide that make the dough light.
18059.m: Yeast makes dough rise with gas bubbles.

18060.q: Where in Switzerland can you have mushrooms you have gathered yourself checked by experts?
a: At an official mushroom inspection office
18060.e: Many municipalities and regions offer official mushroom inspection offices. Experts there check whether the mushrooms are edible.
18060.m: Always have mushrooms you have gathered checked at a mushroom inspection office.

18061.q: What do mosses use to hold on to the ground?
18061.e: Mosses have no real roots, but fine anchoring threads called rhizoids. They take in water mainly over their whole surface.
18061.m: Mosses have no real roots, but rhizoids.

18062.e: Mosses form spores in small capsules on stalks. These are spread by the wind.
18062.m: Mosses reproduce with spores instead of seeds.

18063.q: Which moss forms the peat in raised bogs over thousands of years?
18063.e: Peat mosses keep growing at the top while the lower parts die off. In the wet, acidic bog they hardly break down and turn into peat.
18063.m: Peat mosses slowly build up the peat layers of raised bogs.

18064.q: Why are cushions of moss in the forest important for the water balance?
a: They store many times their own weight in water
They let water run off immediately
They use up all the groundwater
18064.e: Mosses soak up rainwater like a sponge and release it slowly. In this way they protect against drying out and flooding.
18064.m: Mosses store water like a sponge.

18065.q: Why do mosses need water for fertilisation?
a: The male sex cells swim to the egg cell
The spores only germinate under water
The flowers only open in the rain
Insects only fly in the rain
18065.e: The male sex cells of mosses move with flagella. They need a film of water, for example after rain or dew, to reach the egg cell.
18065.m: Mosses need a film of water for fertilisation.

18066.q: Where do ferns form their spores?
a: In clusters on the underside of the leaves
18066.e: On the underside of fern fronds there are brown clusters of spores called sori. The spores are released from them.
18066.m: Ferns carry their spores on the underside of their fronds.

18067.q: What do ferns have that mosses do not?
18067.e: Ferns have vessels for water and nutrients as well as real roots. That is why they can grow much bigger than mosses.
18067.m: Unlike mosses, ferns have vascular bundles.

18068.q: From which plants did large parts of coal form around 300 million years ago?
a: From fern plants as tall as trees
18068.e: In the Carboniferous period, giant club mosses, horsetails and tree ferns grew in swamp forests. Over a long time their remains turned into coal.
18068.m: Coal is made of the remains of prehistoric swamp forests.

18069.q: How do young fern fronds unfold in spring?
a: They unroll like a snail shell
They open out like a fan
They burst out of a tuber
They grow out of a flower
18069.e: Young fern fronds are rolled up in a spiral and look like a bishop’s crook. As they grow, they slowly unroll.
18069.m: Young fern fronds unroll from a spiral.

18070.q: In ferns, what forms first when a spore germinates?
18070.e: A tiny, heart-shaped little leaf, the prothallus, grows from the spore. Only after fertilisation on it does a new fern grow.
18070.m: A small prothallus grows first from a fern spore.

18071.q: From the bark of which tree was a remedy for fever and pain once obtained that became the model for aspirin?
18071.e: Willow bark contains salicin, which the body turns into salicylic acid. Acetylsalicylic acid was later developed from this.
18071.m: Willow bark was the model for a well-known painkiller.

18072.q: Which medicinal plant is often used as a tea for inflammation and stomach complaints?
18072.e: Chamomile flowers reduce inflammation and have a calming effect. Chamomile tea is one of the best-known home remedies.
18072.m: Chamomile tea is a trusted home remedy for inflammation.

18073.q: Which mountain plant is used on the skin for bruises?
18073.e: Arnica grows in mountain meadows and is applied to the skin as an ointment or gel. It should not be taken by mouth.
18073.m: Arnica helps with bruises when used on the skin.

18074.q: Which substance gives peppermint its cooling taste?
18074.e: Menthol stimulates the cold receptors and therefore feels cool. Peppermint tea is often drunk for digestive problems.
18074.m: Menthol gives peppermint its cool feeling.

18075.q: Which meadow plant with narrow leaves is traditionally used as a cough remedy?
18075.e: Ribwort plantain contains mucilage that soothes irritated airways. It is often sold as cough syrup.
18075.m: Ribwort plantain is an old home remedy for coughs.

18076.q: Which plant is considered the most poisonous plant in Europe?
18076.e: Monkshood contains the poison aconitine. It can even be absorbed through the skin.
18076.m: Monkshood is the most poisonous plant in Europe.

18077.q: Which poisonous plant is often mistaken for edible wild garlic?
18077.e: The leaves of lily of the valley and wild garlic look very similar. Only wild garlic smells clearly of garlic when you rub it.
18077.m: You can recognise wild garlic by the garlic smell of its leaves.

18078.q: Which telephone number do you call in Switzerland in case of poisoning?
18078.e: On 145 you can reach Tox Info Suisse around the clock. Experts there give advice on poisoning by plants, mushrooms and chemicals.
18078.m: In Switzerland the number 145 helps in cases of poisoning.

18079.q: Which part of the yew is NOT poisonous?
a: The red flesh around the seed
18079.e: Almost all parts of the yew contain poisonous taxines. Only the red, fleshy covering around the seed is harmless, but the seed inside is highly poisonous.
18079.m: Almost everything about the yew is poisonous.

18080.q: What does the famous saying “The dose makes the poison” mean?
a: Whether a substance is harmful depends on the amount
18080.e: The physician Paracelsus realised that almost any substance is harmful in large amounts. That is why poisonous plants can also be remedies in small amounts.
18080.m: Whether a substance is poisonous depends on the amount.

18081.q: Where does the potato originally come from?
18081.e: The potato was grown in the Andes thousands of years ago. Spanish seafarers brought it to Europe in the 16th century.
18081.m: The potato comes from the Andes in South America.

18082.q: Which cereal is harvested in the greatest quantity worldwide today?
18082.e: Maize is grown for food, animal feed and fuel. According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), its worldwide harvest in 2023 was again larger than that of wheat or rice.
18082.m: Maize is the most harvested cereal in the world by quantity.

18083.q: Which plant is sugar mainly made from in Switzerland?
18083.e: In Switzerland the sugar factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld process sugar beet. Sugar cane only grows in warm countries.
18083.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

18084.q: Which crop makes whole fields bloom bright yellow in spring and provides cooking oil?
18084.e: Rapeseed flowers yellow in April and May. Rapeseed oil is pressed from its small seeds.
18084.m: Cooking oil is made from rapeseed.

18085.q: Which part of the cotton plant is made into fabric?
18085.e: Cotton seeds are surrounded by long white hairs. These fibres are spun into yarn.
18085.m: Cotton fibres are the hairs on the plant’s seeds.

18086.q: Why do farmers change the crops they grow on a field from year to year?
a: To protect the soil and reduce pests
Because the seed would otherwise go bad
18086.e: With crop rotation, different plants take different nutrients from the soil. Pests and diseases also cannot spread as much.
18086.m: Crop rotation keeps the soil healthy.

18087.q: Why are legumes like clover or peas often grown as green manure?
a: Their root nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air
They loosen the soil with prickles
They contain a lot of sugar
18087.e: Bacteria living in nodules on the roots fix nitrogen from the air. This enriches the soil with nitrogen.
18087.m: Legumes enrich the soil with nitrogen.

18088.q: In Switzerland, what is the time called when cows spend the summer on the alpine pastures?
18088.e: In early summer the animals are driven up to the alp and brought back down to the valley in autumn. This makes use of the grass on the mountain pastures.
18088.m: In summer many cows graze on the alps.

18089.q: Which use makes up the largest part of Switzerland’s farmland?
18089.e: Because of the climate and the many hills and mountains, most of it is used as grassland. That is why milk and meat production play a big role.
18089.m: In Switzerland meadows and pastures dominate.

18090.q: What is banned in organic farming?
a: Hedges at the edge of fields
18090.e: Organic farms do without synthetic chemical pesticides and artificial fertiliser. They rely on crop rotation, beneficial insects and farmyard manure.
18090.m: Organic farmers do without synthetic chemical sprays.

18091.q: What was the farming system called in the Middle Ages in which a field lay fallow every third year?
18091.e: One field grew winter cereals, one summer cereals and one lay fallow. This let the soil recover.
18091.m: In the three-field system each field lay fallow every third year.

18092.q: Which gaseous plant hormone promotes the ripening of fruits such as apples and bananas?
18092.e: Ethylene is a simple gaseous plant hormone that triggers fruit ripening, leaf fall and ageing. Ripe apples release ethylene and so speed up the ripening of nearby fruit.
18092.m: The gas ethylene makes fruit ripen.

18093.q: Which plant hormone causes the stomata to close during drought stress?
18093.e: When water is scarce, the level of abscisic acid in the leaves rises. It makes the guard cells lose ions and water, so the stomata close and the plant loses less water through evaporation.
18093.m: Abscisic acid is the stress hormone that closes the stomata in dry conditions.

18094.q: Which enzyme fixes carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate in the Calvin cycle?
18094.e: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, Rubisco for short, binds CO2 to a C5 sugar. It is thought to be the most abundant protein on Earth.
18094.m: Rubisco builds CO2 into organic molecules in the Calvin cycle.

18095.q: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place in plant cells?
a: In the stroma of the chloroplasts
18095.e: The photosystems and the electron transport chain sit in the thylakoid membrane. ATP, NADPH and oxygen are produced there; the light-independent reactions then take place in the stroma.
18095.m: The light reactions happen at the thylakoids of the chloroplasts.

18096.q: Which mechanism is the main driving force for water transport in the xylem of tall trees?
18096.e: Evaporation from the leaves creates negative pressure that pulls the continuous column of water upwards thanks to cohesion. Root pressure alone is only enough for a few metres.
18096.m: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water up the tree.

18097.q: In which form are carbohydrates mainly transported in the phloem?
18097.e: Sucrose is a highly soluble and unreactive disaccharide. It is transported from the leaves (sources) to roots, fruits and buds (sinks).
18097.m: In the phloem, sugar mostly travels as sucrose.

18098.q: Which plants take in CO2 mainly at night and store it as malic acid to save water during the day?
18098.e: CAM plants, such as many cacti and stonecrops, open their stomata at night, separating CO2 uptake and the Calvin cycle in time. This way they lose much less water in hot regions.
18098.m: CAM plants separate CO2 uptake and sugar production in time.
